A.q: An 84-year-old woman spent 9 days in the hospital for a large pericardial effusion that needed two procedures. She is now weak and needs help to walk. Besides cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery, which service is most appropriate before she goes home?
opts: Correct. Rehabilitation is listed alongside cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery in the care of older adults with pericardial disease. At 84, weak and needing help to walk after 9 days and two procedures, she fits that need, and older adults also carry higher morbidity and mortality with surgical interventions.

Nothing in her story points to an infection, and the problem to solve before discharge is her weakness and need for help walking. Rehabilitation is the service listed for older adults with pericardial disease, alongside cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery. Tell: pick the service that matches the problem in front of you.

Genetic evaluation is not part of the care of older adults with pericardial disease. The services listed for this group are rehabilitation and cardiology or cardiothoracic surgery, and her new weakness and need for help walking point to rehabilitation. Tell: her problem is function, so choose the service that restores function.

Nothing suggests kidney disease, and her pressing problem is deconditioning: she is weak and needs help to walk after a 9-day stay and two procedures. Rehabilitation is among the services listed for older adults with pericardial disease. Tell: loss of function after a long, procedure-heavy stay calls for rehabilitation.

A.q: Which surgery treats aortic dissection?
opts: Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection seals the leak of a pseudoaneurysm by promoting clot. Surgery for aortic dissection grafts and replaces the diseased portion of the aorta. Thrombin treats a small cavity outside a vessel, not a torn aortic wall.

Correct. Surgery for aortic dissection grafts and replaces the diseased portion of the aorta. It follows measures to stop progression, reducing systolic pressure to 100 to 120 mmHg with esmolol or nitroprusside, and pain management, because acute untreated dissection has a high mortality rate.

Catheter-directed thrombolysis dissolves clot in acute limb ischemia of less than 14 days. A dissection is a tear in the aortic wall, not a clot, and its surgery grafts and replaces the diseased aorta. Lysis has no role here.

Carotid endarterectomy removes plaque from inside the carotid artery and is the gold standard for high-grade carotid stenosis. Dissection surgery replaces the diseased portion of the aorta with a graft. Different vessel, different lesion.

A.q: A 52-year-old man on telemetry has a prolonged QT after starting a new medication and then develops polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (QRS complexes that vary in shape and twist around the baseline). He becomes unresponsive and pulseless. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion needs a consistent QRS to time against and is used in a patient with a pulse. A pulseless polymorphic rhythm is defibrillated (unsynchronized). Tell: no pulse and a changing QRS both point to an unsynchronized shock.
ruled out by a stated finding

Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades in a conscious patient. This man is unresponsive and pulseless, and a hemodynamically unstable patient with torsades is defibrillated. Tell: 'conscious' is the word that puts magnesium first.

Transcutaneous pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms, not a fast polymorphic one. A pulseless patient in polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated. Tell: an unresponsive, pulseless patient with a fast rhythm needs a shock.

Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a prolonged QT is torsades de pointes, and a hemodynamically unstable patient, here unresponsive and pulseless, is treated with defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion). Magnesium is the drug for torsades in a conscious patient; once he is pulseless, the shock comes first.

A.q: A 61-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes describes a continuous burning sensation in both feet that is the same at rest and during exercise. Her pedal pulses are easily palpable. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Peripheral neuropathy, common in elderly patients with diabetes or alcoholism, causes a continuous burning sensation in the foot that is unaffected by exercise. Her long-standing diabetes, burning that is the same at rest and with exercise, and easily palpable pulses all fit.

Ischemic rest pain is worse with elevation and relieved by dangling the leg, and pulses are diminished below the stenosis. Her pulses are easily palpable and her burning does not change with activity. Normal pulses argue against ischemia.

Spinal stenosis gives claudication-like pain with walking, with numbness and weakness, relieved by sitting down or leaning forward. Her burning is constant and unaffected by exercise. Pain that never changes with walking is not stenosis.

Arterial claudication is activity-related pain relieved by rest, with diminished pulses below the lesion. Her burning is the same at rest and with exercise, and her pulses are easily palpable. Those two features point to neuropathy instead.

A.q: A 60-year-old man has a 12-second run of identical wide QRS complexes at 160 per minute on telemetry. He stays alert, with a normal blood pressure, and feels only a flutter. How should this run be classified?
opts: Non-sustained is right, since his run lasted 12 seconds without collapse, but polymorphic is not: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia has QRS complexes that vary in shape, and his were identical. Tell: identical complexes mean monomorphic.
ruled out by a stated finding

Monomorphic is right, but sustained is not: sustained means 30 seconds or more, or hemodynamic collapse in under 30 seconds. His run lasted 12 seconds and he stayed alert with a normal blood pressure. Tell: under 30 seconds without collapse is non-sustained.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Three or more consecutive premature ventricular beats make ventricular tachycardia. His run lasted 12 seconds, under 30, and caused no hemodynamic collapse, so it is non-sustained, and identical complexes make it monomorphic.

Both labels are wrong: his 12-second run caused no collapse, so it is non-sustained, and his identical complexes make it monomorphic, not polymorphic. Tell: check duration and collapse for sustained; check whether QRS shapes match for monomorphic.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.q: A 60-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy has orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat), crackles at both lung bases and diminished breath sounds at the right base. A chest radiograph is ordered. Which finding on the film would indicate pulmonary edema?
opts: A normal film that excludes congestion

A normal film would not fit his crackles and diminished breath sounds; the radiograph in dilated cardiomyopathy shows cardiomegaly, pleural effusions and pulmonary edema, sometimes as Kerley B lines. Tell: the question asks for a sign of edema, and a normal film offers none.
Short horizontal lines meeting the pleura

Correct. His orthopnea and basal crackles suggest pulmonary edema, and on the chest radiograph Kerley B lines, horizontal lines 1 to 2 cm long meeting the pleura at right angles, indicate it. The diminished breath sounds at his right base fit the pleural effusion and cardiomegaly that dilated cardiomyopathy also shows.
A small heart with clear lung fields

A small heart with clear lungs is the opposite of the expected film: dilated cardiomyopathy shows cardiomegaly, pleural effusions and pulmonary edema. Tell: with crackles and diminished breath sounds at the right base, expect a large heart and fluid on the film.

Pericardial thickening is not a chest radiograph sign of pulmonary edema and is not among the dilated cardiomyopathy film findings. Pulmonary edema shows as Kerley B lines, short horizontal lines meeting the pleura at right angles. Tell: edema is in the lungs, so its sign is in the lung fields.

A.q: Which electrocardiogram changes occur in Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Left bundle branch block is not the Takotsubo change. The electrocardiogram shows ST segment elevation and T wave inversion, which is why the syndrome mimics acute coronary syndrome. Tell: Takotsubo looks like an acute coronary event on the tracing.
Low QRS voltage in all leads

Low QRS voltage is not described in Takotsubo. Its electrocardiogram shows ST segment elevation and T wave inversion, matching its resemblance to acute coronary syndrome. Tell: think of the changes an acute coronary event produces.
ST elevation and T wave inversion

Correct. The electrocardiogram in Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy shows ST segment elevation and T wave inversion. Together with elevated troponin and apical wall-motion abnormalities, this mimics acute coronary syndrome, so its protocols are followed until catheterization shows normal coronary arteries.

Inferior and lateral Q waves are not the Takotsubo pattern. The tracing shows ST segment elevation with T wave inversion, along with elevated troponin and mid and apical wall-motion abnormalities on transthoracic echo. Tell: ST elevation is what makes it mimic acute coronary syndrome.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. A.q: A 72-year-old woman has sudden chest pain and diaphoresis an hour after learning she has lost her savings in a financial collapse. The electrocardiogram shows ST elevation and troponin is elevated. No catheterization has been done yet. Which is the most appropriate initial approach?
opts: An emotional trigger does not exclude acute coronary syndrome, and there are no reliable early features to tell the two apart. With ST elevation and raised troponin, she follows acute coronary syndrome protocols and is admitted to cardiology. Tell: a trigger is not a diagnosis; catheterization is still needed.

Correct. Her chest pain after losing her savings, with ST elevation and elevated troponin, may be stress cardiomyopathy, but it mimics acute coronary syndrome with no initial reliable differences. Evaluation and treatment therefore follow established acute coronary syndrome protocols, with admission to cardiology, until catheterization settles the diagnosis.

A positive inotrope is not part of the Takotsubo approach; treatment is empiric and supportive, with beta blockers helpful and diuretics only if heart failure is present. Initially she follows acute coronary syndrome protocols. Tell: start with the coronary pathway, not a drug to push contraction.

Alcohol septal ablation has no role in a woman with chest pain, ST elevation and raised troponin after a stressor. She is managed on acute coronary syndrome protocols and admitted to cardiology. Tell: the first job is to treat this as a possible coronary event.

A.q: A 66-year-old man with stable cardiomyopathy on full medical therapy says he tires after walking a block and feels anxious about exercising. He has no symptoms at rest. Which referral is most appropriate to improve his exercise tolerance?
opts: Hospice referral is for end-stage cardiomyopathy. He is stable on full therapy with no symptoms at rest, so the referral that fits is cardiac rehabilitation, which aims to improve exercise tolerance and quality of life. Tell: stable disease with a function goal points to rehabilitation, not end-of-life care.

Competitive sport is not a goal for a man who tires after walking a block, and clearance would not build his tolerance. The referral that improves exercise tolerance and quality of life is a cardiac rehabilitation program. Tell: his anxiety also fits rehabilitation, which includes psychological support.

Screening his children does nothing for his own exercise tolerance, which is the stated goal. Cardiac rehabilitation programs aim to improve exercise tolerance and quality of life, with education and psychological support. Tell: the question asks about him and his exercise, which rehabilitation addresses.

Correct. His problems are limited exercise tolerance and anxiety about exercising, and cardiac rehabilitation programs aim to improve exercise tolerance and quality of life. Rehabilitative care also provides education on medication adherence, nutrition and symptom monitoring, and psychological support for coping with chronic illness.

A.q: Which is the first treatment for torsades de pointes in a conscious patient?
opts: Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades de pointes for the same reason as amiodarone. The first treatment in a conscious patient is intravenous magnesium. Tell: any drug that lengthens the QT feeds torsades rather than stopping it.

Amiodarone prolongs the QT, so it is avoided in torsades de pointes, the polymorphic tachycardia of a prolonged QT. It may be added in polymorphic tachycardia without a long QT. Tell: in torsades, the first drug is intravenous magnesium.

Metoprolol is avoided in torsades de pointes: beta blockers cause bradycardia and lengthen the R-to-R interval, which indirectly prolongs the QT. The first treatment is intravenous magnesium. Tell: slowing the heart is harmful when the QT is already long.

Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium is given to break torsades de pointes, then more magnesium as an infusion. Amiodarone, procainamide and beta blockers are avoided because they prolong the QT; if the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable, defibrillation replaces drug therapy.

A.q: What is the most frequent presumed cause of myocarditis in developed countries?
opts: Correct. In developed countries, viral infection is presumed to be the most frequent cause of myocarditis, and viral myocarditis accounts for 20% of dilated cardiomyopathy cases. Named viruses include parvovirus B19, human herpesvirus 6, Coxsackie group B enteroviruses, adenoviruses, hepatitis C virus, cytomegalovirus and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

Autoimmune disease is not the presumed leading cause; in developed countries viral infection is presumed most frequent. The infectious list itself is long, from viruses to rheumatic fever, bacteria, parasites, rickettsia, spirochetes and Candida. Tell: the presumed number one cause is viral.

Drug reactions are not presumed to be the most frequent cause. In developed countries viral infection is, including parvovirus B19, enteroviruses and adenoviruses. Tell: when the question asks for the most frequent cause in developed countries, answer viral.

Bacteria such as diphtheria, brucellosis, meningococcus and Mycoplasma can cause myocarditis, but viral infection is presumed to be the most frequent cause in developed countries. Tell: bacteria are on the list; viruses top it.

A.q: A 78-year-old man with recurrent urinary tract infections has aortic valve endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Nafcillin plus rifampin belongs to staphylococcal prosthetic valve therapy (with gentamicin) for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. His cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis. Tell: an enterococcus calls for ampicillin or penicillin G with gentamicin, not antistaphylococcal drugs.

Cefazolin is an option for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus on native valves, not an enterococcal regimen. Tell: enterococcal regimens pair ampicillin, penicillin G or vancomycin with gentamicin, or ampicillin with ceftriaxone; cefazolin appears only under staphylococci.

A single oral dose cannot treat established endocarditis. Every enterococcal regimen is intravenous combination therapy given for 4-6 weeks or longer, such as ampicillin plus gentamicin. Tell: one oral dose is prevention-style dosing, not treatment.

Correct. His cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis, and enterococcal endocarditis is treated with ampicillin plus gentamicin, both for 4-6 weeks. Listed alternatives are penicillin G plus gentamicin, vancomycin plus gentamicin, or ampicillin plus ceftriaxone, each an intravenous combination.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: Erythema extending well beyond the margin of an inflamed vein raises suspicion of which condition?
opts: Correct. Erythema that extends significantly beyond the margin of the vein should raise suspicion of septic thrombophlebitis, an infection within the vein. High fever, fluctuance and purulent drainage point the same way, and septic thrombophlebitis is uncommon without a history of venous cannulation.

Superficial phlebitis brings tenderness, pain, induration and erythema along the course of the vein. Redness spreading well beyond the vein's margin goes past that pattern and suggests septic thrombophlebitis, an infection within the vein.

Lipodermatosclerosis is not among the findings of an inflamed superficial vein. Those findings are tenderness, induration and erythema along the vein, and erythema extending well beyond its margin points to septic thrombophlebitis.

Stasis dermatitis is not a sign of an inflamed superficial vein, whose findings are a tender, indurated palpable cord with erythema and warmth of the overlying skin. When that erythema extends significantly beyond the vein's margin, septic thrombophlebitis should be suspected.

A.q: What must follow chest or back pain in a patient with a known thoracic aortic aneurysm?
opts: Correct. Chest or back pain in a patient with a known or suspected thoracic aortic aneurysm must undergo urgent imaging studies to rule out the aneurysm as the cause of the pain. If the aneurysm is responsible, it is symptomatic, and repair is recommended for all symptomatic thoracic aortic aneurysms.

Routine surveillance is for asymptomatic aneurysms, every 3 to 5 years under 4.5 cm or every 6 to 12 months at 4.5 to 5.4 cm. Pain changes the urgency: it requires urgent imaging to rule out the aneurysm as the cause. A scheduled scan is too slow.

Pain in a patient with a thoracic aortic aneurysm cannot be treated as benign. Urgent imaging must rule out the aneurysm as its cause, because every symptomatic thoracic aneurysm should be repaired. Analgesia without imaging can miss that.

A stress test is not the step named, and it does not image the aneurysm. Chest or back pain with a known thoracic aneurysm requires urgent imaging to rule out the aneurysm as the cause. The question is about the aorta, not about exercise tolerance.

A.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
A.q: A 49-year-old man has 3 weeks of fever and night sweats. Two separate blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus, and a transesophageal echocardiogram shows an oscillating mass on the aortic valve. He has no skin, eye or kidney findings. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Possible is one major plus one minor criterion, or three minor criteria. He already has two major criteria, positive blood cultures and echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement, which goes beyond possible. Tell: two major criteria alone make the diagnosis definite.

No further test is needed to classify him. Two major criteria, positive blood cultures and an oscillating mass on transesophageal echocardiogram, already meet the threshold for definite endocarditis. Tell: absent skin, eye or kidney findings do not matter once two major criteria are met.

Two separate cultures growing Streptococcus gallolyticus and an oscillating valve mass are evidence for endocarditis, not against it; together they are two major criteria. Tell: transesophageal echocardiography is highly sensitive and specific, and here it detects a vegetation that confirms endocardial involvement.

Correct. He meets both major criteria: positive blood cultures (Streptococcus gallolyticus in two separate sets) and echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement (an oscillating mass on the aortic valve). Two major criteria establish definite endocarditis, so the absent minor findings do not matter.

A.q: A 19-year-old swimmer has an electrocardiogram before a sports physical. She has no symptoms. The rate is 72, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS, but the beats come closer together as she breathes in and spread apart as she breathes out. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A rate of 72 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS, beats closer together on inspiration and farther apart on expiration, is sinus arrhythmia. It is a normal, physiologic rhythm at 60 to 100 that is irregular with a pattern, which fits a healthy swimmer with no symptoms.

Sick sinus syndrome is an irregular rhythm with variable P waves, from sinus exit block, sinus arrest or tachy-brady swings with pauses. She has a uniform P wave before every beat and a variation tied to breathing, with no pauses. Tell: a breathing-linked pattern is physiologic; pauses and fast-slow swings suggest a diseased node.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves. She has a normal P wave before every QRS, and her irregularity follows her breathing. Tell: patterned irregularity with P waves is sinus arrhythmia; patternless irregularity without P waves is fibrillation.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm, over 100, with at least three different P-wave shapes in one lead, usually in acutely ill patients. She has one normal P-wave shape at 72. Tell: multifocal needs both tachycardia and changing P waves, and she has neither.

A.q: A 29-year-old woman has superficial thrombophlebitis of the forearm after an intravenous catheter and asks whether the clot can travel to her lungs. Which statement about her outlook is accurate?
opts: Pulmonary embolism is the usual outcome

Pulmonary embolism is far from the usual outcome, because superficial thrombophlebitis rarely embolizes. The accurate answer for her is that serious complications are rare, and the usual care is warm compresses, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug.

Correct. Superficial phlebitis and thrombophlebitis rarely cause serious complications and rarely embolize, so the clot in her forearm vein is unlikely to reach her lungs. Her catheter-related case is managed with warm compresses, compression, elevation and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID).
Chronic venous insufficiency follows in most

Chronic venous insufficiency is not the expected course of superficial thrombophlebitis, which rarely causes serious complications. Her catheter-related forearm clot should settle with compresses, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug, with anticoagulation only for extensive clot or higher thrombotic risk.
Fatal embolism is likely without treatment

A fatal embolism is not expected, because superficial thrombophlebitis rarely embolizes at all. Routine care with warm compresses, compression, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug suits her uncomplicated catheter-related clot.

A.q: A 32-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and outflow tract obstruction has breathlessness and chest tightness on exertion. His blood pressure is 124/78 and heart rate is 76. He takes no cardiac medication yet. Which is the initial medication for his outflow obstruction?
opts: Diuretics reduce preload, and drugs that reduce preload may aggravate outflow tract obstruction; if needed, they are used with caution to avoid dehydration. The initial medication for obstruction is a beta blocker. Tell: obstruction worsens with less filling, so a strong diuretic is the wrong start.
A beta blocker such as metoprolol

Correct. For his outflow tract obstruction with exertional breathlessness and chest tightness, a beta blocker such as metoprolol is the initial medication. As a negative chronotrope and inotrope it reduces heart rate and enhances diastolic filling by reducing ventricular stiffness and decreasing contractility; verapamil or diltiazem is the alternative.

Nitrates reduce preload and afterload, which may increase symptoms by aggravating outflow tract obstruction, so they are avoided if possible. The initial medication is a beta blocker such as metoprolol. Tell: his exertional symptoms come from obstruction, and nitrates make it worse.
A positive inotrope such as digoxin

Digoxin is a positive inotrope, avoided because increased contractility raises the risk of myocardial ischemia and may induce arrhythmias. A beta blocker such as metoprolol, which decreases contractility, is the initial drug. Tell: in obstruction the aim is less squeeze, not more.

A.q: A 36-year-old man has a regular tachycardia at 170 with an identical, abnormally shaped P wave before every QRS. Adenosine briefly slows the ventricular response, but the abnormal atrial rhythm continues unchanged afterward. Which rhythm does this response point to?
opts: Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a circuit within the atrioventricular node and almost always terminates with vagal maneuvers or adenosine; its P waves are hidden. Here a visible abnormal P wave precedes every QRS and the atrial rhythm survives adenosine. Tell: termination with adenosine suggests nodal reentry; persistence suggests focal atrial tachycardia.
ruled out by a stated finding

Orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia runs through the atrioventricular node, and adenosine is first line for it; its P waves are hidden or retrograde, after the QRS. This rhythm shows an abnormal P wave before each QRS that persists after adenosine. Tell: a rhythm that keeps going despite nodal block is atrial, not node-dependent reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A regular tachycardia at 170 with one identical abnormal P wave before every QRS comes from a single ectopic atrial focus. Adenosine is a diagnostic tool here because it is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia than the node-dependent reentry rhythms, so brief slowing with the atrial rhythm carrying on fits.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three different P-wave shapes in one lead from multiple foci. This rhythm is regular with one identical abnormal P wave before every QRS, which takes a single focus. Tell: one abnormal P shape is focal; three or more shapes is multifocal.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.q: A 78-year-old man with no neurologic symptoms has a 90% carotid stenosis on duplex. He has advanced cancer, and his expected survival is about two years. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Repeating the duplex does not change the missing criterion, a life expectancy over five years. Duplex is used for serial monitoring, but his asymptomatic stenosis is managed medically now. Another scan cannot extend his survival past the threshold.

His stenosis exceeds 80%, but surgery for asymptomatic disease also requires a life expectancy over five years. With about two years of expected survival he does not qualify, and medical management is advised. Both criteria must be met, not just the stenosis.

Correct. Surgery for asymptomatic stenosis is advised only above 80% together with a life expectancy over five years. His 90% stenosis meets the first criterion, but advanced cancer limits survival to about two years, so he is managed medically with antiplatelet therapy, comorbidity control and smoking cessation.

Carotid stenting is one of the surgical intervention options and is advised for asymptomatic patients by the same criteria, including a life expectancy over five years. Being a less invasive route for poor surgical candidates does not remove that criterion. He should be managed medically.

A.q: A 29-year-old woman who delivered a healthy baby three months ago now has breathlessness on exertion, orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and swollen ankles. She had no heart disease before pregnancy. Echocardiogram shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy does not explain a dilated, weak left ventricle appearing after pregnancy in a woman with no prior heart disease. Peripartum cardiomyopathy, a dilated cardiomyopathy, develops in the last trimester or up to 6 months postpartum. Tell: a dilated ventricle plus a recent delivery means peripartum.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy does not fit a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a dilated cardiomyopathy that develops in the last trimester of pregnancy or within 6 months after delivery. Tell: her timing, three months postpartum, is the decisive clue.

Correct. Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a rare cause of dilated cardiomyopathy that develops in the last trimester of pregnancy or within the first 6 months postpartum. Her dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%, three months after delivery and with no prior heart disease, fits that window.

Stress cardiomyopathy is not suggested; no stressor is described, and her dilated left ventricle appeared within months of delivery. Peripartum cardiomyopathy develops in the last trimester or the first 6 months postpartum. Tell: the pregnancy timeline, not a stressor, explains her heart.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
A.q: A 19-year-old college athlete has exertional chest pain without coronary disease and a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border. Hypertension and aortic valve disease have been excluded. Which echocardiogram finding confirms the clinical diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Pericardial thickening is not part of the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy echo. The confirming finding is unexplained left ventricular wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more, classically in the septum. Tell: the thickening that confirms this disease is in the ventricular wall.
Unexplained wall of 1.5 cm or more

Correct. With hypertension and aortic valve disease excluded, the clinical diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is confirmed when echocardiography shows unexplained left ventricular wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more anywhere in the wall. The hypertrophy is most often asymmetric and septal, with a small left ventricular cavity.
Dilated thin walls with low fraction

Dilated, thin walls with a low ejection fraction are the reverse of this disease: the hypertrophic echo shows a small left ventricular cavity with an ejection fraction that is usually normal and above 75% in late stages. Tell: hypertrophic means thick walls and a small cavity.

A normal septum argues against hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where septal hypertrophy is the classic pattern. The confirming finding is unexplained wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more. Tell: the septum is usually the thickest part, not the normal part.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 48-year-old man becomes hypotensive and short of breath an hour after a catheter procedure perforates his heart. Echocardiogram shows only a small pericardial effusion, estimated at about 150 mL, with right ventricular diastolic collapse. Which best explains why so little fluid has compromised him?
opts: Rapid filling of an unstretched sac

Correct. His effusion formed within an hour of the perforation, and acute pericardial effusions can cause hemodynamic compromise with small amounts, under 200 mL. Chronic effusions can grow large without tamponade because the pericardium stretches over time; a sudden 150 mL gives the sac no time to stretch.

Stretching of the pericardium over time is what lets a chronic effusion grow large without tamponade, the opposite of his situation. His fluid accumulated within an hour, so an unstretched sac could not accommodate even 150 mL. Tell: slow fluid, large volume tolerated; fast fluid, small volume dangerous.

Nothing suggests a calcified pericardium; the stem points to timing, with fluid arriving within an hour of a perforation. Acute effusions can cause tamponade with under 200 mL because the sac has had no time to stretch. Tell: the clock, not a diseased sac, explains why a small volume caused collapse.

There is no need to assume a measurement error: acute effusions can produce tamponade with under 200 mL of fluid, so 150 mL is enough. His right ventricular diastolic collapse shows the hemodynamic effect directly. Tell: in a sudden effusion, small volumes are expected to cause tamponade.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 58-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for colon cancer comes to the emergency department with three days of left calf swelling that measures 4 cm more than the right, plus tenderness along the deep veins of the calf. He has no history of clots and nothing else explains his leg. The team debates whether to order a D-dimer or go straight to imaging. Using the Wells criteria, which is the best next step?
opts: Correct. Active cancer under treatment 1 + calf swelling 4 cm more than the other leg (over 3 cm) 1 + tenderness along the deep veins 1 = 3, a high likelihood of deep vein thrombosis (DVT). In the emergency department, where the score applies, a high-risk patient goes to ultrasound whether or not a D-dimer is drawn.

The ankle-brachial index is not part of the Wells pathway for suspected deep vein thrombosis. His score of 3 (active cancer, calf swelling over 3 cm, deep venous tenderness) is a high likelihood, which leads to ultrasound of the leg.

Contrast venography is not the next step in the Wells pathway; a high score leads to ultrasound. With active cancer, calf swelling over 3 cm and deep venous tenderness, he scores 3 and goes to venous duplex ultrasound.

Starting with a D-dimer is the low-likelihood path, where a negative result can stop the work-up. His score of 3 is a high likelihood, and in that group even a negative D-dimer is followed by ultrasound, so the test cannot spare him imaging.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 31-year-old man was treated for acute pericarditis 3 months ago and has been symptom-free for 6 weeks. His sharp, positional chest pain has now returned with a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound). C-reactive protein is mildly raised. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Anti-interleukin-1 therapy is preferred for colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent disease, or earlier with an inflammatory phenotype such as a C-reactive protein above 10 mg/L. His marker is only mildly raised, and at a first recurrence the pathway is nonsteroidal drugs plus colchicine for 6 months or more. Tell: interleukin-1 blockers come after colchicine fails.

Prednisone at a recurrence is reserved for patients with underlying systemic autoimmune disease, and then at a low to moderate dose, which does not describe him. His first recurrence calls for a nonsteroidal drug plus colchicine for 6 months or more. Tell: without autoimmune disease, a steroid is not the next step.
Ibuprofen with colchicine, stopped at 2 weeks

The drug pair is right but the colchicine duration is wrong: after a first recurrence colchicine continues for 6 months or more, double the 3 months of a first episode. Two weeks falls far short. Tell: when two options share the same drugs, the duration decides.
Ibuprofen with colchicine for 6 months or more

Correct. His pain returned after 6 weeks symptom-free, a first recurrence. That is treated with nonsteroidal drugs until chest pain resolves and inflammatory markers normalize, plus colchicine for 6 months or more. An interleukin-1 blocker is not needed yet, since his C-reactive protein is only mildly raised and he is not colchicine-resistant.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 37-year-old man with acute pericarditis feels better after 5 days of ibuprofen and colchicine and plans to stop both medicines now. Which counseling point is most important?
opts: Switch to prednisone to finish faster

Swapping to prednisone does not shorten anything and adds a drug the plan did not call for; the counseling point is to complete the full prescribed course to prevent recurrence. Tell: the answer to a patient who wants to stop early is adherence, not a different drug.
Stopping now is safe since the pain is gone

Pain relief at 5 days is not the end point; education stresses adherence to the full treatment course because stopping early risks recurrence. It is lack of response, not improvement, that changes the plan and prompts cardiology referral. Tell: feeling better is the reason patients stop, and the reason counseling targets adherence.
Finish the full course to prevent recurrence

Correct. Feeling better at day 5 is expected, but patient education stresses adherence to the full treatment course to prevent recurrence. That message goes with activity restriction, its rationale and duration, and teaching on red-flag symptoms of recurrence or tamponade.
Colchicine can stop; keep the ibuprofen

Dropping colchicine early breaks the full treatment course that education stresses to prevent recurrence. Nonsteroidal drugs plus colchicine are the standard pair for pericarditis, and both are taken as prescribed. Tell: no part of the regimen stops early just because the pain has eased.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 39-year-old woman with visible varicose veins asks what symptoms she is most likely to have. Which should she be told?
opts: Sharp pain at rest when lying flat

Sharp pain at rest when lying flat is not the varicose vein pattern; her symptoms, if any, would be brought on by standing, when the dilated veins are visible and palpable. The usual complaint is dull, achy heaviness or fatigue after standing.

Correct. Varicose veins can be asymptomatic, but when symptomatic the most common complaint is a dull, achy heaviness or feeling of fatigue brought on by periods of standing. Itching above the ankle or over the veins can also occur, and the veins may be tender.

Numb, burning feet at night are not among the varicose vein symptoms. The typical complaint is dull, achy heaviness or fatigue brought on by standing, sometimes with itching above the ankle or over the veins.
Calf cramping that eases with rest

Calf cramping that eases with rest is not the varicose vein pattern; her symptoms would be provoked by periods of standing rather than relieved by stopping. The most common symptom is a dull, achy heaviness or fatigue after standing.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
A.q: A 72-year-old man with a known abdominal aortic aneurysm reports early satiety and pain isolated to his right groin, with no abdominal tenderness. Which explains the groin pain?
opts: Renal colic is one of the conditions a ruptured aneurysm is often misdiagnosed as, not an explanation for groin pain in a known aneurysm. His early satiety and isolated groin pain without abdominal tenderness fit a symptomatic, unruptured aneurysm pressing on the femoral nerve.

A femoral pseudoaneurysm follows catheterization and causes local swelling and pain; nothing in his history suggests a puncture. With a known aortic aneurysm and early satiety, isolated groin pain reflects pressure on the femoral nerve. The aneurysm explains both symptoms.

Correct. A symptomatic, unruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm causes pain with expansion, including isolated groin pain from pressure on the femoral nerve. His early satiety is another listed symptom, and abdominal, back or flank pain may also occur.

A hernia is not among the aneurysm's described symptoms and would not account for his early satiety. In a symptomatic aneurysm, isolated groin pain comes from pressure on the femoral nerve. One mechanism, the expanding aneurysm, accounts for both complaints.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A slow sinus rhythm that is causing hypotension and confusion is treated first with which drug?
opts: Metoprolol is a beta blocker, and beta blockers are a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, so giving one would slow this patient further. Beta blockers belong in fast rhythms, such as rate control for stable atrial flutter. Tell: a hypotensive, confused patient with a slow sinus rhythm needs atropine first, then a temporary pacemaker.

Digoxin is listed with beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers as a drug cause of sinus bradycardia, so it would worsen this rhythm. Look for it as the culprit in a slow patient, not the rescue. Tell: drugs that cause bradycardia never treat it; atropine does.

Correct. A slow sinus rhythm causing hypotension and confusion is acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia, and atropine is first line. If it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows; chronic symptomatic bradycardia is treated with a permanent pacemaker instead.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia, after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing is the opposite of what an unstable bradycardia needs. Tell: adenosine is for a fast narrow rhythm; atropine is for a slow, unstable one.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
A.q: A 2-month-old infant with a central line has poor feeding, fast breathing, tachycardia and a changing murmur. Blood cultures are positive and echocardiography shows a vegetation. Which complications are particularly common in infants because of septic emboli?
opts: Classic peripheral stigmata, including Janeway lesions and Roth spots, are considerably less common in children than in adults. In infants, septic emboli instead produce osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia. Tell: peripheral skin and eye stigmata are adult findings; infants show deep-organ seeding.

Glomerulonephritis is not among the infant complications listed. In neonates and infants, septic emboli are common and produce osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia, with frequent neurologic signs. Tell: the question asks about emboli, which seed bone, meninges and lung.

Pediatric endocarditis causes less heart failure than adult disease, and valve stenosis is not the listed infant problem. Septic emboli are common in infants, producing osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia. Tell: the stem asks about embolic complications, not valve function.

Correct. In neonates and infants, septic emboli are common and produce osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia, and neurologic signs such as seizures, hemiparesis and apnea are frequent. This infant's central line, sepsis-like picture and changing murmur fit the infant pattern.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
A.q: A 60-year-old woman has viridans streptococcal endocarditis diagnosed early, before any heart failure or abscess, and she starts appropriate antibiotics the same day. Which statement about her outlook is most accurate?
opts: Correct. Her viridans streptococcal endocarditis was diagnosed before any heart failure or abscess, and antibiotics started the same day. That is exactly the condition for a relatively good prognosis: viridans streptococcal disease does relatively well if antibiotic treatment starts before complications occur.

Valve replacement in a large share of patients describes enterococcal endocarditis, where major complications and need for valve replacement reach about 30-40%. Her organism is viridans streptococci, treated early. Tell: high surgery rates go with enterococci, not early-treated viridans streptococci.

The highest mortality belongs to Staphylococcus aureus, the most lethal organism, with about 30% mortality in people who do not inject drugs and 50% in prosthetic valve endocarditis. Tell: most lethal always means Staphylococcus aureus; viridans streptococci treated early do relatively well.

Death within weeks is not expected after early, appropriate treatment of viridans streptococcal disease, which carries a relatively good prognosis when antibiotics start before complications. Tell: her same-day treatment and absence of complications are what make the outlook good.

A.q: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation at 170 has a blood pressure of 74/40 and is drowsy and confused. Which is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Rate control alone suits hemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation without rapid ventricular response. His rate is 170, and he is hypotensive at 74/40 and confused, so he is unstable. Tell: hemodynamic instability calls for synchronized cardioversion, not rate control.

Twenty-one days of anticoagulation is the prerequisite for an elective outpatient cardioversion in stable atrial fibrillation. He is hypotensive and confused now and cannot wait three weeks. Tell: unstable means cardioversion now; stable means anticoagulate first.

Correct. Atrial fibrillation at 170 with a blood pressure of 74/40, drowsiness and confusion is hemodynamically unstable, a medical emergency. Unstable atrial fibrillation is treated with synchronized cardioversion now, not with rate control or a delayed cardioversion.

Intravenous rate control is for hemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. His rate of 170 is rapid, but a blood pressure of 74/40 with confusion makes him unstable. Tell: rapid plus stable means intravenous rate control; rapid plus unstable means synchronized cardioversion.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: A 75-year-old man with complete heart block is stabilized with transcutaneous pacing in the emergency department. Which is the definitive treatment?
opts: An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) detects and shocks fatal fast rhythms; it is not the definitive treatment for a slow, blocked rhythm. Complete block needs a permanent pacemaker. Tell: a block needs pacing, not shocking.

Ablation is itself a named cause of complete heart block, so it cannot be the cure. After transcutaneous pacing stabilizes him, the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker. Tell: a procedure that causes a block cannot treat it.

Correct. In complete (third-degree) block no P waves conduct, and the ventricles rely on a slow escape rhythm. Atropine, epinephrine and transcutaneous pacing are the emergent measures that stabilize him; the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

A beta blocker is a listed cause of atrioventricular block, so it would slow his escape rhythm further. Complete block is paced: transcutaneously as the emergent bridge, then definitively with a permanent pacemaker. Tell: never add a rate-slowing drug to a heart that is already blocked.

A.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic obstructive lung disease is admitted with an exacerbation. She is confused, and the monitor shows runs of skipped beats from frequent early, wide QRS complexes without P waves. Her arterial oxygen tension is low. Which underlying problem should be corrected first?
opts: Correct. Early, wide QRS complexes without P waves are premature ventricular contractions, and hypoxemia is a named cause, along with electrolyte imbalance. Her chronic obstructive lung disease exacerbation, confusion and low arterial oxygen tension make hypoxemia the problem to correct first.

Blood glucose is not a named cause of premature ventricular contractions. Her low arterial oxygen tension is: hypoxemia heads the list with electrolyte imbalance. Tell: correct the abnormal value the stem gives you.

Blood pressure is not a named cause of premature ventricular contractions. The named causes are hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance, and her low arterial oxygen tension during a lung disease flare is the clear one. Tell: the stem hands you a low oxygen value.

Body temperature is not a named cause of premature ventricular contractions. Hypoxemia, along with electrolyte imbalance, is, and her low arterial oxygen tension during a lung disease exacerbation is the cause to correct first. Tell: her lung disease and low oxygen tension point straight to hypoxemia.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: In sick sinus syndrome, a fast run that is irregularly irregular with no P waves alternates with pauses. Which rhythm is the fast run?
opts: Correct. A fast run that is irregularly irregular with no P waves is atrial fibrillation. In tachy-brady syndrome, the form of sick sinus syndrome in which a tachyarrhythmia alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or pauses, atrial fibrillation is the most common cause of the fast rhythm.

Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome, and then the patient needs a permanent pacemaker with an implantable defibrillator. But ventricular tachycardia is regular, at about 150 to 200, while this run is irregularly irregular with no P waves. Tell: an irregularly irregular run without P waves is atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Sinus tachycardia is regular, at over 100 to 160, with a uniform P wave before every QRS. This fast run is irregularly irregular with no P waves, so it is not coming from the sinus node. Tell: a P wave before every beat keeps the rhythm sinus; irregularity without P waves means atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is also irregular, but each QRS has a P wave, in at least three different shapes in the same lead. A fast run with no P waves at all is atrial fibrillation, the most common fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome. Tell: P waves present in several shapes means multifocal; absent P waves means fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
A.q: A 78-year-old man with diabetes and known black, shriveled toe tips now has a moist, swollen, blistered forefoot. His temperature is 39.2 C and heart rate 118. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. A moist, swollen, blistered forefoot with a temperature of 39.2 C and a heart rate of 118 is wet gangrene: bacterial infection, often spore-forming clostridial species, in the affected tissue, with a risk of sepsis. Wet gangrene is a surgical emergency, unlike the dry gangrene of his black, shriveled toe tips.

Cilostazol suppresses platelet aggregation and improves walking distance in chronic arterial disease; it cannot control infected tissue. His moist, blistered forefoot with fever and tachycardia is wet gangrene, a surgical emergency with a risk of sepsis. A delayed recheck wastes critical time.

Clear demarcation between healthy and necrotic tissue is a feature of dry gangrene, which his black toe tips showed. The forefoot is now moist, swollen and blistered with fever, which is wet gangrene, a surgical emergency because of the risk of sepsis. Observation fits none of these wet features.

Exercise therapy is for stable claudication. A moist, blistered, infected foot with fever and tachycardia is wet gangrene, a surgical emergency because of the risk of sepsis. His fever and tachycardia are the urgent clues.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 71-year-old man has been on strict bed rest for six days during an admission for pneumonia and now has swelling and aching of the entire left leg. Which component of the Virchow triad does his prolonged bed rest represent?
opts: Endothelial injury comes from trauma, surgery such as knee or hip replacement, intravenous drug use or burns. Bed rest during pneumonia does not injure the vein wall; it alters blood flow, which places it under venous stasis.

Arterial vasospasm is not one of the three Virchow components, which are venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state and vascular endothelial injury. His risk comes from immobilization, which the triad lists under venous stasis along with long flights and postoperative inactivity.

A hypercoagulable state is a clotting tendency, inherited (factor V Leiden, protein C or S deficiency) or acquired (cancer, estrogen, pregnancy). Lying still changes blood flow rather than the blood's clotting tendency, so his bed rest belongs to venous stasis.

Correct. Six days of strict bed rest is immobilization, which alters blood flow: the venous stasis arm of the Virchow triad. Immobilization carries about a 20-fold increased risk for deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which fits his new swelling and aching of the entire leg.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: Compared with Mobitz type I, Mobitz type II block carries a higher risk of which outcome?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is not the outcome tied to Mobitz type II. Its block usually sits at the bundle of His, and it carries a higher risk of progression to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death. Tell: the danger of type II is a worse block, not an atrial rhythm.

Mobitz type II does not regress into Mobitz type I. Its risk runs the other way, toward complete heart block and sudden cardiac death. Tell: type II is the more dangerous second-degree block, so its feared outcome is complete block.

Sinus tachycardia is not a complication of Mobitz type II. The danger is progression to complete heart block, with a weak, unreliable escape rhythm and sudden cardiac death. Tell: a block worsens toward slower rhythms, not faster ones.

Correct. Mobitz type II usually originates at the bundle of His, so its escape rhythm is weak and unreliable, and it carries a higher risk of progression to complete (third-degree) block and sudden cardiac death. That is why it is considered dangerous even without symptoms and treated with a permanent pacemaker.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 57-year-old woman with a moderate pericardial effusion was stable yesterday. Today her blood pressure is 96/64, her jugular venous pressure is elevated, and she has new sinus tachycardia at 128. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. A known moderate effusion with a new fall in blood pressure to 96/64, an elevated jugular venous pressure and new sinus tachycardia at 128 signals tamponade. Sinus tachycardia may indicate significant hemodynamic compromise and is an indication for immediate pericardiocentesis.

Waiting a week ignores signs of significant compromise that appeared overnight: lower blood pressure, elevated jugular venous pressure and new sinus tachycardia. Sinus tachycardia in this setting is an indication for immediate pericardiocentesis. Tell: a change from stable to tachycardic and hypotensive means act now.

Nothing in her picture calls for diuresis; new hypotension, an elevated jugular venous pressure and sinus tachycardia point to tamponade from her known effusion, and sinus tachycardia here is an indication for immediate pericardiocentesis. Tell: tamponade is relieved by draining the fluid, not by drug therapy.
Rate control with a beta blocker

Her tachycardia is part of the tamponade picture, a marker of significant hemodynamic compromise rather than a rhythm to suppress. Sinus tachycardia in this setting is an indication for immediate pericardiocentesis. Tell: treat the cause of the fast rate, the compressing fluid, rather than the rate itself.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 66-year-old woman has a painful ulcer above the medial malleolus with a clean base, fibrinous exudate and serous drainage, surrounded by brown pigmentation and pitting edema. Her pedal pulses are strong and her ankle-brachial index is 1.10. Which measure is essential for the ulcer to heal?
opts: Her ulcer has a clean base with fibrinous exudate, and a dressing alone does not address the cause. Venous ulcers will not heal unless edema is controlled and compression is applied; antibiotics are for cellulitis, given orally as cephalexin or clindamycin.

Valvuloplasty is only occasionally successful and carries a high incidence of postoperative deep vein thrombosis, so it is not the step that makes an ulcer heal. Healing requires edema control and compression, with wound care referral.

Flavonoids are used to increase venous tone, but no oral medication has yet been proven useful for venous disease. On its own a flavonoid will not heal the ulcer; edema control and compression are required.

Correct. A painful ulcer above the medial malleolus with brown pigmentation and pitting edema is a venous ulcer, and venous ulcers will not heal unless edema is controlled and compression is applied. Wound care referral supports healing, which can take 4 to 6 months.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 59-year-old woman had a left leg deep vein thrombosis 11 months ago. She now has chronic left leg heaviness, edema and brownish ankle skin that worsen with standing and improve with elevation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Post-thrombotic (postphlebitic) syndrome is symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency that follows a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), from 6 to 24 months after the clot. Her left leg clot 11 months ago, followed by heaviness, edema and brownish ankle skin in that same leg, fits the window and the pattern.

Drug-induced edema, a common adverse effect of drugs such as amlodipine, is often bilateral and usually lacks signs of inflammation. Her swelling is one-sided, in the leg that had a clot 11 months ago, with brownish skin change, which points to post-thrombotic syndrome.

Lymphedema is chronic edema usually accompanied by a history of pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy, none of which she has. Her symptoms began in the leg that had a deep vein thrombosis 11 months ago, within the 6 to 24 month window of post-thrombotic syndrome.

A new clot would bring swelling, pain, warmth or erythema, often with a calf cramp that worsens over a few days. Her complaints are chronic, ease with elevation and began 11 months after the first clot, the course of post-thrombotic syndrome rather than recurrence.

A.q: A 72-year-old woman with a femoral pseudoaneurysm after catheterization reports increasing thigh pain and tingling around the swelling. Which explains her pain?
opts: Ischemic rest pain is constant pain in the forefoot and toes, worse on elevation and relieved by dependency. Her pain is in the thigh around the pseudoaneurysm swelling, with tingling, which reflects swelling pressure and nerve compression. Location around the swelling is the clue.

Correct. A pseudoaneurysm presents with pain due to increased pressure from swelling or from nerve compression. Her increasing thigh pain with tingling around the swelling after femoral catheterization matches both mechanisms, the tingling pointing to a compressed nerve.

Retroperitoneal bleeding is the picture of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, with severe abdominal or back pain, a pulsatile mass and hypotension. Her pain and tingling sit around a femoral pseudoaneurysm after catheterization, which fits swelling and nerve compression. The pain is local, not central.

Atheroemboli cause painful blue toes, not pain and tingling around a groin swelling. A pseudoaneurysm causes pain from increased pressure due to swelling or from nerve compression. Her symptoms sit at the swelling, not in the digits.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 66-year-old man has a story strongly suggesting constrictive pericarditis: edema, ascites, an elevated jugular venous pressure with the Kussmaul sign (a rise on inspiration). His chest radiograph shows no pericardial calcification. How should this radiograph be interpreted?
opts: Most patients with constrictive pericarditis do not show calcification on chest radiograph, so its absence cannot exclude the diagnosis. Calcification raises confidence when present; its absence leaves his strong clinical story intact. Tell: a finding that most patients lack cannot be used to rule a disease out.

A radiograph without calcium does not separate constriction from restrictive cardiomyopathy. Echocardiography, magnetic resonance or computed tomography of pericardial thickness, and B-type natriuretic peptide, which tends to be lower in constriction than in restrictive cardiomyopathy, help with that. Tell: absent calcium is simply uninformative.
It shows the cause is tamponade

A radiograph without calcium says nothing in favor of tamponade, and his edema, ascites and Kussmaul sign fit the constrictive story the stem describes. Echocardiography provides the structural and Doppler information that confirms constrictive physiology in many patients. Tell: the film is uninformative, not diagnostic of another disease.

Correct. Pericardial calcification on a chest radiograph is highly consistent with constriction when present, but most patients do not have it, so a film without calcium cannot rule the diagnosis out. With edema, ascites and the Kussmaul sign, echocardiography is the next step and confirms constrictive physiology in many patients.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 26-year-old man has a sudden, regular narrow complex tachycardia at 230 with retrograde (inverted) P waves. An electrocardiogram taken last year in normal sinus rhythm showed a short PR interval and a delta wave (a slurred QRS upstroke). Which diagnosis is most likely?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves, the exception among supraventricular tachycardias, which are otherwise regular. His rhythm is regular with retrograde P waves, and his prior pre-excitation points to an accessory pathway. Tell: regular with retrograde P waves after pre-excitation is atrioventricular reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a circuit within the atrioventricular node, usually at 140 to 180 with hidden P waves. It needs no accessory pathway, so it does not explain the short PR and delta wave on his sinus tracing. Tell: prior pre-excitation plus a rate above 200 points to accessory pathway reentry rather than nodal reentry.

Sinus tachycardia is regular at over 100 to 160 with a uniform P wave before every QRS, driven by a physiologic or pathologic process. A sudden rate of 230 with retrograde P waves is beyond that range and points to reentry. Tell: retrograde P waves and a rate over 200 do not come from the sinus node.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Pre-excitation, a short PR interval and delta wave, on last year's tracing in normal sinus rhythm points to an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) and the potential for atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia. That rhythm is regular and narrow, above 100 and usually 200 to 300, with hidden or retrograde P waves, matching his rate of 230.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
A.q: A 45-year-old woman has 2 months of fever, weight loss and fatigue. A new murmur with a tumor plop (a low-pitched early diastolic sound) is heard, and three sets of blood cultures drawn before any antibiotics are negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Atrial myxoma mimics endocarditis with fever and a new murmur, classically a tumor plop or mid-diastolic rumble. Her 2 months of fever and weight loss could suggest endocarditis, but the tumor plop and three negative culture sets drawn before any antibiotics point to this neoplastic mimic.

Lyme disease causes fever and, rarely, myocarditis, but it does not produce a new murmur with a tumor plop. Tell: in the endocarditis differential, the tumor plop belongs to atrial myxoma, a neoplastic mimic.

Polymyalgia rheumatica causes myalgia with elevated inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein), not a new murmur with a tumor plop. Tell: a heart sound like a tumor plop points to atrial myxoma; girdle aching points to polymyalgia rheumatica.

Subacute endocarditis is usually culture-positive (culture-negative cases are only about 5-17%), yet her three sets drawn before any antibiotics are negative. And a tumor plop is the sound of atrial myxoma. Tell: a plop plus negative cultures favors the tumor over infection.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 45-year-old man has a heart rate of 122 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. His temperature is 39.2°C and he has a productive cough and crackles at the right base. He is alert with a blood pressure of 126/78. Which is the best treatment for his heart rate?
opts: A vagal maneuver is first line for stable reentrant tachycardias such as nodal reentry. His rhythm is sinus, with a normal P wave before every QRS, responding to fever and pneumonia. Tell: an obvious cause with visible normal P waves means appropriate sinus tachycardia, so treat the cause.

Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias such as supraventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter or atrial fibrillation. He is alert with a blood pressure of 126/78, and his rhythm is sinus, driven by infection. Tell: a sinus rhythm with an obvious cause is not shocked; the cause is treated.

Correct. A rate of 122 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus tachycardia, and with a temperature of 39.2°C, a productive cough and crackles it is an appropriate response to an underlying pathologic process, infection. Appropriate sinus tachycardia is managed by treating that cause, here the infection and fever.

Adenosine follows a vagal maneuver in stable supraventricular tachycardia, converting the rhythm or slowing it to reveal P waves. His P waves are already visible and normal, and the rate is a response to fever and pneumonia. Tell: when the P waves are normal and a cause is obvious, treating the cause is the answer.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
A.q: A 66-year-old woman has had six days of worsening left leg pain and coolness. The limb has no sensory loss or weakness, and imaging shows an arterial thrombus. Which intervention fits this time frame?
opts: Supervised exercise therapy improves walking distance in chronic claudication. A new arterial thrombus causing six days of worsening pain and coolness is acute limb ischemia, and under 14 days it is an indication for catheter-directed thrombolysis. Exercise has no role in acute occlusion.

Major amputation is required for irreversibly ischemic limbs with profound sensory loss and paralysis. Her limb has no sensory loss or weakness after six days, so it is not in that category. Within 14 days, catheter-directed thrombolysis fits the time frame.

Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent for chronic peripheral artery disease and does not dissolve an arterial thrombus. Her six-day occlusion falls within the under-14-day indication for catheter-directed thrombolysis with alteplase. The question is about the time frame, and only thrombolysis carries one.

Correct. Her ischemia has lasted six days, well within the indication for intra-arterial catheter-directed thrombolysis, which is acute limb ischemia of less than 14 days' duration, with alteplase as the thrombolytic drug. With no sensory loss or weakness, her limb is far from the irreversible category that requires amputation.
