A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
A.q: Which cardiac condition is listed among the risk factors for infective endocarditis?
opts: Stable angina is not on the risk-factor list. The listed cardiac risk factors are congenital heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, degenerative valve disease, intracardiac devices and prosthetic valves. Tell: endocarditis risk comes from abnormal valves, devices or congenital lesions, not coronary symptoms.

Sinus bradycardia is not a listed risk factor; it is a rhythm, not an abnormal valve, device or structural lesion. The listed cardiac risk factors include congenital heart disease, rheumatic and degenerative valve disease, intracardiac devices and prosthetic valves. Tell: look for a structural substrate.

Correct. Congenital heart disease is a listed risk factor for infective endocarditis, along with rheumatic heart disease, degenerative valve disease, intracardiac devices, prosthetic valves and injection drug use. Degenerative valve disease and intracardiac devices are now the leading predisposing conditions in high-income countries.

White coat hypertension is not on the risk-factor list. The listed cardiac risk factors are structural: congenital heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, degenerative valve disease, intracardiac devices and prosthetic valves. Tell: an office blood pressure reading creates no surface for a vegetation.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: Which definition fits cardiac tamponade?
opts: Inflammation of the sac lasting under four weeks

Inflammation of the pericardial sac lasting less than 4 to 6 weeks defines acute pericarditis, not tamponade. Tamponade is defined by pericardial fluid under pressure compressing the heart. Tell: a time window describes inflammation; compression describes tamponade.
Fibrous scarring that leaves the pericardium inelastic

Fibrous scarring with loss of elasticity of the pericardial sac, leaving it noncompliant, defines constrictive pericarditis. Tamponade involves fluid under pressure, not a stiff sac. Tell: scar means constriction; pressurized fluid means tamponade; both together suggest effusive-constrictive disease.
Pericardial fluid under pressure compressing the heart

Correct. Cardiac tamponade is an accumulation of pericardial fluid under pressure, resulting in compression of the heart. Both parts matter: extra fluid alone is a pericardial effusion, and it becomes tamponade only when that fluid is under enough pressure to compress the heart.
Extra pericardial fluid with no hemodynamic effect

Extra fluid in the pericardial space is the definition of a pericardial effusion; without pressure compressing the heart it is not tamponade. Tamponade requires that fluid to be under pressure, compressing the heart. Tell: effusion names the fluid; tamponade names what the fluid does to the heart.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
A.q: A 71-year-old woman with suspected endocarditis has a urinalysis sent as part of her workup. Which urinalysis result is most consistent with endocarditis?
opts: Glucose and ketones are not part of the endocarditis urinalysis. The expected findings are hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria. Tell: endocarditis puts blood, protein and white cells in the urine, not metabolic products.

Bilirubin and urobilinogen are not part of the endocarditis urinalysis, which shows hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria. Tell: look for blood, protein and white cells; bile pigments in the urine point away from endocarditis.

Correct. Urinalysis in infective endocarditis can show hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria: blood, protein and white cells. It sits alongside the rest of the workup, which includes three sets of blood cultures, transesophageal echocardiography and a complete blood count showing leukocytosis and a normocytic anemia.

Nitrites with no cells are not the endocarditis pattern. Endocarditis urinalysis shows hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria, so red cells and white cells are present. Tell: an absence of cells rules out the expected pattern, which needs blood and white cells.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
A.q: A 73-year-old man with painful blue toes and palpable pulses asks what the emboli in his toes are made of. Which answer is accurate?
opts: A clot from the heart is a thromboembolus, the usual cause of acute limb ischemia, which blocks a larger artery and leaves pulses absent distal to the occlusion. His blue toes with palpable pulses reflect atheroemboli: fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques. Palpable pulses favor small-vessel debris.

Correct. Atheroembolism is multiple small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris embolizing from proximal atherosclerotic lesions. The debris lodges in small vessels of muscle and skin and may not occlude large vessels, which is why his pulses remain palpable despite painful blue toes.

Air embolism is not the process described. His painful blue toes with palpable pulses are atheroembolism: small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques. The material comes from plaque, not from a line.

Valve vegetations are not the source named for blue toe syndrome. The debris is fibrin, platelets and cholesterol shed from proximal atherosclerotic plaques. Cholesterol debris from plaque answers what these emboli are made of.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 69-year-old woman in stable, rate-controlled atrial flutter of unknown duration is to have elective outpatient cardioversion. Which must come first?
opts: An adenosine challenge is not the listed preparation for cardioversion. Adenosine is a step for stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, and her flutter is already diagnosed and controlled. Tell: preparing for any elective outpatient cardioversion means 21 days of anticoagulation first.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia and is not a prerequisite for cardioversion. Her flutter is stable and rate controlled, and what must come first is 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: pacemakers answer slow rhythms; elective cardioversion needs anticoagulation.

Correct. Her flutter is stable and rate controlled, and elective outpatient cardioversion of atrial flutter is done after 21 days of anticoagulation. Anticoagulation is part of flutter management in its own right, alongside rate control and ablation as the definitive treatment.

Catheter ablation is the definitive management of atrial flutter, which has a substantial recurrence rate, not a step that must precede cardioversion. Before an elective outpatient cardioversion she needs 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: the prerequisite is about clot risk, which anticoagulation addresses.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: A 34-year-old woman has an electrocardiogram before a sports tryout. The QRS is 0.14 seconds, with an rsR' pattern (a small upward wave, a dip, then a taller second upward wave) in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in leads I and aVL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: An accessory pathway does not produce rsR' in V1 to V3 with a slurred S wave in I and aVL. Those findings, with a QRS of 0.14 seconds, are the criteria for right bundle branch block. Tell: bunny ears in the right precordial leads mean right bundle branch block.

Ventricular tachycardia is a fast rhythm, which nothing in this routine tracing describes. A QRS of 0.14 seconds with rsR' in V1 to V3 and a slurred S in I and aVL is right bundle branch block. Tell: a wide QRS at a resting rate with bunny ears is a bundle branch block, not a tachycardia.

Left bundle branch block gives a dominant S wave in V1 and a monophasic R in the lateral leads, not rsR' in V1 to V3. Her pattern is right bundle branch block. Tell: bunny ears in V1 mean right; a deep S in V1 means left.

Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds (here 0.14), an rsR' pattern ('bunny ears') in V1, V2 and V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL are the criteria for right bundle branch block. The right ventricle is activated late from across the septum, and new block can occur without any underlying heart disease.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 66-year-old man is readmitted 3 weeks after coronary artery bypass surgery with fever, pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) chest pain eased by sitting forward, and a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound). His sternal wound looks clean. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Constrictive pericarditis is uncommon, estimated at under 0.05% of patients with viral pericarditis, and his picture is acute: fever, pleuritic positional pain and a rub weeks after surgery. Those findings fit post-cardiotomy Dressler syndrome. Tell: an acute, painful presentation with a rub is pericarditis, not constriction.

Correct. Fever, pleuritic pain eased by sitting forward and a friction rub 3 weeks after coronary artery bypass surgery, with a clean sternal wound, point to post-cardiotomy pericarditis. Pericarditis after myocardial infarction or after cardiac surgery is Dressler syndrome, a listed cause of pericardial disease.

His sternal wound looks clean, and pleuritic pain eased by sitting forward with a friction rub localizes the problem to the pericardium. Weeks after cardiac surgery, that picture is Dressler syndrome. Tell: a rub and positional pain point to the pericardium, not the incision.
ruled out by a stated finding

Nothing points to a new coronary event; fever with pain eased by sitting forward and a friction rub is pericardial. Post-cardiotomy pericarditis, Dressler syndrome, is a listed cause that follows cardiac surgery, as here 3 weeks after bypass. Tell: positional pain plus a rub after cardiac surgery means Dressler syndrome.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
A.q: A 71-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy has fatigue and exercise intolerance along with leg edema, hepatomegaly and ascites, but her lungs are relatively clear. Which pattern of heart failure is expected to dominate in this condition?
opts: Isolated left-sided failure does not fit her relatively clear lungs. Restrictive cardiomyopathy raises filling pressures in both ventricles, and right heart failure may dominate, giving hepatomegaly, bilateral pedal edema and ascites. Tell: congestion in the abdomen and legs with clear lungs points right.

Correct. Her leg edema, hepatomegaly and ascites with relatively clear lungs are the right-sided pattern. In restrictive cardiomyopathy, filling pressures are elevated in both ventricles, but right heart failure may dominate over left, with an elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pedal edema and ascites.

Pure systolic failure is not the pattern described; the restrictive problem is raised filling pressure in both ventricles, and right heart failure may dominate over left. Tell: her leg edema, hepatomegaly and ascites are right-sided findings, and the question asks which side dominates.

High-output failure does not fit, because her exercise intolerance comes from poor cardiac output. Right heart failure may dominate in restrictive cardiomyopathy, matching her edema, hepatomegaly and ascites. Tell: restrictive disease lowers output, and the dominant side is the right.

A.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
A.q: A 60-year-old woman with a prosthetic valve and a past episode of anaphylaxis to penicillin needs a dental cleaning and can take pills. Which prophylactic agent should be avoided?
opts: Azithromycin is an appropriate choice: azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg by mouth is listed for penicillin-allergic patients who can take oral medication, and the anaphylaxis warning applies only to cephalosporins. Tell: the warning covers cephalexin, cefazolin and ceftriaxone, not macrolides.

Correct. She had anaphylaxis to penicillin, and cephalexin (like cefazolin and ceftriaxone) should not be used in patients with a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria to penicillin or ampicillin. Her prosthetic valve still calls for prophylaxis, so an oral macrolide or doxycycline is used instead.

Doxycycline 100 mg by mouth is listed for penicillin-allergic patients who can take oral medication, and the anaphylaxis warning is not about it. Tell: only the cephalosporins (cephalexin, cefazolin, ceftriaxone) carry the anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria restriction.

Clarithromycin 500 mg by mouth is listed with azithromycin for penicillin-allergic patients who can take oral medication, and her anaphylaxis history does not restrict it. Tell: the restricted drugs are the cephalosporins, which are avoided after anaphylaxis to penicillin.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 74-year-old woman with newly diagnosed deep vein thrombosis has chronic kidney disease with a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min. Which approach should be avoided?
opts: Admission is exactly what a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min requires: she is hospitalized and given unfractionated heparin as an intravenous loading bolus followed by a continuous infusion. This is the recommended plan, not one to avoid.

Adjusting the dose by laboratory results is standard for unfractionated heparin, which is titrated to the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT). That monitoring is part of the inpatient plan her kidney function requires, so it is not the approach to avoid.

Overlapping heparin with warfarin is the standard plan: unfractionated heparin continues alongside warfarin for at least 5 days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2 for at least 24 hours. It is part of her inpatient treatment, not an error.

Correct. With a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min, she needs to be hospitalized to start treatment, so beginning therapy at home is the approach to avoid. In hospital she receives unfractionated heparin (UFH) as an intravenous bolus followed by a continuous infusion, adjusted by laboratory results and overlapped with warfarin.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: A 59-year-old man in ventricular fibrillation arrest is shocked several times, and his rhythm changes to a flat line with no electrical activity in two leads. What does this change mean for his outlook?
opts: The change matters: ventricular fibrillation is one of the best-prognosis arrest rhythms, while asystole has a poor prognosis and is usually an end-of-life rhythm. Tell: moving from a shockable rhythm to asystole moves the outlook down.

Correct. A flat line with no electrical activity is asystole. Ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation have the best prognosis of the arrest rhythms, while asystole is unshockable, carries a poor prognosis and is usually an end-of-life rhythm, so his outlook has worsened; compressions and epinephrine continue.

A flat line is not a successful conversion; it is asystole, with no organized activity and no perfusion. It is unshockable and carries a poor prognosis. Tell: success would be an organized rhythm with a pulse, not a flat line.

Asystole carries a poorer prognosis than ventricular fibrillation, not a better one; it is usually an end-of-life rhythm. Tell: of the arrest rhythms, ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation have the best prognosis, asystole and pulseless electrical activity the worst.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: What most commonly causes a lower extremity arteriovenous fistula?
opts: Blunt trauma to the thigh is not the leading cause of a lower extremity fistula. Most lower extremity arteriovenous fistulas are iatrogenic, the result of groin access during endovascular procedures.

Correct. Lower extremity arteriovenous (AV) fistulas are most commonly iatrogenic, caused by groin access for endovascular procedures. Upper extremity fistulas, by contrast, are most commonly created on purpose for hemodialysis access.

Fistulas created for long-term hemodialysis access are placed in the upper arm or forearm, which are generally preferred over the lower extremity. That is the most common cause of an upper extremity fistula; in the leg, iatrogenic groin access leads.

Fistulas can exist almost anywhere in the body depending on their cause, but a congenital origin is not the most common one in the leg. Lower extremity fistulas are most commonly iatrogenic, from groin access for endovascular procedures.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 40-year-old woman has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 182 with palpitations and mild anxiety. Her blood pressure is 128/80, oxygen saturation 98%, and she is alert without chest pain. Which treatment should be tried first?
opts: Amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, not as the opening step for a stable narrow complex tachycardia. Her stable presentation starts with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine. Tell: the first step in stable supraventricular tachycardia needs no drug at all.

Correct. A regular narrow complex tachycardia at 182 with a blood pressure of 128/80, normal oxygen saturation and an alert patient without chest pain is stable supraventricular tachycardia. A vagal maneuver is first line, then adenosine (repeated once if needed), with synchronized cardioversion kept for instability.

Adenosine is the second step in stable supraventricular tachycardia, given if a vagal maneuver does not work, and it may be repeated once. It may convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Tell: the question asks what to try first, and the vagal maneuver comes before any drug.

Synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, is immediate treatment for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia. She is alert with a normal blood pressure and no chest pain, so she is stable. Tell: stability means a vagal maneuver first, not a shock.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
B.q: A 52-year-old man becomes ill over 4 days with a temperature of 40.1 °C (104.2 °F), shaking chills and confusion. He looks toxic, a new loud regurgitant murmur is heard, and painless hemorrhagic macules appear on his soles, which are Janeway lesions (painless, nontender spots). Which form of infective endocarditis fits his course?
opts: Correct. Four days of illness with 40.1 °C (104.2 °F), shaking chills, confusion and a toxic appearance fit acute endocarditis: a hectically febrile illness from a virulent, invasive organism, with rapid onset typically over 3-10 days. The new loud murmur reflects rapid valve damage, and Janeway lesions show seeding beyond the heart.

Subacute endocarditis is indolent, with lower fevers, malaise and weight loss over weeks or months, slow structural damage and rare metastasis. His 4-day, 40.1 °C, toxic illness is the opposite. Tell: high fever and toxicity within days mean acute; weeks to months of low-grade symptoms mean subacute.

Libman-Sacks disease is not one of the two courses infective endocarditis takes, acute or subacute. His 4-day illness with 40.1 °C fever, shaking chills, toxicity and embolic Janeway lesions is the hectically febrile, rapidly destructive acute form. Tell: an infectious, toxic, embolizing picture names a tempo, acute.

Device endocarditis requires an implanted cardiac device, and none is described. The question asks which course his illness fits, and a 4-day, toxic, 40.1 °C illness with rapid valve damage and skin seeding is acute endocarditis. Tell: device endocarditis names a site; acute and subacute name a tempo.

B.topic: Differential diagnosis of a swollen leg

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
B.q: A 68-year-old man who started amlodipine for hypertension five weeks ago has bilateral, symmetric ankle swelling without warmth, redness or tenderness. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A D-dimer belongs to the work-up of suspected deep vein thrombosis, guided by the Wells criteria. His swelling is bilateral and noninflamed and began after amlodipine, the picture of drug-induced edema, so clot testing is not the next step.
Review the medication as the cause

Correct. Bilateral, symmetric ankle swelling without warmth, redness or tenderness, beginning weeks after amlodipine, is the pattern of drug-induced edema. It is a common adverse effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, so reviewing the medication as the cause is the logical next step.

Ultrasound of both legs would be a search for clot, but nothing here suggests one: the swelling is symmetric, without warmth, redness or tenderness. Drug-induced edema from amlodipine is often bilateral and lacks inflammation, so the medication is reviewed first.

Anticoagulation would treat a clot that has not been suspected, let alone shown. Bilateral swelling without signs of inflammation five weeks after starting amlodipine fits drug-induced edema, which calls for reviewing the drug.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: Which patient with recurrent pericarditis is described as a candidate for anti-interleukin-1 therapy?
opts: Correct. Recurrent or colchicine-resistant disease, or steroid-dependent disease, makes anti-interleukin-1 therapy (anakinra or rilonacept) the preferred option. Current guidance also supports using it earlier when there is an inflammatory phenotype: C-reactive protein above 10 mg/L, fever or evidence of pericardial inflammation.

Tamponade is treated with pericardiocentesis, not an interleukin-1 blocker; the immediate problem is fluid compressing the heart. Anti-interleukin-1 therapy targets recurrent, colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent disease. Tell: an emergency of compression needs drainage first.
One with a normal C-reactive protein

A normal C-reactive protein argues against the inflammatory phenotype (C-reactive protein above 10 mg/L, fever or evidence of pericardial inflammation) that supports earlier anti-interleukin-1 therapy. Tell: candidates show more inflammation, not less; steroid dependence or colchicine resistance is the other route in.
One with a first, mild episode

A first episode is treated with high-dose nonsteroidal drugs until chest pain resolves and C-reactive protein normalizes, plus colchicine for 3 months. Anti-interleukin-1 therapy is for recurrent, colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent disease. Tell: a first, mild episode sits at the start of the pathway, not the end.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
B.q: A 66-year-old woman with viridans streptococcal endocarditis had positive blood cultures on days 1 and 2 and her first negative culture on day 4. She asks how long her antibiotics will last. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: Correct. Antibiotic therapy must be bactericidal and prolonged, typically 4-6 weeks counted from the first NEGATIVE culture. Her cultures were positive on days 1 and 2 and first negative on day 4, so day 4 starts the count, because all bacteria in the vegetation must be killed.

Admission day is not the anchor. The typical 4-6 weeks are counted from the first negative blood culture, which for her was day 4, not day 1. Tell: the days of positive cultures (days 1 and 2) do not count toward the course.

Fever resolution does not decide the length of therapy. The course is bactericidal, parenteral and prolonged, typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture, here day 4. Tell: the stopping point is set by time from culture clearance, not by how she feels.

Ten days falls far short of the typical 4-6 weeks, and the count runs from the first negative culture, not the first dose. Tell: endocarditis therapy is measured in weeks from culture clearance, because all bacteria in the vegetation must be killed.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
B.q: A 38-year-old woman has three months of worsening breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. Dilated cardiomyopathy is suspected, but her 12-lead electrocardiogram is completely normal. Which interpretation of the normal tracing is most accurate?
opts: It points to restrictive disease instead

A normal tracing does not point to any particular alternative; it only makes dilated cardiomyopathy unlikely, because that disease usually produces an abnormal electrocardiogram. Tell: a normal result lowers the probability of one diagnosis without naming another.
It is what most dilated cardiomyopathy shows

The opposite holds: the electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, with left ventricular hypertrophy, atrial fibrillation, premature ventricular contractions or conduction delays. Tell: usually abnormal means a normal tracing argues against the disease.
It excludes every cause of heart failure

A normal electrocardiogram speaks only to dilated cardiomyopathy, which it almost rules out; it cannot exclude every cause of heart failure. Her symptoms still need explaining with tests such as a blood count for anemia and thyroid function. Tell: one normal test narrows one diagnosis, not all of them.
It makes dilated cardiomyopathy very unlikely

Correct. The electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, with findings such as left ventricular hypertrophy, atrial fibrillation, premature ventricular contractions or left bundle branch block, so her completely normal tracing will almost rule it out. An echo with dilated, thin walls would be needed to support it.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
B.q: A 50-year-old woman with a diagnosed leg deep vein thrombosis, not yet treated, develops sudden shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. Which complication has occurred?
opts: Correct. Part of a deep vein thrombus can break off and travel to the lungs, causing a pulmonary embolism. Her untreated leg clot followed by sudden shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain fits that complication.

Post-thrombotic syndrome is not a sudden chest event; it develops in the leg over time after a clot. Sudden shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain in someone with an untreated leg clot point to a piece of thrombus traveling to the lungs.

Nothing in her story suggests a heart attack; the decisive clue is an untreated leg clot followed by sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. That sequence fits a fragment of thrombus breaking off and lodging in the lungs, a pulmonary embolism.

Septic thrombophlebitis is an infection within a superficial vein and would not explain sudden breathlessness and pleuritic pain. Her known, untreated deep vein thrombosis is the source, with part of the clot traveling to the lungs as a pulmonary embolism.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
B.q: A 75-year-old man is newly diagnosed with restrictive cardiomyopathy caused by hemochromatosis, with iron deposited in the heart tissue. He has congestion and fatigue. Which is the first principle of his management?
opts: Correct. Management of restrictive cardiomyopathy begins with treating the underlying disorder, here hemochromatosis. Diuretics are then used with caution for his congestion, beta blockers or verapamil and diltiazem may improve filling, and anticoagulants or a pacemaker are added as needed.

An inotrope is not on the restrictive cardiomyopathy list; the drugs used are cautious diuretics, beta blockers or cardioselective calcium channel blockers, and anticoagulants. The first principle is treating the underlying disorder. Tell: the listed drugs slow and relax the heart rather than push it harder.

Septal myectomy is not part of restrictive cardiomyopathy care; the steps are treating the underlying disorder, cautious diuretics, rate-slowing drugs, anticoagulants, a pacemaker and transplantation. Tell: his problem is iron in the heart muscle, so the cause is treated, not cut away.

A high-intensity exercise program does not treat hemochromatosis or the stiff ventricle. Management starts by treating the underlying disorder. Tell: he has a known cause, iron deposited in heart tissue, and the first principle is to treat it.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: A 67-year-old man has repeated dizziness and near-fainting while climbing stairs. His electrocardiogram shows the PR interval lengthening until a beat is dropped, in a repeating pattern. He takes no atrioventricular nodal blocking drugs, and no reversible cause is found. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Correct. A PR that lengthens until a beat drops is Mobitz type I, and his dizziness and near-fainting on stairs fit its symptoms, which usually appear when exertion induces the block. With no nodal blocking drugs or reversible cause, a permanent pacemaker is considered for this symptomatic patient.

Amiodarone is not used for Mobitz type I; it is an antiarrhythmic for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation. Symptomatic Mobitz type I with no reversible cause is managed with a permanent pacemaker. Tell: blocks are paced, not suppressed with antiarrhythmics.

Synchronized cardioversion terminates tachycardias with a pulse. His problem is a conduction block causing exertional symptoms, which is paced, not shocked. Tell: there is no fast rhythm here to convert.

Reassurance fits silent Mobitz type I. His repeated dizziness and near-fainting with exertion, with no reversible cause, make him a candidate for a permanent pacemaker. Tell: symptoms are what change the plan in type I.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
B.q: A 69-year-old man has sudden severe pain in his right leg. Pulses are absent below the knee. Which examination finding is often the earliest neurologic sign of acute vascular insufficiency?
opts: Sensory loss over the foot's dorsum

Correct. His sudden severe pain with absent pulses below the knee is acute limb ischemia. Light-touch sensory fibers are highly susceptible to ischemia, so sensory deficits over the dorsum of the foot are often the earliest neurologic sign of acute vascular insufficiency, which is why sensory testing is part of the examination.
Loss of hair on the shin

Hair loss is a chronic sign of peripheral artery disease, part of the loss of dermal appendages from long-standing poor flow, not a neurologic sign. In his sudden ischemia, the earliest neurologic sign is sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Chronic skin changes do not appear in hours.

Paralysis is a late finding; profound weakness with paralysis marks an irreversibly ischemic limb. The earliest neurologic sign is sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot, because light-touch fibers are most susceptible to ischemia. Early is sensory, late is motor.

Reflex testing is not named as the early sign. Light-touch sensory fibers are highly susceptible to ischemia, so loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot comes earliest. The examination emphasizes sensory and muscle strength testing.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
B.q: Idarucizumab is the reversal agent for which anticoagulant?
opts: Warfarin has its own reversal options: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, fresh frozen plasma or intravenous vitamin K, or oral vitamin K. Idarucizumab is not among them; it is specific to dabigatran.

Unfractionated heparin and low molecular weight heparin are both reversed by protamine sulfate in life-threatening bleeding. Idarucizumab plays no part in heparin reversal; its single partner is dabigatran.

Correct. Idarucizumab is the reversal agent for dabigatran when it causes life-threatening or intracranial hemorrhage, the most serious adverse effect of anticoagulation. Each anticoagulant group has its own reversal agent, so matching drug to antidote is the point.
Apixaban is reversed by andexanet alfa, the same agent used for rivaroxaban and off-label for edoxaban. Idarucizumab does not reverse apixaban; it is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: A 61-year-old woman with recurrent pericarditis over several years now has leg edema, ascites and an elevated jugular venous pressure. Constrictive pericarditis is suspected. Which echocardiogram finding would best support it?
opts: A dilated, weakly contracting ventricle is not among the echocardiographic features of constriction, which are increased pericardial thickness, septal bounce toward the left ventricle, pronounced respiratory variation in filling and moderate biatrial enlargement. Tell: constriction is recognized by how the pericardium and septum behave, not by a failing ventricle.

Asymmetric septal hypertrophy is not a feature of constriction. In constriction the septum moves abnormally, bouncing toward the left ventricle, and it is the pericardium that is thickened. Tell: a thick septum is a muscle finding; a bouncing septum with a thick pericardium is constriction.

Right ventricular diastolic collapse is not among the echocardiographic features of constriction. Those features are increased pericardial thickness, septal bounce toward the left ventricle, pronounced respiratory variation in filling and moderate biatrial enlargement, while subacute tamponade stays a separate diagnosis in the differential. Tell: pick the finding on the constriction list.
Septal bounce toward the left ventricle

Correct. Years of recurrent pericarditis, a listed antecedent of constriction, now with edema, ascites and an elevated jugular venous pressure fit constrictive pericarditis. A septal bounce toward the left ventricle is one of its echocardiographic features, along with increased pericardial thickness, pronounced respiratory variation in ventricular filling and moderate biatrial enlargement.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
B.q: After a positive D-dimer in the low likelihood Wells category, which test comes next?
opts: Contrast ascending venography is the definitive gold standard but has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound. After a positive D-dimer, ultrasound is the next test, not venography.

Repeating the D-dimer adds nothing, since the test is sensitive but not specific and a second positive would still not confirm a clot. The next step after a positive result is venous duplex ultrasound.

Stopping is the response to a negative D-dimer in the low-likelihood group, not a positive one. A positive result reflects increased fibrinolysis, which is not specific for a clot, so it must be followed by ultrasound.

Correct. In a low-likelihood patient, a negative D-dimer ends the work-up, but a positive one leads to ultrasound, because D-dimer is sensitive but not specific. A negative ultrasound then stops the evaluation, and venous duplex ultrasound has replaced contrast venography as the imaging test.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
B.q: A 44-year-old man arrives with a temperature of 40.2 °C (104.4 °F), rigors and a new murmur, and he looks toxic. Acute endocarditis is suspected. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Two cultures within 1-2 hours, then antibiotics

Correct. His temperature of 40.2 °C (104.4 °F), rigors and toxic appearance suggest acute endocarditis, so 2 blood cultures are drawn within the first 1-2 hours rather than over 24 hours. Empiric therapy then starts, but ONLY after the cultures have been drawn.

Observation without treatment is inappropriate for a toxic patient with suspected acute endocarditis. When the presentation suggests acute disease, 2 cultures are drawn within the first 1-2 hours and empiric antibiotics follow. Tell: a toxic presentation shortens the culture window to hours, not a day of watching.

Echocardiography is part of the workup, but it does not come before cultures in a toxic patient. Suspected acute disease calls for 2 cultures within the first 1-2 hours, then empiric antibiotics. Tell: cultures are the time-critical first step; imaging can follow.

Empiric therapy is started ONLY after blood cultures have been drawn, so antibiotics first with cultures tomorrow reverses the required order. Tell: in suspected acute disease, cultures are drawn within 1-2 hours and then antibiotics start, never the other way around.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
B.q: A 6-year-old with repaired congenital heart disease has 3 weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue, joint aches and weight loss. A new murmur is heard. Which organism most commonly causes endocarditis in this age group?
opts: Enterococci are less common in children than in adults and are not the leading organism after age 1. Children over 1 year with congenital heart disease develop indolent viridans group streptococcal disease. Tell: an indolent course in a child with congenital heart disease means viridans streptococci.

Candida is a neonatal and infant organism, tied to central venous catheters, hyperalimentation, neonatal intensive care and prematurity. A 6-year-old with an indolent course and repaired congenital heart disease fits viridans streptococci. Tell: Candida goes with the catheter-bearing infant.

Correct. Children over 1 year with congenital heart disease develop indolent viridans group streptococcal disease (Streptococcus sanguis, mitis, mutans), with Staphylococcus aureus next. This 6-year-old's 3 weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue, joint aches and weight loss is that indolent course.

Group B Streptococcus is a less common organism of neonates and infants under 1 year, not of a 6-year-old. Tell: after age 1 with congenital heart disease, viridans group streptococci dominate, while group B Streptococcus belongs on the newborn list.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
B.q: Which organism is a classic cause of acute infective endocarditis?
opts: Correct. Acute infective endocarditis is caused by virulent organisms: beta-hemolytic streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible or methicillin-resistant), sometimes Staphylococcus lugdunensis (a coagulase-negative staphylococcus), and enterococci. Staphylococcus aureus, a skin organism, is the classic acute cause.

Viridans streptococci are a subacute organism, listed with enterococci, coagulase-negative staphylococci and the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group, and they come from the oral cavity. Tell: viridans means subacute; Staphylococcus aureus means acute.

Streptococcus gallolyticus is the gastrointestinal tract organism, not one of the listed acute causes (beta-hemolytic streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus lugdunensis, enterococci). Tell: Streptococcus gallolyticus answers a bowel-source question, not an acute-course one.

The gram-negative coccobacilli of the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group are listed under subacute endocarditis and come from the upper respiratory tract. Tell: HACEK organisms are slow, subacute causes; Staphylococcus aureus is the acute one.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: An 81-year-old man has known tachy-brady syndrome (a fast rhythm alternating with slow rates and pauses) and asks which fast rhythm is behind his palpitations. An ambulatory monitor is arranged. Which rhythm is it most likely to record during the fast episodes?
opts: A junctional rhythm is a slow, regular rhythm usually at 40 to 60 with inverted or hidden P waves, and it can follow sinus arrest. It could appear in his slow phases, not his fast ones. Tell: junctional rhythm belongs to the brady side; atrial fibrillation is the usual tachy side.

Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in some patients with tachy-brady syndrome, who then need a permanent pacemaker with an implantable defibrillator. It is not the most common one; atrial fibrillation is. Tell: ventricular tachycardia changes the device, not the most likely rhythm.

Atrial flutter is an organized atrial rhythm with sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, but it is not the named most-common fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome. That is atrial fibrillation. Tell: in tachy-brady syndrome, expect an irregularly irregular fast phase, not a regular sawtooth.

Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome, the form of sick sinus syndrome in which a fast rhythm alternates with slow rates or pauses, the tachyarrhythmia is most commonly atrial fibrillation. During his fast episodes the monitor would most likely show an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: A 58-year-old man with acute pericarditis is starting ibuprofen and colchicine. He has a history of dyspepsia. Which addition to his regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Antibiotics have no part in the regimen for acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis, which is anti-inflammatory therapy with colchicine. His dyspepsia calls for gastrointestinal protection with a proton pump inhibitor. Tell: the add-on should guard against the anti-inflammatory drug's side effects, not treat an infection he does not have.

Correct. Ibuprofen and colchicine are the initial therapy for most acute pericarditis, and gastrointestinal protection is provided alongside anti-inflammatory treatment, for example a proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole. His history of dyspepsia makes that protection especially relevant.

Anticoagulation is not part of pericarditis therapy, and patients already on oral anticoagulants are a higher-risk group that may need hospitalization. His dyspepsia calls for gastrointestinal protection instead. Tell: an anticoagulant raises risk in pericarditis; a proton pump inhibitor lowers the risk of the anti-inflammatory drug.

Nothing in his presentation calls for diuresis, and diuretics are not part of the anti-inflammatory regimen for acute pericarditis. The addition that matches his dyspepsia is gastrointestinal protection with a proton pump inhibitor. Tell: tie the add-on to his stated risk, a sensitive stomach.

B.q: A 69-year-old man receiving an unfractionated heparin infusion for deep vein thrombosis develops life-threatening bleeding. Which agent reverses the heparin?
opts: Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban, with off-label use for edoxaban; it is not the antidote for heparin. His bleeding on an unfractionated heparin infusion is reversed with protamine sulfate.

Correct. He is on an unfractionated heparin (UFH) infusion and has life-threatening bleeding, the most serious adverse effect of anticoagulation. Protamine sulfate is the reversal agent for UFH and for low molecular weight heparin.

Oral vitamin K is one of the reversal options for warfarin, alongside prothrombin complex concentrate and fresh frozen plasma. He is bleeding on an unfractionated heparin infusion, which is reversed with protamine sulfate.
Idarucizumab is the reversal agent for dabigatran and does not reverse heparin. For life-threatening bleeding on an unfractionated heparin infusion, the reversal agent is protamine sulfate.

B.q: A 70-year-old man has an asymptomatic infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 3.4 cm on ultrasound. Which follow-up is most appropriate?
opts: Ultrasound or computed tomography every 6 to 12 months is for aneurysms of 4.0 to 5.4 cm. At 3.4 cm his aneurysm sits in the 3.0 to 3.9 cm band, imaged with ultrasound every three years. Check the size band before picking the interval.

Correct. Once identified, an aneurysm needs routine follow-up of size and growth rate, with frequency set by size. His asymptomatic 3.4 cm aneurysm is in the 3.0 to 3.9 cm band, which is imaged with ultrasound every three years.

Elective repair is advised at 5.0 cm or larger in women and over 5.5 cm in men, or with rapid growth of 0.5 cm in six months. A 3.4 cm asymptomatic aneurysm meets none of these. It needs ultrasound every three years.

Every identified aneurysm needs routine follow-up of size and growth rate. At 3.4 cm, that means ultrasound every three years. A small aneurysm still needs surveillance, so stopping imaging is not an option.

B.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
B.q: A 73-year-old man who lives at home has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and a new murmur. He has had no recent hospital stay, procedure or urinary symptoms, and no primary source of infection is found. Two separate blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis. How do these cultures count under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: A positive culture counts as the minor microbiologic criterion only when it does not meet the major criterion. Community-acquired enterococci without a primary focus are a typical organism, so two separate positive cultures meet the major criterion. Tell: typical organism plus two separate cultures equals major.

Correct. Community-acquired enterococci in the absence of a primary focus count as a typical organism for endocarditis. He lives at home, has had no hospital stay, procedure or urinary source, and two separate cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis, so the major blood culture criterion is met.

Only single positive cultures of coagulase-negative staphylococci or diphtheroids, or of organisms that rarely cause endocarditis, are excluded as contaminants. Enterococcus faecalis in two separate cultures is a typical organism. Tell: two separate cultures of a typical organism are never dismissed.

Blood cultures count on their own. Echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement is a separate major criterion, not a prerequisite for the culture criterion. Tell: each major criterion stands independently, and these cultures already meet one.

B.q: A 52-year-old man who smokes and has diabetes and hypertension asks whether he is too young to have peripheral artery disease. Which age threshold applies to him?
opts: Seventy is later than either age threshold. With risk factors such as smoking, diabetes and hypertension, peripheral artery disease is a concern from age 50; without them, from over 60. At 52 with three risk factors, he is already past his threshold.

Over 60 is the threshold for people without other risk factors. His smoking, diabetes and hypertension lower the threshold to age 50, so at 52 he already qualifies. Risk factors move the age down by a decade.

Correct. Age is a risk factor for peripheral artery disease at over 60 without other risk factors, or at 50 with risk factors such as smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, sedentary lifestyle or obesity. At 52 with smoking, diabetes and hypertension, he is not too young.

A family history of peripheral artery disease, cardiovascular disease or stroke is a risk factor, but 40 is not a stated age threshold, and the stem gives no family history. The thresholds are 50 with risk factors and over 60 without. His age of 52 already qualifies.

B.q: A 64-year-old woman has two weeks of exertional breathlessness and chest pressure. Her electrocardiogram shows a left bundle branch block; a tracing from last year was normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. A left bundle branch block absent a year ago is new, and a new left bundle branch block should always be considered a sign of pathology, an ST-elevation myocardial infarction equivalent. With exertional breathlessness and chest pressure, she needs evaluation for underlying heart disease rather than reassurance.

Synchronized cardioversion terminates tachycardias; a conduction block is not shocked. A new left bundle branch block is a sign of pathology that needs evaluation for heart disease. Tell: there is no fast rhythm to convert.

Some new right bundle branch blocks occur without heart disease, but a new left bundle branch block is always considered a sign of pathology. With new exertional symptoms, she needs evaluation, not reassurance. Tell: a new right block can be benign; a new left block never is.

A pacemaker is not the next step: left bundle branch block is usually left untreated, and a biventricular pacer is reserved for symptomatic block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Her new block first needs evaluation for underlying disease. Tell: evaluate before any device.

B.q: A 70-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has three months of progressive hoarseness. A chest radiograph shows widening of the mediastinal shadow. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: An abdominal aortic aneurysm causes abdominal, back or flank pain and cannot widen the mediastinal shadow or affect the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Her hoarseness and mediastinal widening place the aneurysm in the chest, at the arch. The chest film finding rules out the abdomen.

A descending thoracic aneurysm compresses the trachea or esophagus, causing dyspnea, stridor, wheezing, cough or dysphagia. Her symptom is hoarseness, which localizes the aneurysm to the arch through the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Match the symptom to the segment.

Correct. Thoracic aneurysm symptoms depend on location, and an arch aneurysm causes hoarseness through the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Her long-standing hypertension is the common history, and the widened mediastinal shadow on chest radiograph is a typical finding.

An ascending thoracic aneurysm causes aortic regurgitation and heart failure rather than hoarseness. Her progressive hoarseness localizes the aneurysm to the arch, where it involves the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Valve problems point to the ascending aorta.

B.q: A 27-year-old woman has had 20 minutes of sudden palpitations. Her heart rate is 188, blood pressure 122/76, and she is alert with no chest pain or breathlessness. The electrocardiogram shows a regular narrow complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. Which is the most appropriate first step?
opts: Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 122/76 and no chest pain or breathlessness, so she is stable. Tell: a fast rate alone is not instability; look at blood pressure and mental status.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; it is not a first step. Her rhythm is regular and narrow with no pre-excitation described. Tell: a stable regular narrow tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver.

Correct. A sudden, regular narrow complex tachycardia at 188 with no visible P waves is supraventricular tachycardia, and with a blood pressure of 122/76, a clear mind and no chest pain or breathlessness she is stable. A vagal maneuver is first line, followed by adenosine, which may slow the rhythm enough to show P waves.

Adenosine is the second step for stable supraventricular tachycardia, given if a vagal maneuver fails, and it may be repeated once. The question asks for the first step, which needs no drug. Tell: vagal maneuver first, then adenosine.

B.q: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes has nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and a high CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) score. Which anticoagulant class is preferred?
opts: Warfarin can be used, with a target international normalized ratio (INR) of 2 to 3, but it is not the preferred class. In nonvalvular atrial fibrillation the direct oral anticoagulants are preferred. Tell: preferred means a direct oral anticoagulant; warfarin is the alternative with its own target range.

Aspirin is not among the anticoagulants listed for atrial fibrillation, and it appears on the HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score as a medication that predisposes to bleeding. Her high stroke-risk score calls for anticoagulation, preferably a direct oral anticoagulant. Tell: aspirin adds bleeding risk without being the recommended stroke protection.

Her age adds to stroke risk rather than ruling out anticoagulation: 75 or older scores 2 points on the stroke-risk score. With a high score, patients typically require anticoagulation unless bleeding risk is high, a HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score of 3 or more. Tell: only a high bleeding score withholds anticoagulation, not age itself.

Correct. Her CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score is high (age 75 or older 2, female 1, hypertension 1, diabetes 1 = 5), so she typically requires anticoagulation unless bleeding risk is high. In nonvalvular atrial fibrillation the direct oral anticoagulants (dabigatran, apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) are preferred.

B.q: An 81-year-old man with 3 months of weight loss presents with dyspnea and a large pericardial effusion. He has had no recent viral illness, chest surgery or radiation. Which etiology should be most strongly suspected?
opts: Nothing in his story points to rheumatic disease, and at 81 with weight loss and a large effusion the age-specific guidance is a higher index of suspicion for malignancy. Tell: older age plus a large effusion plus weight loss points to cancer.

Correct. In older adults there is a higher index of suspicion for malignancy, especially with an effusion or tamponade. At 81, with 3 months of weight loss, a large effusion and no viral illness, surgery or radiation to explain it, malignancy is the cause to pursue.

He has had no recent viral illness, so a viral cause has nothing to anchor it. In an older adult with a large effusion and 3 months of weight loss, suspicion for malignancy is higher. Tell: the stem removes the usual explanations (virus, surgery, radiation) to leave cancer.
ruled out by a stated finding

His history contains no recent chest surgery and no cardiac event, so there is no trigger for Dressler syndrome. Older adults with an effusion warrant a higher index of suspicion for malignancy, and his weight loss reinforces it. Tell: without a preceding cardiac injury, Dressler syndrome is off the table.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.q: A 61-year-old woman has scleroderma with Raynaud phenomenon, acid reflux, osteoporosis and long-standing pulmonary hypertension. Her electrocardiogram shows a right bundle branch block. Which of her conditions is a named cause of this block?
opts: Raynaud phenomenon is not a listed cause of right bundle branch block. Of her conditions, only long-standing pulmonary hypertension is named. Tell: the listed causes are degeneration, ischemic heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary embolism, cardiomyopathies and myocarditis or amyloidosis.

Osteoporosis is not a listed cause of right bundle branch block. Long-standing pulmonary hypertension, which she also has, is. Tell: look among her conditions for the one that loads the right side of the heart.

Acid reflux is not among the causes of right bundle branch block. Of her conditions, long-standing pulmonary hypertension is the named one. Tell: a gastrointestinal condition cannot explain a right-sided conduction block.

Correct. Pulmonary hypertension is a named cause of right bundle branch block, alongside a sudden rise in right ventricular pressure from pulmonary embolism, ischemic heart disease, cardiomyopathies and degeneration. Her Raynaud phenomenon, reflux and osteoporosis are not on the list, and treatment depends on the underlying condition.

B.q: A 32-year-old man has typical acute viral pericarditis with stable vital signs and no high-risk features. A transthoracic echocardiogram is ordered. Which result is most expected?
opts: A normal study or only a small effusion

Correct. In typical acute viral pericarditis with stable vital signs and no high-risk features, the echocardiogram is often normal unless there is an associated effusion, so a normal study or a small effusion is expected. The chest radiograph is typically normal too, and most such patients need no invasive workup.
Apical ballooning with a normal base

Apical ballooning is not a finding of acute pericarditis, where the echocardiogram is often normal unless an effusion is present. Tell: in uncomplicated pericarditis, expect a normal study or a little fluid, not a wall-motion abnormality.
A thick pericardium with septal bounce

A thickened pericardium with septal bounce is not what a first, uncomplicated episode shows; in acute pericarditis the echocardiogram is often normal unless an effusion is present. Tell: a stable patient with typical, low-risk disease should have an unremarkable study.

Right ventricular diastolic collapse is not expected in a stable patient with typical, low-risk disease; the echocardiogram in acute pericarditis is often normal unless an effusion is present. Cardiac tamponade, when it does occur, is an indication for pericardiocentesis. Tell: stable vital signs and no high-risk features predict a normal study.

B.q: A 24-year-old woman with chest pain and breathlessness after a recent viral illness is being evaluated for myocarditis. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia. Which laboratory result would indicate cardiac myonecrosis?
opts: A natriuretic peptide is not the listed myonecrosis marker, and a low value would indicate nothing abnormal. Serum troponin is the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis in the myocarditis work-up. Tell: necrosis raises a marker, and the one named for heart muscle is troponin.

The blood count in myocarditis shows leukocytosis, a raised white cell count, not a low one, and it does not measure heart muscle injury. Serum troponin indicates cardiac myonecrosis. Tell: leukocytosis is the expected count; troponin is the necrosis marker.

Correct. In this young woman with chest pain and breathlessness after a viral illness, serum troponin is the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis. Her sinus tachycardia fits the electrocardiogram of myocarditis, and the rest of the work-up looks for leukocytosis and a possibly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

The erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated in myocarditis, so a normal value is not the expected finding, and either way it is not the myonecrosis marker. Serum troponin is the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis. Tell: a normal result cannot indicate necrosis.

B.q: A 20-year-old man has just been diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on echocardiography. He has two younger sisters and a brother. His mother had unexplained sudden death at 44. Which step for his family is most appropriate?
opts: Most hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so each of his siblings may carry the mutation, in a disease that carries a high incidence of sudden death. Tell: his mother's unexplained sudden death at 44 suggests the family already shows the pattern.

Autosomal dominant inheritance does not spare males; in fact males are affected more often than females. His brother needs evaluation as much as his sisters. Tell: males outnumber females in this disease, so leaving out his brother is the worst possible choice.

Waiting for symptoms is risky in a disease that carries a high incidence of sudden death and is the leading cause of sudden death in preadolescent and adolescent children. His siblings should be evaluated now. Tell: in an inherited disease with sudden death, the family is evaluated before symptoms appear.

Correct. Most cases of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, in which one copy of the mutated gene from an affected parent is sufficient to cause the condition. His diagnosis and his mother's unexplained sudden death at 44 make evaluation of his siblings the right step.

B.q: A 70-year-old woman has Mobitz type II block found on a routine tracing; she has no symptoms. Her family prefers to avoid procedures. Which approach should be avoided?
opts: Referral to cardiology is appropriate, since a permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment. The approach to avoid is simple observation of Mobitz type II, which is dangerous even without symptoms. Tell: referral moves toward the right treatment, so it is not the one to avoid.

A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II, so it is the approach to pursue, not avoid. Observation alone is what should be avoided. Tell: the question asks which option is unsafe.

Correct. Observation without pacing should be avoided: Mobitz type II is considered dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression to complete block and poor prognosis, with a higher risk of sudden cardiac death. The definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker, even for a symptom-free patient.

Reviewing her medication list is reasonable and harmless. What should be avoided is observation without a pacemaker, because Mobitz type II is dangerous even without symptoms. Tell: the question asks which step to avoid, and a safe, sensible step never fits that.

B.q: Adenosine slows a tachycardia and reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Which drug is used?
opts: A repeat dose of adenosine is allowed for ordinary stable supraventricular tachycardia, but once atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White is revealed, adenosine must never be used. Intravenous procainamide takes its place. Tell: the moment a pre-excited atrial fibrillation appears, adenosine is off the table.

Intravenous magnesium is not the listed drug for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. When adenosine slows a tachycardia and reveals this combination, intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is not repeated. Tell: pre-excited atrial fibrillation has one named drug answer, procainamide.

Correct. Slowing from adenosine has unmasked atrial fibrillation conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White, and in that setting intravenous procainamide is used, never adenosine. The same rule applies whenever Wolff-Parkinson-White is already known; adenosine stays first line only for ordinary orthodromic reentry.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. This patient has a fast atrial fibrillation conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White, the opposite problem, which is treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: atropine is for a slow rate; procainamide is for pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

B.q: A 68-year-old man is 4 days into his recovery from a large anterior myocardial infarction when he suddenly becomes hypotensive, with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. Which is the most likely explanation?
opts: Constrictive pericarditis develops when acute, chronic or relapsing pericarditis leaves pericardial fibrosis, with progressive exertional dyspnea, edema and ascites, not sudden collapse on day 4. His abrupt Beck triad signals tamponade. Tell: sudden and catastrophic means fluid; slow and progressive means a scarred sac.

Dressler syndrome is pericarditis after myocardial infarction and presents like other pericarditis, with pleuritic, positional chest pain and possibly a rub. Sudden hypotension with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds on day 4 is the Beck triad of tamponade from a mechanical complication. Tell: pain and a rub suggest pericarditis; abrupt collapse suggests rupture.

Nothing points to a clot; muffled heart sounds belong to fluid around the heart, and free-wall rupture after infarction is a listed cause of tamponade that fits day 4 after a large infarction. Tell: muffled heart sounds with distended neck veins and hypotension complete the Beck triad of tamponade.

Correct. Sudden hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds are the Beck triad of tamponade, and 4 days after a large myocardial infarction the listed cause that fits is free-wall rupture. Rapidly accumulating fluid causes tamponade early because the pericardium cannot stretch to accommodate it.

B.q: Which electrical treatment is delivered for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is used for unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. Polymorphic tachycardia is defibrillated (unsynchronized) instead, because it is never truly stable. Tell: monomorphic with a pulse gets synchronized; polymorphic gets unsynchronized.

Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, even when the patient looks fine, because it is a short-lived transitional state. It is treated with defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion), followed by urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization.

Transcutaneous pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms such as Mobitz type II or complete block, not a fast ventricular rhythm. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is treated with defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion). Tell: pace the slow, shock the fast.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, even if the patient looks well; it is a short-lived transitional state. So there is no drug trial first: the patient is defibrillated, and intravenous metoprolol or amiodarone may be added. Tell: drugs-first fits stable monomorphic tachycardia only.

B.q: A 71-year-old woman hospitalized after surgery has had a peripheral intravenous catheter in her arm for a week. She has a high fever, fluctuance over a tender vein, and redness spreading well past the vein. Which is the most appropriate approach?
opts: Treat as infection within the vein

Correct. High fever, fluctuance and erythema extending significantly beyond the vein margin suggest infection within the vein, suppurative or septic thrombophlebitis. Her week-long peripheral catheter is the expected setting, since septic thrombophlebitis is uncommon without a history of venous cannulation.
Compresses and ibuprofen with a recheck in 7 to 10 days

A routine plan of compresses, an anti-inflammatory drug and a later recheck treats the vein as simply inflamed. Her high fever, fluctuance and redness spreading well past the vein suggest infection within the vein, septic thrombophlebitis, so it must be managed as an infection.

Anticoagulation alone addresses clot, not infection, and her findings point to infection: high fever, fluctuance and erythema extending well beyond the vein suggest septic thrombophlebitis. Fever and fluctuance are the clues that separate infection from a sterile clot.
Reassure that the process is self-limited

Reassurance ignores three warning signs: high fever, fluctuance and redness spreading well beyond the vein, which together suggest septic thrombophlebitis. Her week of intravenous cannulation makes that infection plausible, since it is uncommon without such a history.

B.q: A 79-year-old man has enterococcal endocarditis of the aortic valve after recurrent urinary infections. Which outcome is he at notable risk for?
opts: Septic lung emboli are not the outcome singled out for enterococcal endocarditis; embolic occlusion of larger peripheral arteries is the complication highlighted for fungal disease. Enterococci are difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance. Tell: enterococci mean resistance and valve surgery in about 30-40%.

Correct. His enterococcal aortic valve endocarditis is difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance, and major complications with need for valve replacement occur in about 30-40% of patients. Needing heart surgery is the notable risk for this organism.

Spontaneous cure is not described for endocarditis, and enterococcal disease in particular is difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance. Tell: enterococcal disease is the one tied to resistance and a 30-40% rate of major complications and valve replacement.

The lowest death rate is not an enterococcal feature. Viridans streptococci carry a relatively good prognosis when treated early, while enterococci are difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance. Tell: enterococci mean resistance and valve replacement in about 30-40%.
