Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 64-year-old man in atrial flutter has a heart rate of 150, a blood pressure of 70/40, and is confused. Which is the next step?
opts: Oral rate control is not the step for unstable flutter; it is stable flutter that is rate controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker. His blood pressure of 70/40 and confusion make him unstable. Tell: hypotension and confusion take rate control off the table and call for synchronized cardioversion.

Twenty-one days of anticoagulation precedes an elective outpatient cardioversion of stable flutter. He is hypotensive and confused now and cannot wait three weeks. Tell: unstable means cardioversion now; stable means anticoagulation first for an elective cardioversion.

A vagal maneuver is first line for stable supraventricular tachycardia, not for unstable flutter. His blood pressure of 70/40 and confusion call for synchronized cardioversion. Tell: unstable atrial flutter goes straight to a synchronized shock.

Correct. Atrial flutter at 150 with a blood pressure of 70/40 and confusion is hemodynamically unstable, and unstable atrial flutter is treated with synchronized cardioversion. Flutter usually does not cause hemodynamic collapse, so instability like this calls for a prompt shock.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 71-year-old woman admitted with stress cardiomyopathy after a house fire has a repeat echocardiogram that shows a thrombus in the akinetic left ventricular apex. She is in sinus rhythm. Which treatment is now indicated?
opts: A nitrate infusion is not part of the Takotsubo plan and does not treat a thrombus. The supportive options are beta blockers, anticoagulation if a left ventricular thrombus is present, and diuretics if heart failure is present. Tell: her new finding is a clot, and clot means anticoagulation.

A pacemaker is not indicated: she is in sinus rhythm, and nothing suggests a conduction problem. The new finding is a left ventricular thrombus, and Takotsubo care adds anticoagulation when a thrombus is present. Tell: match the treatment to the finding, thrombus to anticoagulant.

Correct. Treatment of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is empiric and supportive and depends on the presentation, and a thrombus in her akinetic left ventricular apex is the finding that calls for anticoagulation. Beta blockers are helpful, and diuretics are added only if heart failure is present; most patients completely recover.

Surgical myectomy is not part of Takotsubo care; treatment is empiric and supportive. Her thrombus in the akinetic apex is treated with anticoagulation. Tell: the new finding is a ventricular clot, and the supportive plan answers it with anticoagulation.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
C.q: A 26-year-old woman had a peripherally inserted central catheter placed in her right arm two weeks ago for long-term antibiotic therapy. She reports aching and swelling of the arm. Examination shows diffuse swelling of the entire right upper arm with mild redness, and there is no palpable cord and no purulent drainage. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Venous duplex ultrasound of the arm

Correct. Upper extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT) often presents only with limb swelling and arm discomfort, which is her picture: diffuse swelling of the whole upper arm two weeks after a catheter was placed. With no cord or purulence to suggest a superficial process, imaging the arm veins with duplex ultrasound confirms or excludes the clot.

Treating symptoms with compresses and ibuprofen skips the question that matters, whether the swollen arm holds a deep clot. She has no palpable cord, and swelling of the entire upper arm with aching is the usual presentation of upper extremity deep vein thrombosis.

Cellulitis brings painful erythema and may be accompanied by fever and chills; she has only mild redness and no fever is described. Diffuse aching swelling of the whole arm two weeks after catheter placement fits upper extremity deep vein thrombosis, which needs imaging, not antibiotics.

Reassurance and elevation would leave a possible deep clot undiagnosed. Upper extremity deep vein thrombosis often presents only with limb swelling and arm discomfort, exactly her complaint, so the arm must be imaged first.

C.q: A 45-year-old woman with varicose veins has a small, tender, red cord along the great saphenous vein of the calf. Venous duplex ultrasound confirms a short segment of superficial clot. She has no other risk factors for thrombosis. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: An inferior vena cava filter is not part of the care of superficial thrombophlebitis, which rarely embolizes. Her short clot with no other risk factors is treated with warm compresses, compression, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug such as ibuprofen.

Nothing here suggests infection: she has a small, tender, red cord confirmed as a short superficial clot. Superficial thrombophlebitis is treated with warm compresses, compression, elevation and anti-inflammatory drugs, not antibiotics.

Correct. Her clot is a short superficial segment, she has no other thrombotic risk factors, and superficial thrombophlebitis rarely embolizes or causes serious complications. Typical treatment is warm compresses, compression, elevation and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) such as ibuprofen, with anticoagulation kept for extensive clot or higher risk.

Thrombolysis is not used for superficial thrombophlebitis, which rarely causes serious complications and rarely embolizes. A short superficial clot without other risk factors gets warm compresses, compression, elevation and ibuprofen or diclofenac.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 33-year-old man has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 190 with hidden P waves. He is alert with a blood pressure of 128/80. A properly performed vagal maneuver does not change the rhythm. Which is the next step?
opts: Intravenous magnesium is not part of the sequence for stable supraventricular tachycardia, which runs vagal maneuver, then adenosine. With the vagal maneuver failed, adenosine is the next step. Tell: in stable supraventricular tachycardia, the drug after a failed vagal maneuver is adenosine.

Correct. He is stable, alert with a blood pressure of 128/80, and his regular narrow tachycardia at 190 with hidden P waves has not responded to a proper vagal maneuver. Adenosine is next and may be repeated once; it may convert the rhythm to normal sinus rhythm or slow it enough to show whether P waves are there.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. His rhythm is fast at 190, the opposite problem. Tell: atropine is for slow rates; a stable supraventricular tachycardia after a failed vagal maneuver gets adenosine.

Synchronized cardioversion is immediate treatment for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia. He is alert with a blood pressure of 128/80, so he is stable and moves from the vagal maneuver to adenosine. Tell: a failed vagal maneuver does not by itself make a patient unstable.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 67-year-old woman is recovering in hospital from stress cardiomyopathy that followed news of her son's serious illness. Her chest pain has resolved, and she asks whether her heart will stay damaged. Which answer about her prognosis is most accurate?
opts: Correct. Most patients with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy completely recover. Care in hospital is empiric and supportive, with beta blockers, anticoagulation if a left ventricular thrombus is present and diuretics if heart failure is present, so she can be told her heart is expected to recover.

Takotsubo does not routinely progress to heart failure; diuretics are used only if heart failure is present, and most patients completely recover. Tell: always is the giveaway, since the expected course is recovery.

The poorest outlook is the opposite of the Takotsubo course: most patients completely recover. Tell: her resolved chest pain and supportive treatment fit a syndrome with an expected full recovery, which answers her worry about lasting damage.

Half dying within five years is not the Takotsubo outlook; most patients completely recover after empiric, supportive treatment. Tell: Takotsubo is the cardiomyopathy with the good prognosis, which is the answer to her question.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 31-year-old woman has inappropriate sinus tachycardia at about 110 after a full workup excluded other causes. Her only symptom is awareness of her heartbeat, and she asks whether she needs medication. Which response is most accurate?
opts: She needs a lifelong beta blocker

Beta blockers are not well tolerated in inappropriate sinus tachycardia, which is why it is generally left untreated. Her only symptom is awareness of her heartbeat. Tell: patients tolerate the symptoms better than the treatment, so a lifelong drug is not the usual plan.

Anticoagulation belongs to atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a sinus rhythm with a usually benign prognosis, and anticoagulation is not part of its management. Tell: a sinus rhythm, even a fast one, does not bring an anticoagulation decision.

Correct. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is generally left untreated because patients tolerate the symptoms better than the treatment and the prognosis is usually benign. Management centers on removing influencing factors, such as night-shift work, illicit drugs and medications, rather than on beta blockers, which are poorly tolerated.

Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias such as supraventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter or atrial fibrillation. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a sinus rhythm in a stable patient and is generally left untreated. Tell: a sinus rhythm is not shocked; management is removing influencing factors.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: A 62-year-old woman with suspected tamponade undergoes right heart catheterization before drainage. Which pressure finding is expected?
opts: An isolated high left atrial pressure

An isolated rise in one chamber does not fit tamponade, where elevated intrapericardial pressure compresses cardiac filling and catheterization shows equal pressures in all chambers. Tell: tamponade affects every chamber at once, so look for equalization, not a single high reading.

Right-sided pressure is high, not low, in tamponade: the jugular venous pressure is greatly elevated and the neck veins are distended as part of the Beck triad. Catheterization shows equal pressures in all chambers. Tell: distended neck veins mean a high right atrial pressure.

Correct. Cardiac catheterization in tamponade shows equalization of pressures in all chambers of the heart. Elevated intrapericardial pressure compresses filling of every chamber, which also explains the greatly elevated jugular venous pressure and the venous waveform with a prominent x descent and absent y descent.
A gradient across the aortic valve

A gradient across the aortic valve is not a feature of tamponade, in which pericardial fluid mechanically impairs diastolic filling rather than obstructing outflow. Catheterization shows equalization of pressures in all chambers. Tell: tamponade is a diastolic, all-chamber problem; a single valve gradient points elsewhere.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 76-year-old woman has episodes of lightheadedness and one faint. A 24-hour ambulatory monitor shows runs of a fast, irregular rhythm that alternate with slow rates and long pauses. Which fast rhythm is most likely on her monitor?
opts: Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a regular narrow tachycardia, usually 140 to 180, typically in women without heart disease. Her fast runs are irregular and alternate with slow rates and pauses, the pattern of tachy-brady syndrome. Tell: irregular fast runs plus pauses in an older patient point to atrial fibrillation.

Correct. Runs of a fast, irregular rhythm alternating with slow rates and long pauses, with lightheadedness and a faint, are tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sick sinus syndrome. The tachyarrhythmia in tachy-brady syndrome is most commonly atrial fibrillation, which fits an irregular fast run.

Sinus tachycardia is regular with a uniform P wave before every QRS. Her fast runs are irregular, and in tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm is most commonly atrial fibrillation. Tell: an irregular fast phase alternating with pauses is not sinus; it is atrial fibrillation until proven otherwise.

Ventricular fibrillation is not the listed fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome, and she has recurring runs she lives through between slow spells. The tachyarrhythmia there is most commonly atrial fibrillation; ventricular tachycardia occurs in some patients and calls for a pacemaker with a defibrillator. Tell: recurring irregular fast runs with pauses are atrial fibrillation.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: Why is renal function checked in peripheral artery disease?
opts: Homocysteine is an amino acid, and an elevated level is a risk factor linked to earlier-onset atherosclerosis; it is not what a renal test measures. Renal function is checked because patients with peripheral artery disease are at risk for renal insufficiency. The reason is kidney risk.

Kidney stones are not the concern named. Renal function is checked because patients with peripheral artery disease are at risk for renal insufficiency. The worry is reduced kidney function, not stone formation.

Claudication is graded by history and the ankle-brachial index, not by kidney tests. Renal function is checked because these patients are at risk for renal insufficiency. The renal panel answers a different question.

Correct. Patients with peripheral artery disease are at risk for renal insufficiency, so renal function is part of the work-up, alongside an electrocardiogram, complete blood count, lipid profile, metabolic panel, fasting glucose and hemoglobin A1c, which reflects average glucose over three months.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: A 72-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has a routine electrocardiogram. The QRS is 0.16 seconds wide, with a dominant S wave in V1, a broad single-peaked R wave in leads I, V5 and V6, and no Q waves in those leads. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds (here 0.16) with a dominant S wave in V1, a broad monophasic R in I, V5 and V6 and no Q waves in those leads is left bundle branch block. The left ventricle is activated by current crossing the septum from the right, and chronic hypertension, his long-standing condition, is a named cause.

Right bundle branch block gives an rsR' pattern ('bunny ears') in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL, not a dominant S in V1. His pattern is left bundle branch block. Tell: a deep S in V1 means left.

Ventricular tachycardia is a fast rhythm of 100 to 250 with no P waves. A routine tracing with a wide QRS, a dominant S in V1 and monophasic lateral R waves is left bundle branch block. Tell: a wide QRS at a normal rate is a bundle branch block.

First-degree block lengthens the PR interval with a narrow QRS. His QRS is 0.16 seconds with a dominant S in V1 and monophasic lateral R waves, which is left bundle branch block. Tell: first degree changes the PR; a bundle branch block widens the QRS.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 41-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy also has enlarged hilar lymph nodes and skin nodules, and an infiltrative process such as sarcoidosis is suspected. Coronary angiography showed no disease. Which imaging test best identifies an inflammatory or infiltrative cause?
opts: Ambulatory rhythm monitoring for forty-eight hours

Rhythm monitoring records arrhythmias and cannot show infiltration of the heart muscle. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium identifies inflammatory, ischemic or infiltrative processes such as sarcoidosis. Tell: the question asks for imaging of tissue, which gadolinium imaging provides.
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium

Correct. Sarcoidosis is suspected, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium contrast is helpful in identifying inflammatory, ischemic or infiltrative processes such as sarcoidosis or hemochromatosis in dilated cardiomyopathy. Endocardial biopsy is rarely useful but may be considered for systemic disease with possible cardiac involvement.
A repeat resting electrocardiogram in six months

Repeating the electrocardiogram in six months delays the answer and cannot characterize heart tissue. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium contrast helps identify infiltrative processes such as sarcoidosis now. Tell: suspected sarcoid infiltration calls for gadolinium-enhanced imaging.

Catheterization does not identify inflammation or infiltration, and her coronary angiography is already done. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium contrast identifies inflammatory, ischemic or infiltrative processes such as sarcoidosis or hemochromatosis. Tell: infiltration is shown by enhanced imaging, not by pressures.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 24-year-old man whose Wolff-Parkinson-White was found on a school electrocardiogram presents with palpitations. The rhythm is irregular and wide-complex, at rates up to 260, with varying delta waves (slurred upstrokes). He is alert with a blood pressure of 118/74. Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Correct. An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia up to 260 with varying delta waves in a man with known Wolff-Parkinson-White is atrial fibrillation conducting over the accessory pathway. When Wolff-Parkinson-White is known, intravenous procainamide is used, never adenosine; he is alert with a normal blood pressure, so a drug is appropriate.

Atropine is the first-line drug for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia. This man has a very fast, irregular rhythm conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White, the opposite problem, so atropine has no role. Tell: atropine is for slow rates; known Wolff-Parkinson-White with a fast rhythm calls for procainamide.

Intravenous magnesium is not the listed treatment for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Irregular, wide complexes with varying delta waves in a patient with a known accessory pathway call for intravenous procainamide. Tell: known Wolff-Parkinson-White plus a fast irregular rhythm means procainamide.

Adenosine must never be used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White is present; it is first line only for ordinary orthodromic reentry. His irregular, wide, delta-wave complexes in known Wolff-Parkinson-White are exactly that exception. Tell: an irregular wide rhythm with delta waves rules adenosine out.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: A 70-year-old man had 20 minutes of weakness and numbness in his right hand four months ago that fully resolved. Duplex ultrasonography shows 75% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. A friend with no symptoms was told surgery waits until stenosis passes 80%, and he asks whether the same applies to him. Which response is accurate?
opts: Yes; resolved symptoms do not count

A transient ischemic attack resolves by definition, lasting under 24 hours, yet it still counts. Asymptomatic means no ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack within the last six months, and his attack four months ago makes him symptomatic. Full recovery does not reset his status.

Correct. His 20 minutes of hand weakness and numbness was a transient ischemic attack (a focal loss of neurologic function lasting under 24 hours) within the last six months, so he is symptomatic. Surgery is advised for symptomatic stenosis over 70%, which his 75% meets; the over-80% rule is for asymptomatic patients.

Over 80%, with a life expectancy over five years, is the threshold for asymptomatic stenosis like his friend's. His transient ischemic attack four months ago, within the last six months, makes him symptomatic, so the over-70% threshold applies, and his 75% stenosis qualifies. Symptom status changes the number.
No; he needs medical therapy only

Medical management alone is advised for low-grade stenosis under 50%. At 75% with a transient ischemic attack four months ago, he is symptomatic and meets the over-70% threshold for surgery. His stenosis is well above the medical-only range.

C.q: A 50-year-old man with acute pericarditis says the pain keeps him awake because it is worse when he lies down. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Keep the head of the bed elevated

Correct. Pericardial pain is worse when supine, which is why lying down keeps him awake, and keeping the head of the bed elevated is part of follow-up counseling. That advice sits with adherence to the full treatment course, activity restriction and recognizing red-flag symptoms.
Sleep prone to splint the chest

Sleeping prone is not advised for pericardial pain; the recommendation is to keep the head of the bed elevated, because the pain worsens when lying flat. Tell: the fix for pain that is worse supine is to sit him up, not to turn him over.
Sleep flat to rest the heart

Lying flat is exactly what worsens pericardial pain, so sleeping flat would keep him awake. Counseling advises keeping the head of the bed elevated. Tell: pain worse when supine means raise the head of the bed, never lower it.
Take an extra dose at bedtime

Changing the dose on his own is not advised; counseling stresses the prescribed full treatment course and medication side effects. His pain is positional, worse when supine, and keeping the head of the bed elevated addresses that directly. Tell: positional pain gets a positional fix.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: Where do atherosclerotic lesions most often form?
opts: In the smallest arterioles of the skin

Atherosclerosis affects intermediate and large arteries, such as the coronary, cerebral, carotid and femoral arteries and the aorta, not the smallest skin arterioles. Lesions favor arterial bifurcations and sites of increased turbulence. Vessel size is the first clue.
In straight segments with laminar flow

Lesions do not favor smooth, straight segments; they form at arterial bifurcations and at sites of increased turbulence. Branch points and disturbed flow are where plaques start, developing over many decades. Turbulence, not laminar flow, is the setting.
In the veins draining the lower legs

Atherosclerosis is a disease of intermediate and large arteries, not veins. Its lesions form at arterial bifurcations and sites of increased turbulence. Leg veins belong to venous disease, a different process.
At branch points and turbulent sites

Correct. Atherosclerotic lesions often form at arterial bifurcations (branching) and at sites of increased turbulence, and they develop over many decades. Plaque can lead to stenosis, thrombus can form at the plaque site, and atheroemboli can originate from it.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
C.q: When are palliative care discussions raised for elderly patients with cardiomyopathy?
opts: The first visit is too early; palliative care discussions for the elderly are placed in advanced stages of disease. Earlier care focuses on tailored therapy, cautious diuretics and vasodilators, and symptom control. Tell: the timing word is advanced.

Palliative care discussions are explicitly part of elderly cardiomyopathy care, held in advanced stages, and palliative care also covers advance care planning and goals-of-care discussions. Tell: never contradicts a strategy written for this age group.

Transplant is considered in advanced adult cases, but palliative discussions in the elderly are not tied to it; they come in advanced stages of disease. Tell: palliative care discussions follow the stage of disease, not a surgical event.

Correct. For elderly patients with cardiomyopathy, palliative care discussions are held in advanced stages, alongside therapy tailored to comorbidities and frailty, cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators, and a focus on symptom control and quality of life.

C.q: A 76-year-old woman has constant throbbing, burning pain in her toes and forefoot that is worse lying flat, not relieved by narcotic pain medicine, and eased by dangling her leg or walking around. Her feet are cool. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Claudication is activity-related muscle pain relieved by rest, usually in about 10 minutes. Her pain is constant, worse lying flat and eased by walking or dangling, which is ischemic rest pain. Walking relieves her pain, whereas claudication is caused by it.

Peripheral neuropathy gives a continuous burning sensation in the foot that is unaffected by exercise. Her pain is worse lying flat and eased by dangling or walking, and her feet are cool, which is arterial rest pain. Position dependence points to ischemia.

Acute limb ischemia is a sudden occlusion with abrupt onset of severe pain and absent pulses, a vascular emergency. Her constant pain that worsens lying flat and eases with dangling is the established pattern of critical limb ischemia. Nothing in the stem describes an abrupt onset.

Correct. Ischemic rest pain of critical limb ischemia is constant, throbbing or burning, in the forefoot and toes, with cool feet. It worsens with elevation or reclining, is not readily controlled even by narcotics, and is relieved by dependency or walking around, which use gravity to aid perfusion.

C.q: Which acute event can cause right bundle branch block by suddenly raising right ventricular pressure?
opts: A hypertensive crisis is not a named cause of right bundle branch block. The acute event that suddenly raises right ventricular pressure is a pulmonary embolism. Tell: the cause must load the right ventricle, which pumps into the lungs.

Aortic dissection is not on the list of causes of right bundle branch block. A pulmonary embolism is the acute event named for a sudden rise in right ventricular pressure. Tell: the right ventricle pumps into the lungs, so look for a lung vessel problem.

Correct. A sudden increase in right ventricular pressure, as from a pulmonary embolism, is a named cause of right bundle branch block. The chronic counterpart is pulmonary hypertension, and other causes include degeneration, ischemic heart disease and cardiomyopathies; treatment depends on the underlying condition.

Acute gastroenteritis does not raise right ventricular pressure and is not a named cause of right bundle branch block. A pulmonary embolism is. Tell: only one option is an acute event in the lung circulation.

C.q: A 69-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure, ascites and a raised jugular venous pressure has cardiac magnetic resonance imaging to decide between restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis. Which imaging finding would point to constrictive pericarditis instead?
opts: A preserved left ventricular ejection fraction is typical of restrictive cardiomyopathy, which keeps it until late stages, so it does not separate the two. Pericardial thickening on magnetic resonance imaging points to constrictive pericarditis. Tell: shared features cannot decide between them.

Normal or near normal left ventricular cavity size is expected in restrictive cardiomyopathy and does not favor pericarditis. The magnetic resonance imaging finding for constrictive pericarditis is pericardial thickening. Tell: the deciding image is of the pericardium, not the ventricle.

Correct. Echocardiography alone cannot separate restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis, so cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is used, and pericardial thickening points to pericarditis. Big atria, a preserved ejection fraction and normal cavity size are restrictive features that do not decide the question.

Marked enlargement of one or both atria is a feature of restrictive cardiomyopathy on echo, so it does not point to pericarditis. The finding on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging that does is pericardial thickening. Tell: look for a pericardial finding to diagnose a pericardial disease.

C.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
C.q: A 58-year-old woman with previous infective endocarditis needs a root canal. She developed hives (urticaria) after amoxicillin years ago and can take pills. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Amoxicillin caused her hives, so she is penicillin-allergic and the standard oral amoxicillin regimen is out. Her previous endocarditis and a root canal still require prophylaxis. Tell: a penicillin allergy with the ability to take pills moves to azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline.
ruled out by a stated finding

Cephalexin, cefazolin and ceftriaxone should not be used in patients with a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria to penicillin or ampicillin, and she had hives (urticaria) with amoxicillin. Tell: urticaria removes the cephalosporin options and leaves the macrolides or doxycycline.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Previous endocarditis qualifies her, and a root canal manipulates the periapical region of the tooth, so she needs prophylaxis. She can take pills but had urticaria with amoxicillin, which rules out penicillins and cephalexin, leaving azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg (or doxycycline) 30-60 minutes before.

Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. For a penicillin-allergic patient with urticaria who can take pills, azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline is used. Tell: clindamycin has been removed from every regimen.

C.q: A 66-year-old woman in torsades de pointes (a polymorphic rhythm whose QRS complexes twist around the baseline) becomes unresponsive with a blood pressure of 60/30 and only a faint pulse. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Unresponsive with a blood pressure of 60/30, she is hemodynamically unstable, and an unstable patient in torsades de pointes is defibrillated (unsynchronized cardioversion). Magnesium is the drug for a conscious patient, and amiodarone, procainamide and beta blockers are avoided because they prolong the QT.

Intravenous lidocaine is the one antiarrhythmic that can be used in torsades de pointes, but a drug is not the step for an unstable patient. Unresponsive with a blood pressure of 60/30, she needs defibrillation. Tell: instability moves torsades from drugs to a shock.

Transcutaneous pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms, not a fast polymorphic one. Unresponsive with a blood pressure of 60/30, she is unstable and needs defibrillation. Tell: pace the slow, shock the fast.

Synchronized cardioversion needs a consistent QRS to time the shock to, and a polymorphic rhythm such as torsades has none. A hemodynamically unstable patient in torsades is defibrillated. Tell: polymorphic rhythms are never synchronized.

C.q: A 68-year-old man has had 6 weeks of low-grade fever and weight loss and has a new murmur. Subacute endocarditis is suspected. Which complete blood count finding is most likely?
opts: Eosinophilia is not part of the expected blood count in endocarditis. The complete blood count with differential shows leukocytosis and anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume. Tell: expect more white cells overall and a normocytic anemia, not an eosinophil rise.

Correct. Six weeks of low-grade fever, weight loss and a new murmur suggest subacute endocarditis, and the complete blood count with differential shows leukocytosis and anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume, which is a normocytic anemia.

Microcytic anemia is the wrong red cell size. The anemia of endocarditis is an anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume, so it is normocytic. Tell: normal-sized red cells with leukocytosis is the expected pattern.

Polycythemia is the opposite of what is expected. Endocarditis produces an anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume, together with leukocytosis. Tell: the red cell count falls rather than rises.

C.q: A 65-year-old woman with a normal pulse examination and ankle-brachial index has had her venous ulcer heal after months of compression. She asks why it opened again after she bumped her leg. Which feature of a healed venous ulcer explains this?
opts: Correct. A venous ulcer heals with a thin scar that can break down easily with minor trauma or increased leg edema. Her bump to the leg is exactly that kind of minor trauma, so the reopening reflects the fragile scar rather than a new disease process.

Nothing suggests infection: her ulcer had healed and reopened right after a bump. A healed venous ulcer leaves a thin scar that breaks down with minor trauma or increased leg edema, which explains the timing.
Lymphatic obstruction does not explain an ulcer reopening at a healed site right after a bump. Healed venous ulcers leave a thin scar that breaks down easily with minor trauma or rising leg edema.

Her normal pulse examination and ankle-brachial index argue against arterial ischemia. The reopening after a bump reflects the thin scar a venous ulcer heals with, which breaks down easily with minor trauma or increased edema.

C.q: A 30-year-old woman with known atrioventricular nodal reentry has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 178. She is stable. Which treatment almost always terminates it?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is rarely required in atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia and is held for hemodynamic instability. She is stable, so she gets vagal maneuvers or adenosine first. Tell: a stable patient with nodal reentry almost never needs a shock.

Catheter ablation offers a definitive cure, over 95 percent, for a select subset of patients with nodal reentry, but it is a planned procedure, not how an acute episode is stopped. Her stable episode now responds to vagal maneuvers or adenosine. Tell: the question asks what terminates the episode, not what prevents the next one.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or when adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. She has known nodal reentry, a circuit within the node with no accessory pathway. Tell: procainamide answers an accessory pathway; nodal reentry answers to vagal maneuvers or adenosine.

Correct. She is stable with a regular narrow tachycardia at 178 and known nodal reentry, and atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia almost always terminates with vagal maneuvers or adenosine. An educated patient whose vagal maneuver works at home usually does not need urgent medical attention.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: A 54-year-old man has a moderate-to-large pericardial effusion on echocardiogram with no hemodynamic compromise. Viral, uremic, thyroid and rheumatologic workups are unrevealing. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Nothing supports treating an undiagnosed effusion empirically; the cause is still unknown, and further management depends on the underlying etiology. Sampling the fluid by diagnostic pericardiocentesis comes first. Tell: unknown cause plus a moderate-to-large effusion means sample the fluid.

Pericardiectomy or a pericardial window is performed for recurrent effusions or loculated effusions, especially posterior ones, and neither applies to a first, unexplained effusion without compromise. Diagnostic pericardiocentesis is indicated first. Tell: a first effusion of unknown cause gets sampled, not removed surgically.

Correct. A moderate-to-large effusion whose viral, uremic, thyroid and rheumatologic workups are unrevealing is an effusion of unknown etiology, an indication for diagnostic pericardiocentesis. The fluid is sent for cell count, Gram stain, bacterial and fungal culture, acid-fast stain with mycobacterial culture, and cytology.

An unexplained moderate-to-large effusion is itself an indication for diagnostic pericardiocentesis, and malignancy should be considered once common causes are excluded. Discharging him without a diagnosis skips that step. Tell: unknown etiology plus a moderate-to-large effusion triggers sampling, not reassurance.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: A 72-year-old man with extensive atherosclerosis develops painful, tender, bluish discoloration of several toes on his left foot, with localized pallor. His dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are easily palpable. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Atheroemboli of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques lodge in small vessels of muscle and skin, causing blue toe syndrome with localized tenderness, pallor and livedo reticularis. Because large vessels may not be occluded, distal pulses usually remain palpable, as his are.

A thromboembolus occluding a limb artery produces a cold, pale limb with absent pulses distal to the occlusion. His dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are easily palpable, with tender blue toes, which points to atheroembolism. Palpable pulses argue against a large-artery occlusion.

Dry gangrene is hard, dry, necrotic tissue with clear demarcation between healthy and dead tissue. His toes are tender and bluish with localized pallor, not black and demarcated. Gangrene may develop later, but the current picture is atheroembolism.

Critical limb ischemia is chronic rest pain, ulcers and tissue loss with diminished pulses below the stenosis. His tender, bluish toes with easily palpable pulses fit atheroembolism instead. Preserved pulses separate small-vessel emboli from chronic large-vessel disease.

C.q: A 23-year-old previously healthy man has breathlessness, chest pain and exercise intolerance ten days after a flulike illness with fever, myalgia and diarrhea. He is tachycardic with a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) and crackles at both bases. Troponin is elevated and coronary angiography is normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Takotsubo is not suggested by this history; his trigger is a flulike illness with fever, myalgia and diarrhea 10 days earlier, the prodrome of viral myocarditis. Tell: a young male with a viral prodrome, low cardiac risk and acute heart failure points to myocarditis.

Correct. A previously healthy young man with heart failure symptoms ten days after fever, myalgia and diarrhea fits viral myocarditis, which follows a recent (1 to 2 week) flulike syndrome; young males are particularly susceptible. His tachycardia, third heart sound and crackles match the examination.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy does not fit acute heart failure in a previously healthy 23-year-old after a flulike illness. Viral myocarditis follows a 1 to 2 week flulike syndrome with fever, myalgia or gastroenteritis. Tell: his diarrhea counts as gastroenteritis, part of the viral prodrome.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy does not explain acute heart failure arriving 10 days after a flulike illness in a previously healthy man. Viral myocarditis presents exactly this way, with acute decompensation and no underlying cardiac dysfunction. Tell: the timing after a viral illness is the key clue.

C.q: A 71-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted with an exacerbation and respiratory failure. His pulse is 128 and irregular. The electrocardiogram shows a P wave before every QRS, with at least three different P-wave shapes in lead II. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no PR interval. His rhythm is irregular too, but every QRS has a P wave before it, in three shapes. Tell: in an irregular narrow tachycardia, look for P waves; absent means fibrillation, multiple shapes mean multifocal atrial tachycardia.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. An irregular rhythm at 128 with a P wave before every QRS and at least three distinct P-wave shapes in lead II is multifocal atrial tachycardia, from multiple atrial foci. It typically occurs in acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure, as with his exacerbation and respiratory failure.

Atrial flutter with variable conduction can be irregular, but it shows sawtooth flutter waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more that outnumber the QRS complexes. He has one discrete P wave before each QRS, in three different shapes. Tell: one P wave per QRS in changing shapes is multifocal; more sawtooth waves than QRS complexes is flutter.

Focal atrial tachycardia comes from a single ectopic atrial focus, so it is regular with one consistent abnormal P-wave shape. His rhythm is irregular and his P waves take at least three shapes. Tell: one shape in a regular rhythm is focal; three or more shapes in an irregular rhythm is multifocal.
ruled out by a stated finding

C.q: A 28-year-old woman with a malar rash, painful joints and a positive antinuclear antibody test has a new murmur. She has no fever, repeated blood cultures are negative, and echocardiography shows small sterile-appearing valve vegetations. Which is the most likely cause of her valve lesion?
opts: Subacute infective endocarditis would be expected to bring fever and positive cultures; she has neither, and her lupus features point to a non-infective valve lesion. Tell: malar rash, painful joints and a positive antinuclear antibody with sterile-appearing vegetations mean Libman-Sacks, not infection.
ruled out by a stated finding

Device endocarditis requires an implanted cardiac device, and none is described. Her lupus features, absent fever and negative cultures point to non-infective Libman-Sacks endocarditis. Tell: with no device in the history, device endocarditis cannot be the answer.

Acute infective endocarditis would bring fever and positive cultures; she has no fever, repeatedly negative cultures and sterile-appearing vegetations, so she meets neither the fever nor the culture criterion. Tell: lupus features with sterile vegetations point to Libman-Sacks, a non-infective mimic.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. She has features of systemic lupus erythematosus (malar rash, painful joints, positive antinuclear antibody), and lupus may present with non-infective Libman-Sacks endocarditis. No fever, repeatedly negative blood cultures and sterile-appearing vegetations fit this autoimmune mimic rather than infection.

C.q: A 57-year-old woman in ventricular fibrillation arrest has received shocks, epinephrine and amiodarone, and she remains in ventricular fibrillation. Which drug may be considered next?
opts: Metoprolol is not part of the cardiac arrest algorithm. With fibrillation persisting after shocks, epinephrine and amiodarone, a lidocaine push may be considered, along with calcium gluconate or sodium bicarbonate. Tell: after amiodarone, the next antiarrhythmic is lidocaine.

Adenosine has no place in the cardiac arrest algorithm. Ventricular fibrillation that stays refractory to shocks after amiodarone may be treated with a lidocaine push. Tell: the only two antiarrhythmics in arrest are amiodarone and lidocaine.

Correct. She has had shocks, epinephrine and amiodarone and is still in ventricular fibrillation, so a lidocaine push may be considered for rhythm refractory to shock after the antiarrhythmic. Calcium gluconate and sodium bicarbonate may also be considered while cardiopulmonary resuscitation continues.

Verapamil is not part of the cardiac arrest algorithm. With ventricular fibrillation persisting after shocks, epinephrine and amiodarone, lidocaine may be considered. Tell: once amiodarone has been given, the next antiarrhythmic in arrest is lidocaine.

C.q: A 66-year-old man with a known ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm develops a new diastolic murmur, exertional dyspnea and leg swelling. Which complication does the aneurysm's location explain?
opts: Esophageal compression with dysphagia is an effect of a descending thoracic aneurysm. An ascending aneurysm produces aortic regurgitation and heart failure, matching his murmur, breathlessness and edema. He has no swallowing complaint.

Correct. An ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm can cause aortic regurgitation and heart failure. That explains his new diastolic murmur, exertional dyspnea and leg swelling, while arch aneurysms cause hoarseness and descending ones cause compression symptoms.

Tracheal compression, with dyspnea, stridor and wheezing, comes from a descending thoracic aneurysm. His ascending location explains aortic regurgitation with heart failure, which fits a diastolic murmur and leg swelling. Stridor would point to the descending aorta.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, with hoarseness, comes from an arch aneurysm. His ascending aneurysm explains aortic regurgitation and heart failure, matching the diastolic murmur, exertional dyspnea and leg swelling. He has no hoarseness.

C.q: In the low likelihood Wells category, what happens after a negative D-dimer?
opts: Ultrasound follows a positive D-dimer in the low-likelihood group, not a negative one. A negative result in that group ends the work-up, because the test is sensitive enough to serve as a rule-out.

Contrast venography is the definitive gold standard but has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound, and nothing calls for imaging here. In the low-likelihood category a negative D-dimer simply ends the work-up.
The test is repeated in a week
Repeat testing in a week belongs to the high-likelihood arm, as a repeat thigh ultrasound after a negative first scan. A low-likelihood patient with a negative D-dimer stops there.

Correct. In the low-likelihood Wells category (score zero or less), a negative D-dimer ends the work-up. The test is sensitive, so a negative result reliably rules out deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in these patients, while a positive one would lead to ultrasound.

C.q: A 52-year-old man with a pacemaker implanted two weeks ago has three days of swelling and aching of the left arm. The pacemaker lead has injured the wall of the subclavian vein. Which component of the Virchow triad does this injury represent?
opts: A hypercoagulable state is a tendency of the blood itself to clot, not damage done to a vessel. The decisive clue is a lead that injured the vein wall, a mechanical injury to the lining, which is endothelial trauma.

Correct. The lead has physically injured the wall of the subclavian vein, which is damage to the vessel lining: endothelial trauma. Pacemakers, internal cardiac defibrillators and indwelling central venous catheters are the most common causes of upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which makes up only 5% to 10% of all DVTs.

Venous stasis means altered blood flow, and nothing in the stem describes immobility. The stated problem is a lead that injured the vein wall, which is endothelial trauma; pacemakers and similar devices are the most common cause of upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis.

Impaired lymphatic drainage is not a component of the Virchow triad, which is venous stasis, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury. A pacemaker lead injuring the subclavian vein wall is endothelial trauma, and devices like his are the most common cause of upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis.

C.q: A 37-year-old man was treated for acute pericarditis 4 weeks ago and now feels well. A repeat electrocardiogram shows widespread T-wave inversions without ST elevation, and troponin is normal. Which best explains the tracing?
opts: Correct. Four weeks after acute pericarditis, in a man who feels well with a normal troponin, widespread T-wave inversion without ST elevation is stage 3 of the classic evolution. ST elevation with PR depression comes first, then ST normalization with T-wave flattening at 1 to 3 weeks, then inversion from 3 weeks on, and finally a normal tracing.

His troponin is normal, and the tracing fits the timeline of his known pericarditis: T waves flatten at 1 to 3 weeks and invert from about 3 weeks onward before the tracing normalizes. Tell: a normal troponin plus timing that matches stage 3 means expected evolution, not a new infarction.
ruled out by a stated finding

Tamponade from a large effusion shows electrical alternans on the tracing, and he feels well with nothing to suggest compromise. Widespread T-wave inversion 4 weeks after treatment is stage 3 of the expected pericarditis evolution. Tell: inverted T waves in a well patient weeks after pericarditis are evolution, not a new complication.

No electrolyte problem is suggested, and the timing alone explains the tracing: in pericarditis, flattened T waves become inverted from about 3 weeks onward, before the electrocardiogram returns to normal. Tell: widespread T-wave inversion 4 weeks after treated pericarditis, in a patient who feels well, is stage 3.

C.q: A 71-year-old man admitted with pneumonia develops frequent early, wide QRS beats with no preceding P wave on telemetry, and he feels his heart skipping. His oxygen saturation on the monitor is drifting down. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Amiodarone is not part of managing premature ventricular contractions. New frequent premature beats in a patient whose oxygen saturation is falling call for finding and correcting their named causes: hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance. Tell: fix the cause before reaching for a drug.

Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. He has premature beats with a pulse and feels them skipping. Tell: a patient who can describe his palpitations is not in cardiac arrest.

Catheter ablation is reserved for symptoms refractory to a beta blocker or isolated premature-beat cardiomyopathy. In a man with pneumonia and falling oxygen saturation, the first step is checking oxygenation and electrolytes. Tell: a reversible cause comes before any procedure.

Correct. Early, wide beats with no P wave are premature ventricular contractions, and hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia) are the main causes. With pneumonia and a drifting oxygen saturation, checking a blood gas and electrolytes, then correcting what is found, comes first.

C.q: An 80-year-old man is found on the floor two days after collapsing. His right leg has profound sensory loss, paralysis with rigid muscles, and no arterial or venous Doppler signal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Vascular imaging suits viable and marginally threatened limbs. For an irreversibly damaged limb, with profound sensory loss, paralysis and absent arterial and venous signals, imaging is generally not immediately needed because the limb requires amputation. Imaging would not change the plan.

Catheter-directed thrombolysis can restore flow to a salvageable limb within 14 days. His leg, after two days on the floor with profound sensory loss, rigid paralysis and no venous signal, is irreversibly damaged and needs major amputation regardless of therapy.

Clot removal is for limbs that can still be saved. Profound sensory loss, paralysis with rigid muscles and absent arterial and venous Doppler signals mark an irreversibly ischemic limb that requires major amputation regardless of therapy. Restoring flow cannot revive this limb.

Correct. Profound sensory loss, paralysis with rigid muscles and inaudible arterial and venous Doppler signals define an irreversibly ischemic limb with major tissue loss or permanent nerve damage. Nonviable extremities require major amputation regardless of the therapy instituted.

C.q: What is the first-line treatment for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is the treatment for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia, not the first step in an acute, unstable episode. The acute sequence is atropine first, then a temporary pacemaker. Tell: acute and unstable means atropine; chronic and symptomatic means a permanent pacemaker.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing a heart that is already too slow and causing instability is the opposite of the goal. Tell: adenosine treats fast narrow rhythms; atropine treats unstable slow ones.

Amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, a fast rhythm, and is not used to raise a slow rate. Unstable bradycardia is treated with atropine first, then a temporary pacemaker. Tell: amiodarone belongs to the fast-rhythm toolbox; atropine to the slow.

Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia is treated first with atropine. If it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows; chronic symptomatic bradycardia is managed with a permanent pacemaker, and asymptomatic bradycardia is not treated at all.

C.q: A 49-year-old man has a first proximal deep vein thrombosis with no surgery, trauma, hormone use, travel, cancer or other identifiable trigger, and no inherited disorder has been found. How long should anticoagulation continue?
opts: Three to six months is for a clot provoked by a minor transient factor such as estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery, prolonged travel or minor leg injury. He has none of these; with no identifiable trigger, treatment is indefinite.

Correct. His first proximal deep vein thrombosis had no surgery, trauma, hormones, travel, cancer or other trigger, which makes it an unprovoked first venous thromboembolism (VTE). An unprovoked first VTE is treated for an indefinite length of time, beyond the 3-month minimum that applies to every first episode.
Six weeks is shorter than the minimum, since every acute first venous thromboembolism is treated for at least 3 months. An unprovoked first clot like his goes further still, to indefinite treatment.

Three months is the course for a clot provoked by a major transient factor, such as surgery under general anesthesia over 30 minutes, 3 or more days of bed rest, or major trauma or fracture. He had no trigger, so his unprovoked clot is treated indefinitely.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 21-year-old man has mild breathlessness and fatigue two weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. Troponin is mildly raised, echocardiogram shows mildly reduced function, and he is hemodynamically stable. Which is the mainstay of his treatment?
opts: Correct. This stable young man with mild symptoms, a mildly raised troponin and mildly reduced function after a viral illness has myocarditis, and supportive care is the mainstay of treatment. Treatment is directed toward the clinical scenario, adding vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics or anticoagulation as needed.

Septal ablation is not among the treatments for myocarditis. Treatment is supportive, directed toward the clinical scenario, with medications as needed. Tell: myocarditis care is support and drugs, not a procedure on the septum.

Endomyocardial biopsy is recommended for acute deterioration of heart function of unknown origin that is not responding to medical treatment. He is stable with mild symptoms, so supportive care is the mainstay. Tell: biopsy is for the patient who keeps getting worse, not the stable one.

Transplant listing has no place in a stable patient with mild symptoms; myocarditis is managed with supportive care directed toward the clinical scenario. Tell: mild and stable means supportive care, with drugs added only as needed.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 53-year-old man has had positive blood cultures for 10 days despite an antibiotic regimen that matches his organism's sensitivities, and he still has fevers. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Ten days of positive cultures and ongoing fevers despite an antibiotic matched to the organism's sensitivities is infection not resolving with appropriate antibiotic therapy, an indication for surgery. Cardiothoracic surgery evaluates him; other indications are heart failure from valvular dysfunction, abscess and fungal infection.

Stopping antibiotics would abandon treatment of an active, persistent bacteremia. Infection not resolving with appropriate antibiotic therapy is an indication for surgery, so the next step is surgical evaluation. Tell: failure of the right antibiotic escalates care rather than ending it.

Anticoagulation does not treat infection and is not beneficial in native valve infection (it is controversial with prosthetic valves). His problem is persistent bacteremia despite appropriate antibiotics, an indication for surgery. Tell: a blood thinner is not a fix for antibiotic failure.

Switching to oral therapy does not address infection that is not resolving with appropriate antibiotic therapy, which is an indication for surgery. Tell: when the right drug fails after 10 days, the next step is surgical evaluation, not a different route.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 77-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve has endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. His son asks how serious this organism is. Which statement is most accurate?
opts: A relatively good prognosis belongs to viridans streptococcal endocarditis treated before complications occur, not to Staphylococcus aureus. Tell: Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve is the worst combination, with mortality of about 50%.

Surgery is not a rarity to dismiss: it is indicated for heart failure from valvular dysfunction (the most common indication), infection not resolving with appropriate antibiotics, or abscess. Staphylococcus aureus is the most lethal organism, with about 50% mortality in prosthetic valve endocarditis. Tell: this organism on a prosthetic valve is high stakes, not a minor infection.

Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis does not resolve within a week; it is the most lethal organism, with mortality of about 50% in prosthetic valve endocarditis. Tell: the son's question is about seriousness, and the accurate answer is that this is the highest-risk organism.
It is the most lethal cause

Correct. Staphylococcus aureus is the most lethal organism in infective endocarditis, with mortality of about 30% in people who do not inject drugs, 50% in prosthetic valve endocarditis and 5% in people who inject drugs. His prosthetic aortic valve puts him in the highest-mortality group.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. D.q: A 46-year-old man with frothy urine and leg swelling is found to have a moderate pericardial effusion. Which tests best evaluate the suspected cause?
opts: A urine culture looks for a urinary infection, which is not part of the effusion workup and does not fit frothy urine with leg swelling. Those clues point to nephrotic syndrome, tested with albumin and urine protein. Tell: frothy urine signals protein, not bacteria.

Thyroid function tests evaluate myxedema, another cause in the effusion workup, but nothing in his history suggests a thyroid problem. His frothy urine and edema point to nephrotic syndrome, which albumin and urine protein address. Tell: each test in the workup matches a clinical clue.

Correct. Frothy urine and leg swelling suggest nephrotic syndrome, and albumin and urine protein are the tests in the effusion workup for that cause. The underlying etiology is usually uncovered through a careful history and examination, as his urinary clue shows.

An antinuclear antibody belongs to the rheumatologic workup, which fits when the history suggests autoimmune disease. His clues are renal: frothy urine and leg swelling point to nephrotic syndrome and to albumin and urine protein testing. Tell: match the test to the organ the history points to.

D.q: A 68-year-old man with dilated non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, an ejection fraction of 25% and breathlessness on minimal exertion despite optimal medical therapy has a left bundle branch block with a QRS of 0.16 seconds. Which treatment addresses the conduction problem?
opts: Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes; it does nothing for a conduction delay. Symptomatic left bundle branch block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is treated with a biventricular pacer. Tell: a conduction problem is fixed with a device.

Correct. Left bundle branch block is usually left untreated, but his is symptomatic, with breathlessness on minimal exertion and an ejection fraction of 25% despite optimal therapy. Symptomatic block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is treated with a biventricular pacer, and dilated non-ischemic cardiomyopathy is itself a named cause.

A single-chamber pacemaker is not the treatment named here. Symptomatic left bundle branch block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is treated specifically with a biventricular pacer. Tell: 'biventricular' is the word that goes with this block and a low ejection fraction.

Catheter ablation cannot restore conduction through a blocked left bundle. Symptomatic left bundle branch block with reduced ejection fraction is treated with a biventricular pacer. Tell: removing tissue cannot fix a conduction delay.

D.q: A 58-year-old woman five days after hip replacement develops sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain and a heart rate of 118. Her electrocardiogram shows a new right bundle branch block. Which acute cause of the block should be suspected?
opts: A pericardial effusion is not a named cause of right bundle branch block. The acute cause listed is a pulmonary embolism, a sudden increase of right ventricular pressure, which fits her setting after hip replacement. Tell: sudden breathlessness after surgery plus a new right bundle branch block suggests embolism.

A hypertensive crisis is not a named cause of right bundle branch block. The acute cause on the list is a sudden increase in right ventricular pressure from a pulmonary embolism, which fits her postoperative breathlessness and pleuritic pain. Tell: the cause must load the right ventricle suddenly.

Aortic dissection is not on the list of causes of right bundle branch block. The acute named cause is a sudden rise in right ventricular pressure from a pulmonary embolism, which matches her postoperative breathlessness and pleuritic pain. Tell: right bundle branch block points to the right ventricle and lungs.

Correct. A sudden increase in right ventricular pressure from a pulmonary embolism is a named acute cause of right bundle branch block. Five days after hip replacement, with sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain and a heart rate of 118, she fits that picture, and treatment of the block depends on the underlying condition.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: Which pair of drugs can cause pericarditis through drug-induced lupus?
opts: Neither metoprolol nor lisinopril is a listed cause of pericarditis. The drug-induced lupus pair is procainamide and hydralazine, listed under the iatrogenic causes with trauma and radiation therapy. Tell: memorize the pair, procainamide and hydralazine.

Colchicine and ibuprofen are not on the list of iatrogenic causes, which names trauma, radiation therapy and drug-induced lupus from procainamide and hydralazine. Tell: the question asks for drugs that cause disease through lupus, and only procainamide and hydralazine do.

Amoxicillin and azithromycin are not named causes of pericarditis. Drug-induced lupus pericarditis comes from procainamide and hydralazine, grouped with trauma and radiation therapy as iatrogenic causes. Tell: infection is a cause of pericarditis, but antibiotics are not.

Correct. Iatrogenic causes of pericarditis include trauma, radiation therapy and drug-induced lupus from procainamide and hydralazine. Through lupus, the pair connects to the autoimmune causes of pericarditis such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 71-year-old man with a permanent pacemaker has severe claudication, and an intervention is planned. His pacemaker system is an older one, implanted 20 years ago. Which imaging study should be avoided?
opts: Computed tomography angiography is limited by contrast allergy and decreased renal function, not by a pacemaker. It remains usable for him if his kidneys and allergy history allow. The pacemaker steers away from the magnetic study instead.

Duplex ultrasound uses no contrast media or radiation and has no listed conflict with a pacemaker. It is the mainstay initial noninvasive imaging for suspected stenosis. The pacemaker rules out magnetic resonance angiography, not ultrasound.

Correct. Magnetic resonance angiography is contraindicated with pacemakers and intracranial aneurysm clips, so with his pacemaker it is the study to avoid. It is otherwise the alternative to computed tomography angiography in contrast allergy.

Conventional angiography is the invasive gold standard used to guide a planned intervention, and a pacemaker is not among its contraindications. The study to avoid with his pacemaker is magnetic resonance angiography. Devices matter for the magnetic study only.

D.q: A 64-year-old woman has an asymptomatic ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm that now measures 5.9 cm. Repair is planned. Which approach is usually required for this location?
opts: Imaging every 3 to 5 years is for aneurysms under 4.5 cm. At 5.9 cm in the ascending aorta she is past the 5.5 cm repair threshold, and repair is already planned. Surveillance intervals no longer apply.

Endovascular aortic repair is an option for descending thoracic aneurysms. The ascending aorta often requires an open surgical approach with aortic root replacement. Her aneurysm's ascending location is the deciding clue.

The ascending threshold is over 5.5 cm; 6.0 cm applies to descending aneurysms, and 6.5 cm is not a threshold at all. Her 5.9 cm ascending aneurysm already qualifies for repair, usually open with root replacement. Waiting longer is not supported.

Correct. Surgical repair is generally indicated for ascending aneurysms over 5.5 cm, and hers is 5.9 cm. An ascending thoracic aneurysm often requires an open surgical approach with aortic root replacement, whereas a descending one can be repaired open or endovascularly.

D.q: A 57-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy returns with recurring ankle edema and increasing abdominal girth. She admits to eating canned soups and fast food most days. Which dietary counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Drink extra fluids with every meal

Extra fluids are not part of dilated cardiomyopathy education, and she already has recurring edema and rising abdominal girth. The dietary point is sodium restriction to less than 2 g/day. Tell: her canned soups and fast food are the target.
Restrict sodium to under two grams a day

Correct. Her recurring edema and growing abdominal girth with daily canned soup and fast food point to her diet, and patient education in dilated cardiomyopathy includes sodium restriction to less than 2 g/day. The same education covers the medication regimen, follow-up and removing any offending source.
Raise salt intake to protect pressure

Raising salt runs directly against the education for dilated cardiomyopathy, which is sodium restriction to less than 2 g/day. Tell: her diet of canned soups and fast food is the problem, and her edema keeps returning.
No diet change is needed with drugs

Medication does not replace diet: sodium restriction to less than 2 g/day is part of dilated cardiomyopathy education alongside the medication regimen and follow-up. Tell: her recurring edema despite treatment points to the diet.

D.q: A 27-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is examined by a student who hears a loud systolic murmur at the left sternal border. Respiration does not change it. Which bedside maneuver would soften her murmur?
opts: Standing decreases preload, and anything that decreases blood flow in the heart increases outflow obstruction, so the murmur gets louder, not softer. Tell: standing and Valsalva make it louder; handgrip, squatting and leg raising make it softer.

Correct. Anything that increases blood flow in the heart reduces outflow obstruction and softens the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Sustained handgrip increases afterload, and rapid squatting or passive leg raising increase preload, so each decreases the murmur, while respiration has no effect.

The Valsalva maneuver decreases preload, which increases outflow obstruction and makes the murmur louder. Handgrip, squatting or passive leg raising soften it. Tell: less filling means more obstruction and a louder murmur.

Amyl nitrite decreases afterload, which increases outflow obstruction and makes the murmur louder. Increasing afterload with handgrip softens it. Tell: afterload up softens the murmur; afterload down makes it louder.

D.q: A 65-year-old woman has new atrial fibrillation at 146 with palpitations. She is alert, her blood pressure is 132/84, and she has no chest pain or breathlessness. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. Her atrial fibrillation is already fast at 146, so raising the rate is the opposite of the goal. Tell: atropine is for slow and unstable; a stable rapid ventricular response needs intravenous rate control.

Correct. New atrial fibrillation at 146 is rapid ventricular response, and with a blood pressure of 132/84, a clear mind and no chest pain or breathlessness she is hemodynamically stable. Stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is treated with intravenous rate control, with anticoagulation planned for all.

Mapping and ablation is a later option in atrial fibrillation management, not the first treatment of a new rapid ventricular response. Her immediate need is to slow the rate with intravenous rate control. Tell: new, fast and stable atrial fibrillation starts with intravenous rate control.

Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation, such as with severe heart failure, hypotension or an acute myocardial infarction. She is alert with a blood pressure of 132/84 and no chest pain or breathlessness. Tell: a fast rate alone is not instability; check blood pressure and symptoms.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. D.q: What may the electrocardiogram show in aortic dissection?
opts: Low voltage is not described for dissection, and no electrocardiographic finding is constant. The electrocardiogram may be normal, so diagnosis depends on computed tomography of the chest and abdomen, magnetic resonance imaging or transesophageal echocardiography. Distrust the word always with this test.

ST elevation is not described as a feature of dissection, and the word always is the giveaway. The electrocardiogram may be entirely normal, which is exactly why imaging is needed. A test that may be normal cannot always show any one finding.

Q waves are not described as a finding in aortic dissection. The point to remember is the opposite: the electrocardiogram may be normal, so it cannot exclude dissection. Diagnosis rests on computed tomography of the chest and abdomen, magnetic resonance imaging or transesophageal echocardiography.

Correct. The electrocardiogram may be normal in aortic dissection, so a normal tracing does not rule it out. The diagnosis rests on computed tomography of the chest and abdomen to delineate extent, magnetic resonance imaging, which is good but slower, or transesophageal echocardiography.
