D.q: A 79-year-old man with multiple serious medical conditions is a poor surgical candidate. He had a transient ischemic attack and has a 90% symptomatic carotid stenosis. Which intervention is most appropriate?
opts: Medical management alone is advised for stenosis under 50%. His symptomatic 90% stenosis is far above the over-70% threshold for intervention, so revascularization is needed, here by stenting because he is a poor surgical candidate. Observation undertreats him.

Correct. His transient ischemic attack and 90% stenosis meet the over-70% threshold for intervention in symptomatic patients. Because he is a poor surgical candidate, carotid angioplasty with stenting, most often through the common femoral artery, is chosen: it is less invasive and allows intervention in poor surgical candidates.

Carotid endarterectomy is the gold standard for high-grade stenosis but requires open surgery, with risks of stroke or nerve damage. In a poor surgical candidate, the less invasive stenting approach is chosen. His surgical risk is the deciding clue.

Digital subtraction angiography guides therapeutic interventions but does not treat the stenosis. His symptomatic 90% stenosis needs revascularization, and as a poor surgical candidate he should have carotid stenting. A guiding study is not a treatment.

D.q: A 51-year-old woman with dilated, tortuous leg veins has a duplex ultrasound confirming superficial venous reflux. Which vein is most commonly involved in this condition?
opts: The popliteal vein is a deep vein behind the knee, and varicose veins are a disease of the superficial veins. The superficial vein most commonly involved is the great saphenous vein.
The femoral vein belongs to the deep system, while varicose veins involve the superficial veins. Of those, the great saphenous vein is the most commonly involved, ahead of the short saphenous vein.

The short saphenous vein is a superficial vein that can be involved in varicose veins, but it is not the most common one. The great saphenous vein is the most commonly involved, which makes it the better answer.

Correct. Dilated, tortuous veins with superficial reflux are varicose veins, which result from venous reflux and venous hypertension. Superficial veins are involved, most commonly the great saphenous vein, with the short saphenous vein also affected.

D.q: A 64-year-old man has heart-failure-like edema, ascites and an elevated jugular venous pressure. The differential is narrowed to constrictive pericarditis or restrictive cardiomyopathy. Which laboratory finding would favor constrictive pericarditis?
opts: A markedly high B-type natriuretic peptide leans the other way, since levels are likely lower in constriction than in restrictive cardiomyopathy. No single threshold confirms or excludes either diagnosis. Tell: the comparison is relative, and the higher value favors restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Inflammatory markers such as sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are often elevated in constriction, so a normal value does not favor it. Tell: in constriction, inflammation markers tend to run high; the laboratory clue that separates it from restrictive cardiomyopathy is a relatively low natriuretic peptide.

Correct. No B-type natriuretic peptide threshold confirms or excludes constriction, but the level is likely lower in constrictive pericarditis than in restrictive cardiomyopathy. With the differential narrowed to those two, a relatively low value tips toward constriction.

Positive blood cultures do not separate constriction from restrictive cardiomyopathy; the laboratory clue between those two is the B-type natriuretic peptide, likely lower in constriction. Inflammatory markers are often elevated in constriction. Tell: choose the test that compares the two diagnoses directly.

D.q: A 66-year-old woman learns her electrocardiogram shows a constant PR interval of 0.22 seconds with every beat conducted. She feels well and asks at what point this kind of delay usually starts to cause symptoms. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: A PR of 0.12 seconds is within the normal range, and her 0.22 seconds already exceeds that without symptoms. Symptoms of first-degree block usually begin when the PR exceeds 0.3 seconds. Tell: 0.12 is normal, 0.20 defines the block, 0.3 brings symptoms.

A PR over 0.20 seconds defines first-degree block, which she already has at 0.22 seconds, yet she feels well, like most such patients. Symptoms usually begin above 0.3 seconds. Tell: the diagnostic cutoff is not the symptom cutoff.

Dropped QRS complexes would mean second-degree block, a different rhythm, not the point at which first-degree block causes symptoms. Symptoms usually appear once the PR exceeds 0.3 seconds. Tell: the symptom threshold in first-degree block is a PR number, not a dropped beat.

Correct. Her constant PR of 0.22 seconds is first-degree block, and the vast majority of such patients have no symptoms. Fatigue, shortness of breath, palpitations and chest pain usually appear once the PR interval exceeds 0.3 seconds, the point at which a permanent pacemaker is also considered.

D.q: A 67-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is being discharged after treatment of an embolic leg occlusion. Which warning symptoms should prompt him to return immediately?
opts: Dry, shiny skin on the shins

Dry, shiny, hairless skin is a chronic sign of severely diminished flow in peripheral artery disease, not a warning of a new embolus. Recurrent embolism announces itself suddenly, with the six P's: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis and poikilothermia. Chronic skin change is not an emergency trigger.
Mild ankle swelling in the evening

Evening ankle swelling is not an arterial warning sign; swelling fits venous problems such as venous insufficiency. The return warnings are the six P's of acute limb ischemia: sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis and poikilothermia. Arterial occlusion makes the limb cold and pale.

Correct. Atrial fibrillation is a named embolic source, so he is at risk of another embolus. Sudden pain, pallor, coldness and numbness match the six P's of arterial assessment (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis and poikilothermia), the signs of acute limb ischemia, a vascular emergency needing immediate care.

Exertional calf cramping relieved by rest is intermittent claudication, a chronic symptom of narrowing, not a sign of a new embolus. Recurrent embolism presents suddenly with pain, pallor, coldness and numbness. Predictable exertional pain is chronic; abrupt change at rest is acute.

D.q: A 58-year-old woman has a slow sinus rhythm at 38 six hours after an inferior myocardial infarction. She feels faint and her blood pressure is 80/50. Each narrow QRS has a normal P wave before it. Which drug should be given first?
opts: Metoprolol is a beta blocker, and beta blockers are a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, so it would slow her further at a rate of 38. Beta blockers are used for fast rhythms, such as rate control in stable atrial flutter. Tell: a hypotensive, faint patient with a slow sinus rate needs atropine, not a rate-slowing drug.

Diltiazem is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, a class listed with beta blockers and digoxin as a drug cause of sinus bradycardia. Giving it at a rate of 38 with a blood pressure of 80/50 would deepen the problem. Tell: drugs that cause bradycardia never rescue it; atropine does.

Correct. A sinus rhythm at 38 with a normal P wave before each narrow QRS, faintness and a blood pressure of 80/50 is acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable sinus bradycardia; sinus node ischemia is a listed cause, fitting the infarction. Atropine is first line, followed by a temporary pacemaker if it fails.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing a sinus rhythm already at 38 is the opposite of what she needs. Tell: adenosine is for a fast narrow rhythm; unstable sinus bradycardia gets atropine.

D.q: A 67-year-old woman with tamponade from a malignant effusion has a blood pressure of 76/48 while the team prepares for pericardiocentesis. Which measure best supports her in the meantime?
opts: Slowing the heart does nothing to relieve the compression, and the stated bridge to drainage is intravenous fluid resuscitation to raise preload and prevent right ventricular collapse. Tell: the bridge to pericardiocentesis supports filling; it does not suppress the heart.

Nitroglycerin is not part of tamponade support; her compressed heart needs more preload, which intravenous fluids provide, not a drug that lowers it. Tell: the temporizing measure for tamponade increases preload until expedient pericardiocentesis.

Correct. At 76/48 while pericardiocentesis is prepared, intravenous fluid resuscitation is given in tamponade to increase preload and prevent right ventricular collapse. It is a temporizing, stabilizing measure; expedient pericardiocentesis remains the definitive treatment.

A diuretic removes volume, the opposite of the intravenous fluid resuscitation given in tamponade to increase preload and prevent right ventricular collapse. Tell: in tamponade the bridge to drainage adds volume, and taking volume away risks collapse.

D.q: A 27-year-old woman has a first deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. Genetic testing shows factor V Leiden, an inherited clotting abnormality. Which component of the Virchow triad does this finding represent?
opts: Venous insufficiency is listed under venous stasis, the altered blood flow component, along with immobilization and heart failure. Factor V Leiden is a genetic change in clotting, an inherited hypercoagulable state.

Correct. Factor V Leiden is an inherited hypercoagulable state, listed with prothrombin gene mutation and protein C, protein S or antithrombin deficiency. In the Virchow triad it represents a clotting tendency of the blood, separate from stasis or vessel injury.

Endothelial injury comes from trauma, surgery, intravenous drug use or burns. Factor V Leiden is a gene finding that changes the blood's clotting tendency, which makes it an inherited hypercoagulable state.

Venous stasis is altered blood flow from immobilization, venous insufficiency or heart failure. Her finding is a genetic clotting abnormality, which the triad places under the hypercoagulable state, inherited or acquired.

D.q: A 63-year-old woman with chest pain after a car accident that killed her sister has ST elevation and an elevated troponin; stress cardiomyopathy is suspected. Her pain has eased and she is hemodynamically stable in the emergency department. Which disposition is most appropriate?
opts: Feeling better does not make discharge safe: with ST elevation and an elevated troponin, she cannot yet be told apart from acute coronary syndrome, so she is admitted to cardiology. Tell: the diagnosis is confirmed only by catheterization, which has not happened yet.

Transplant listing has no place in Takotsubo, where treatment is empiric and supportive and most patients completely recover. She is admitted to cardiology under acute coronary syndrome protocols. Tell: an expected full recovery rules out transplant.

Outpatient follow-up skips the acute coronary syndrome evaluation she needs; the syndrome mimics acute coronary syndrome, so its protocols apply and she is admitted to cardiology. Tell: elevated troponin plus ST elevation means admission, whatever the suspected cause.

Correct. Even though her pain has eased and she is stable, Takotsubo mimics acute coronary syndrome with no initial reliable differences, so she is evaluated and treated on established acute coronary syndrome protocols and admitted to cardiology. Treatment is then empiric and supportive, and most patients completely recover.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: In a stable narrow complex tachycardia, which step comes before any drug?
opts: Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or when adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; it is not a first step. Stable narrow complex tachycardia begins with a vagal maneuver. Tell: procainamide answers pre-excited atrial fibrillation; a stable narrow tachycardia starts drug-free.

Synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, is immediate treatment only for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia. A stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine. Tell: the word stable in the question takes the shock off the table.

Correct. In stable supraventricular tachycardia, the narrow complex tachycardias, a vagal maneuver is first line, before any drug. Adenosine follows if needed, may be repeated once, and may convert the rhythm or slow it enough to show P waves; synchronized cardioversion is kept for instability.

An echocardiogram is not part of the acute sequence for stable supraventricular tachycardia, which runs vagal maneuver, then adenosine. The question asks for the step before any drug, and that is the vagal maneuver. Tell: the first move in a stable narrow tachycardia is a bedside, drug-free maneuver.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 65-year-old man has a painful, swollen right groin two days after a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery. Ultrasound shows a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall, communicating with the lumen. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A pseudoaneurysm is a communication between the arterial lumen and overlying connective tissue after arterial rupture, forming a blood-filled cavity outside the vessel wall. The common site is the femoral artery after cardiac catheterization, from laceration by the access needle, and pain comes from swelling or nerve compression.

A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall, as a saccular outpouching or a fusiform dilation. His ultrasound shows a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall after a femoral puncture, which is a false aneurysm, a pseudoaneurysm. Outside the wall means false.

Acute limb ischemia is sudden occlusion of a previously patent artery, with a cold, pale, pulseless limb. He has a painful, swollen groin and a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall after catheterization, which is a pseudoaneurysm. Local swelling, not distal pulselessness, is his problem.

Atheroembolism causes painful blue toes from small-vessel debris, usually with palpable pulses. A swollen, painful groin with a cavity outside the arterial wall after catheterization is a pseudoaneurysm. The finding is at the puncture site, not in the toes.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
D.q: Which cardiomyopathy strategy applies specifically to adolescents?
opts: Palliative care discussions in advanced stages are an elderly strategy, not an adolescent one. Adolescents get genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and activity restriction if high risk. Tell: palliative care sits at the elderly end of the age list.
Cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators

Cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators is an elderly strategy, tailored to comorbidities and frailty. Adolescents get genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Tell: caution with these drugs reflects frailty, which is an elderly concern.

An assist device or transplant is considered in advanced adult cases. The adolescent strategy is genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, plus activity restriction for high risk. Tell: devices and transplant sit in the adult list.

Correct. The age-specific strategies for adolescents are genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and activity restriction for high-risk individuals, with medication for symptomatic relief and an implantable defibrillator in select cases.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: In tachy-brady syndrome, which tachyarrhythmia is most common?
opts: Atrial flutter is a fast atrial rhythm with sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, but it is not the named most-common tachyarrhythmia of tachy-brady syndrome. That is atrial fibrillation. Tell: the fast phase is classically irregularly irregular without P waves, which is fibrillation, not a regular sawtooth.

Ventricular tachycardia can be the tachyarrhythmia in some patients with tachy-brady syndrome, who then need a permanent pacemaker with an implantable defibrillator. It is not the most common one; atrial fibrillation is. Tell: ventricular tachycardia changes the device, not the most-common answer.

Correct. Tachy-brady syndrome is the form of sick sinus syndrome in which a tachyarrhythmia alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or offset pauses. The most common cause of the fast phase is atrial fibrillation, which appears as an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves.

Sinus tachycardia is a regular rhythm at over 100 to 160 with a P wave before every QRS, usually driven by a physiologic or pathologic process. The fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome is most commonly atrial fibrillation, not a sinus rhythm. Tell: the named most-common tachyarrhythmia is irregularly irregular without P waves.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: For recurrent, colchicine-resistant pericarditis with an inflammatory phenotype, which therapy do the 2025 guidelines now support earlier in the course?
opts: Correct. The 2025 guidelines support anti-interleukin-1 therapy earlier in the course when there is an inflammatory phenotype: C-reactive protein above 10 mg/L, fever or evidence of pericardial inflammation. For recurrent, colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent disease, anakinra or rilonacept is the preferred agent.

Pericardiectomy may be considered for frequent, highly symptomatic recurrences with effusion or for constriction, and its role in multiple recurrences remains uncertain; it is not what the 2025 guidelines move earlier. They move anti-interleukin-1 therapy earlier. Tell: the guideline change concerns a drug class, not surgery.

Intravenous immunoglobulin is not the therapy the 2025 guidelines bring forward. For recurrent, colchicine-resistant disease with an inflammatory phenotype, anti-interleukin-1 therapy (anakinra or rilonacept) is preferred. Tell: anakinra and rilonacept are the named agents of the guideline change.

Azathioprine is not the agent the 2025 guidelines move earlier; with fever, a C-reactive protein above 10 mg/L or pericardial inflammation on imaging, an interleukin-1 blocker is supported earlier. Tell: the inflammatory phenotype points specifically to interleukin-1 blockade.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. D.q: A 64-year-old man with crushing chest pain develops a wide QRS tachycardia whose complexes vary in shape from beat to beat; his QT before the episode was normal. He is still talking and has a pulse. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion needs a consistent QRS to time against and suits unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. His complexes vary in shape, so he is defibrillated. Tell: monomorphic with a pulse gets synchronized; polymorphic gets unsynchronized.

Correct. A wide tachycardia with complexes that vary in shape is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, and with a normal QT and crushing chest pain, acute ischemia is the likely driver. It is never truly stable, so he is defibrillated even with a pulse, then sent for urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization.

Intravenous amiodarone may be added after the shock, but drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Complexes that vary in shape mean polymorphic tachycardia, which is never truly stable and is defibrillated. Tell: a talking patient with polymorphic tachycardia still needs a shock.

Observation is unsafe: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, only a short-lived transitional state that will need defibrillation. Tell: looking well does not make a polymorphic rhythm safe.

D.q: A 70-year-old woman with a medial ankle venous ulcer has used compression, elevation and wound care for seven months and the ulcer has not healed. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Nonhealing ulcers are one of the reasons to refer to a vascular specialist. Healing can take 4 to 6 months with compression and wound care, and an ulcer still open at seven months needs further workup for underlying infection or other causes.

Infection is one cause to search for when an ulcer fails to heal, but the referral for a nonhealing venous ulcer is to a vascular specialist. Her ulcer has outlasted the 4 to 6 months that healing can take, which is the trigger.

A dermatologist is not the referral for a nonhealing venous ulcer. After seven months of compression, elevation and wound care, past the 4 to 6 months healing can take, she is referred to a vascular specialist.

Physical therapy does not address an ulcer that has failed seven months of compression, elevation and wound care. Nonhealing ulcers are a reason for referral to a vascular specialist, since an ulcer open beyond 4 to 6 months needs further workup.

D.q: A 21-year-old man collapses while playing basketball and arrives with a very fast regular tachycardia. He is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70. A vagal maneuver fails, and adenosine slows the rate to reveal an irregular rhythm with wide QRS complexes, each with a delta wave (slurred upstroke). Which is the next step?
opts: Oral beta blockers serve as chronic therapy for focal atrial tachycardia or as a pill-in-the-pocket option for nodal reentry, not as the acute drug here. Atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White revealed by adenosine is treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: a pre-excited, irregular wide rhythm calls for intravenous procainamide, not an oral rate-control drug.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. His problem is a very fast rhythm conducting over an accessory pathway, the opposite of what atropine treats. Tell: atropine answers slow rates; atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White gets procainamide.

Adenosine may be repeated in ordinary stable supraventricular tachycardia, but once it reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White it must never be used again. Irregular wide complexes with delta waves are exactly that finding. Tell: delta waves on an irregular rhythm switch the drug to procainamide.

Correct. Adenosine has slowed the rate and revealed an irregular rhythm with wide complexes and delta waves, which is atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. In that situation intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is never repeated; he is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70, so a drug is appropriate.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: How many points does an alternative diagnosis at least as likely as deep vein thrombosis subtract in the Wells criteria?
opts: One point is the value of each positive item, such as active cancer or calf swelling over 3 cm. The alternative diagnosis item works in the other direction and subtracts 2 points.

Correct. An alternative diagnosis at least as likely as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) scores minus 2, the only negative item in the Wells criteria. Every other item adds 1 point, and the total sorts patients into low (zero or less), moderate (1 to 2) or high (3 or more) likelihood.

Three is not the value of any single item; it is the total at which the likelihood of deep vein thrombosis becomes high. The alternative diagnosis item subtracts 2 points, the only negative entry in the score.

No Wells item is worth 5 points; the positive items add 1 each and the alternative diagnosis item subtracts 2. Remembering that only one item is negative, and that it is worth 2, separates this choice from the key.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 55-year-old woman taking a loop diuretic for heart failure has new palpitations felt in her neck. Telemetry shows frequent premature ventricular contractions. Which laboratory values should be checked first?
opts: Troponin and lipase do not test for the named causes of premature ventricular contractions. The named causes are hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance (low potassium, low magnesium, high calcium). Tell: her loop diuretic is the clue that points to potassium and magnesium.

Glucose and lactate are not among the named causes of premature ventricular contractions. The named causes are hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia). Tell: a patient on a diuretic with new premature beats needs her electrolytes checked.

Correct. Electrolyte imbalance (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia) and hypoxemia are the named causes of premature ventricular contractions, and her loop diuretic puts potassium and magnesium at risk. Palpitations felt in the neck are the classic symptom of these beats, which occur with or without structural heart disease.

Thyroid hormone and cortisol are not among the named causes of premature ventricular contractions. The named causes are hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance, so a patient on a loop diuretic needs potassium and magnesium checked first. Tell: the drug in the stem points to an electrolyte.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: A 36-year-old woman who smokes and takes an oral contraceptive has mild calf aching. Her Wells score is low, and her D-dimer returns positive. What is the next step?
opts: Correct. Her Wells score is low, so she started with a D-dimer, and a positive result leads on to ultrasound. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific, so it cannot confirm a clot, and venous duplex ultrasound has replaced contrast venography for diagnosis.

Empiric anticoagulation would treat a clot that has not been shown; a positive D-dimer implies fibrinolysis but is not specific for deep vein thrombosis. In the low-likelihood pathway a positive result leads to ultrasound, which decides whether treatment is needed.

Reassurance and discharge are for a negative D-dimer in a low-likelihood patient. Her result is positive, and because the test is not specific, ultrasound is needed to find out whether a clot is present.

Repeating a test that is sensitive but not specific cannot settle whether a clot is present. In the low-likelihood pathway a positive D-dimer moves straight to ultrasound, which has replaced venography for diagnosis.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: Which electrolyte is given as an intravenous push and then as an infusion to break torsades de pointes?
opts: Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium is given to break torsades de pointes, followed by more magnesium as an infusion. Amiodarone, procainamide and beta blockers are avoided because they prolong the QT, and lidocaine is the only antiarrhythmic that can be used.

Phosphate has no role in torsades de pointes. The conscious patient gets intravenous magnesium to break the rhythm, then a magnesium infusion, while an unstable patient is defibrillated. Tell: magnesium is the only electrolyte repeated as push and infusion.

Potassium is not the drug that breaks torsades de pointes. Hypokalemia is a cause of acquired long QT and should be corrected, but the push-then-infusion treatment is magnesium. Tell: torsades is 'mag, mag, mag'; an unstable patient is defibrillated instead.

Calcium is not the treatment that breaks torsades de pointes; hypocalcemia is a cause of acquired long QT. Calcium gluconate is only considered in refractory ventricular fibrillation arrest. Tell: the electrolyte given as a push and then an infusion for torsades is magnesium.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for ventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
D.q: An 80-year-old man has an incidental finding on a preoperative electrocardiogram: a constant PR interval in conducted beats with occasional P waves that are not followed by a QRS complex, and no PR lengthening before the dropped beats. He has no symptoms. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. A constant PR in conducted beats with occasional dropped QRS complexes and no PR lengthening is Mobitz type II. It is considered dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression and poor prognosis, with a higher risk of complete block and sudden cardiac death, so the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

Reassurance suits silent first-degree or Mobitz type I block. A constant PR with dropped beats and no PR lengthening is Mobitz type II, which needs a permanent pacemaker even without symptoms. Tell: in type II, being symptom-free does not change the plan.
Repeat the tracing in a year

Repeating the tracing in a year ignores the unpredictable progression of Mobitz type II to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death. Guidelines treat it as dangerous even without symptoms. Tell: an incidental type II finding is treated, not watched.

An oral beta blocker is not among the listed treatments for Mobitz type II, which usually originates at the bundle of His and is considered dangerous even without symptoms because of its higher risk of complete heart block and sudden cardiac death. Tell: the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker, not a rate-slowing drug.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 52-year-old woman with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has new palpitations. Her pulse is irregularly irregular and the electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation. Echocardiogram shows left atrial enlargement. Which treatment prevents embolic stroke in her?
opts: Diuretics may be necessary but are used with caution to avoid dehydration, and they do not prevent thromboembolism. Anticoagulation is the stroke-prevention step in atrial fibrillation. Tell: amiodarone controls the rhythm; anticoagulation protects against stroke.

Nitrates reduce preload or afterload and are avoided if possible because they may aggravate outflow tract obstruction; they do nothing to prevent emboli. Anticoagulation prevents embolic stroke. Tell: the question asks about stroke, which only an anticoagulant addresses.

Correct. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, as in this woman with an irregularly irregular pulse and left atrial enlargement, is treated with anticoagulation to prevent embolic stroke. Antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone convert and suppress it, and radiofrequency ablation is another option.

Digoxin is a positive inotrope avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because increased contractility raises ischemia risk and may induce arrhythmias. It does not prevent stroke; anticoagulation does. Tell: stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation means anticoagulation.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
D.q: Which group has the highest incidence of abdominal aortic aneurysm?
opts: Male sex fits, but aneurysm is uncommon in Asian populations. Caucasian men have the highest incidence, with men outnumbering women 2:1 under age 80. Race is the element that disqualifies this option.

Both features lower the odds: aneurysm is uncommon in Hispanic populations, and women are affected less than men under 80. Caucasian men have the highest incidence. Each element of this option points away from the high-risk group.

Aneurysm is uncommon in African American populations and less common in women under 80, so both features point away. The highest incidence is in Caucasian men. Look for the option combining male sex with Caucasian race.

Correct. Caucasian men have the highest incidence of abdominal aortic aneurysm. Men outnumber women 2:1 under age 80, evening out to 1:1 over 80, and aneurysm is uncommon in African American, Asian and Hispanic populations.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 52-year-old man with end-stage dilated cardiomyopathy is listed for cardiac transplantation, but his breathlessness and fatigue worsen despite full medical therapy and a biventricular defibrillator. Which device strategy fits his situation?
opts: A pacemaker for isolated heart block does not fit; nothing in his story describes heart block, and he already has a biventricular defibrillator. His failing pump needs a left ventricular assist device as a bridge to the transplant he is listed for. Tell: worsening pump failure, not a conduction problem, is his issue.
Assist device as a bridge to transplant

Correct. He is already listed for transplantation and worsening despite full therapy and a biventricular defibrillator. A left ventricular assist device (LVAD), a pump that helps the left ventricle in heart failure, is indicated as bridge therapy for cardiac transplantation or while waiting for cardiac function to return.

Alcohol septal ablation does nothing for a dilated, failing ventricle and is not part of dilated cardiomyopathy management. A left ventricular assist device, a pump that helps the left ventricle, serves as a bridge to transplantation. Tell: he needs pump support while he waits.

Destination therapy is for patients who are not candidates for cardiac transplantation. He is already listed, so the device serves as bridge therapy instead. Tell: listed for transplant means bridge; not a candidate means destination.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 40-year-old woman with right lower lobe pneumonia has sharp chest pain. A rubbing sound is heard over the lower chest that is present only while she breathes in and vanishes when she holds her breath. Which is the most likely source of the sound?
opts: A rub is not a valve sound, and nothing about this one links it to the mitral valve. A sound present only on inspiration and gone with breath-holding is a pleural rub, which fits her pneumonia. Tell: a sound that depends on breathing comes from the pleura.

Correct. Her rub is heard only during inspiration and vanishes with breath-holding, the pattern of a pleural rub, which fits her right lower lobe pneumonia. A pericardial rub behaves differently: its intensity increases when the patient holds a breath, leans forward or the diaphragm is pressed firmly.

A pericardial rub does not vanish with breath-holding; its intensity actually increases when the breath is held. It is loudest at the left sternal border and classically triphasic and scratchy. Her inspiration-only rub over the lower chest is pleural. Tell: breath-holding silences a pleural rub but not a pericardial one.
ruled out by a stated finding

The chest wall is not the source of a rub heard only during inspiration that stops with breath-holding; that pattern defines a pleural rub. A pericardial rub, by contrast, grows louder with breath-holding. Tell: inspiration-only plus disappears on breath-holding equals pleural.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 62-year-old man with fever, a new murmur and positive blood cultures is stable. A transthoracic study is limited by his body habitus. Which imaging test best detects vegetations and defines the extent of disease?
opts: Correct. Transesophageal echocardiography is highly sensitive and specific, detects vegetations on the valve leaflets and defines the extent of disease. With his transthoracic study limited by body habitus, it is the test to order, although a normal result does not necessarily rule out endocarditis.

A chest radiograph is not among the listed diagnostic tests and cannot show vegetations on valve leaflets. Transesophageal echocardiography detects vegetations and defines the extent of disease. Tell: the question asks for a valve-level image, which only echocardiography provides.

Repeating a transthoracic study that his body habitus already limited would not solve the problem. Transesophageal echocardiography is the highly sensitive and specific test that detects vegetations and defines the extent of disease. Tell: a limited view calls for a different window, not the same one.

Coronary angiography is not among the listed diagnostic tests for endocarditis and does not show valve vegetations. Transesophageal echocardiography detects vegetations on valve leaflets and defines the extent of disease. Tell: a vegetation sits on a valve, so image the valve.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: What causes congestive heart failure in infective endocarditis?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is not the cause given for heart failure in endocarditis. Congestive heart failure results from valvular dysfunction, as infection damages the valve or ruptures the chordae tendineae. Tell: heart failure in endocarditis traces back to a damaged valve, not to a rhythm alone.

Correct. Congestive heart failure in infective endocarditis is due to valvular dysfunction: infection damages the valve, producing a new murmur, and can rupture the chordae tendineae. A new murmur together with heart failure points to a failing infected valve.

Fluid from antibiotics is not the cause; congestive heart failure in endocarditis is due to valvular dysfunction from valve damage or ruptured chordae tendineae. Tell: heart failure here is a structural complication of the infection, not of its treatment.

Coronary vasospasm is not the mechanism. Congestive heart failure in endocarditis is due to valvular dysfunction, the same valve damage that produces a new murmur. Tell: think valve, not coronary artery, when heart failure complicates endocarditis.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: Which condition is a contraindication to anticoagulation for deep vein thrombosis?
opts: An extensive proximal clot is a reason to treat, not to withhold treatment; anticoagulation is the mainstay of deep vein thrombosis therapy, and some patients also need thrombolysis. The contraindications are bleeding problems such as acute intracranial hemorrhage.

Active cancer is not on the list of contraindications, which are active bleeding, acute intracranial hemorrhage, major trauma and severe bleeding disorders. A patient with cancer and a deep vein thrombosis can still be anticoagulated.

A recent long flight is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation. The contraindications are all bleeding-related: active bleeding, acute intracranial hemorrhage, major trauma and severe bleeding disorders.

Correct. Contraindications to anticoagulants are active bleeding, acute intracranial hemorrhage, major trauma and severe bleeding disorders. Anticoagulation is otherwise the mainstay of treatment for deep vein thrombosis (DVT), so a bleeding problem is what stops it.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 75-year-old man with peripheral artery disease has a hard, dry, black distal toe with a clear line between healthy and dead tissue. There is no swelling, moisture or fever. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atheroembolism causes painful, tender blue toes with pallor and livedo reticularis, usually with palpable pulses. A hard, dry, black distal toe with a clear line between healthy and dead tissue is dry gangrene. Blue and tender differs from black and hard.

Wet gangrene has a moist appearance, edema and blistering, with bacterial infection and a risk of sepsis, and it is a surgical emergency. His toe is hard and dry with no swelling, moisture or fever. The absence of moisture and fever separates dry from wet.

Correct. Dry gangrene has a hard, dry texture, usually involves the distal toes, shows clear demarcation between healthy and necrotic tissue, and is common in patients with peripheral artery disease. His toe matches every feature, with no swelling, moisture or fever to suggest infection.

Gas gangrene is a wet gangrene in which spore-forming clostridial species release toxins and gas into infected tissue. His dry, clearly demarcated toe without swelling, moisture or fever is dry gangrene. Gas gangrene sits on the wet, infected side.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for pericardial disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 9. adult 10. elderly
D.q: A 78-year-old man with chronic kidney disease, pulmonary hypertension and hyponatremia is diagnosed with constrictive pericarditis. His family asks what to expect. Which statement about his long-term outlook is most accurate?
opts: Survival without treatment is usually normal

Without treatment, survival in constrictive pericarditis is low, not normal. Pericardiectomy increases 5-year survival to nearly 80% and 10-year survival to nearly 60%, and earlier surgery is associated with better outcomes. Tell: untreated constriction carries poor survival.
His age and comorbidities predict a worse outcome

Correct. Older age, worse functional class and comorbidities such as renal dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension and hyponatremia are independent predictors of poor long-term outcome in constrictive pericarditis. At 78 with kidney disease, pulmonary hypertension and hyponatremia, he carries several of them.
His prognosis is as good as a young patient's

His age and his renal dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension and hyponatremia are each independent predictors of a poor long-term outcome, so his prognosis is worse than that of a younger, healthier patient. Tell: count the listed predictors he carries.
Age does not influence the outcome of surgery

Older age is itself an independent predictor of poor long-term outcome in constriction, so age does matter. Earlier surgical intervention is also associated with improved outcomes. Tell: age appears on the list of predictors, so it cannot be neutral.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: A 66-year-old man taking apixaban for deep vein thrombosis develops an acute intracranial hemorrhage. Which agent reverses the anticoagulant?
opts: Oral vitamin K is one of the reversal options for warfarin, along with prothrombin complex concentrate, fresh frozen plasma and intravenous vitamin K. He takes apixaban, whose reversal agent is andexanet alfa.

Correct. He is taking apixaban and has an acute intracranial hemorrhage, one of the situations that calls for reversal. Andexanet alfa (Andexxa) is the reversal agent for apixaban and rivaroxaban, and it is used off-label for edoxaban.
Idarucizumab is the reversal agent for dabigatran and does not act on apixaban. For his intracranial bleed on apixaban, the reversal agent is andexanet alfa, the same agent used for rivaroxaban.
Protamine sulfate reverses unfractionated heparin and low molecular weight heparin. He takes apixaban, so the reversal agent for his intracranial hemorrhage is andexanet alfa.

D.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
D.q: Which valve-related condition warrants endocarditis prophylaxis before dental work?
opts: A history of rheumatic fever is not on the prophylaxis list, which names prosthetic valves, valve-repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation. Tell: the list is built around prosthetic material and prior infection, not a past illness.

A pacemaker without valve disease is not on the dental prophylaxis list, which applies to patients with valve disease who have prosthetic valves, repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease or transplant valve regurgitation. Tell: a device without valve disease does not qualify.

Correct. Prosthetic cardiac valves, including transcatheter-implanted prostheses and homografts, are on the list for which prophylaxis is reasonable before dental procedures that manipulate gingival tissue or the periapical region of teeth or perforate the oral mucosa. A transcatheter valve counts the same as a surgical one.
Sinus rhythm with a flow murmur

Sinus rhythm with a flow murmur is not a qualifying condition; the list covers prosthetic valves, valve-repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation. Tell: a murmur alone, without prosthetic material or prior infection, does not warrant prophylaxis.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 68-year-old man with a native mitral valve has 5 weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue and a new murmur. Three sets of blood cultures have just been drawn, and the organism is not yet known. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. With the organism unknown, empiric therapy must cover staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci. For a native valve with a subacute presentation (5 weeks of low-grade fever), the empiric regimen is vancomycin plus ceftriaxone, started only after blood cultures are drawn, as they have been here.

A single oral dose cannot treat established endocarditis. Antibiotic therapy must be bactericidal, prolonged (typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture) and given parenterally. Tell: anything oral or single-dose fails the parenteral, prolonged rule; his empiric regimen is vancomycin plus ceftriaxone.

Nafcillin plus rifampin (with gentamicin) is directed therapy for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve. His valve is native and the organism is unknown. Tell: empiric native valve therapy is vancomycin plus ceftriaxone, covering staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci.

Two weeks of oral doxycycline breaks two rules: endocarditis antibiotics must be given parenterally, and therapy is prolonged, typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture. Tell: oral and short both fail; empiric therapy here is vancomycin plus ceftriaxone.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 74-year-old man with restrictive cardiomyopathy is found to have cardiac amyloidosis, with amyloid protein deposited in the heart tissue. He has breathlessness, leg edema and ascites. Which electrocardiogram finding is expected with this infiltrative disease?
opts: ST elevation is not part of the restrictive or amyloid electrocardiogram. In amyloidosis infiltrative disease the tracing may show low QRS voltage, often with atrial fibrillation or a bundle branch block. Tell: amyloid means small complexes, not a raised segment.

Left axis deviation is not the finding described for amyloid infiltration. The restrictive electrocardiogram may show low QRS voltage in amyloidosis, with atrial fibrillation and bundle branch blocks also common. Tell: infiltrative disease is tied to low voltage.

Correct. The electrocardiogram in restrictive cardiomyopathy depends on the stage and diagnosis, and it may show low QRS voltage in amyloidosis infiltrative disease. Rhythm disorders such as atrial fibrillation and conduction disorders such as bundle branch blocks are also common.

Prominent Q waves are not the amyloid finding. Restrictive cardiomyopathy from amyloidosis may show low QRS voltage on the electrocardiogram, along with rhythm and conduction disorders, while the chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly from atrial enlargement. Tell: an infiltrated heart gives low voltage.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 34-year-old woman has frequent, disruptive episodes of atrioventricular nodal reentry and wants a definitive cure. Referral for which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. For a select subset of patients with nodal reentry, such as this woman with frequent, disruptive episodes, catheter ablation offers the opportunity for a definitive cure, in over 95 percent. Acute episodes are otherwise ended with vagal maneuvers or adenosine, with a pill-in-the-pocket beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker as an option.

Septal myectomy is not a treatment for nodal reentry. A reentry circuit within the atrioventricular node is cured by catheter ablation, in over 95 percent of selected patients. Tell: a definitive cure for nodal reentry targets the circuit in the node.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome with symptomatic slow rates. Nodal reentry is a tachycardia from a reentry circuit within the node, which catheter ablation can cure. Tell: pacemakers support slow hearts; ablation removes a fast circuit.

Valve replacement does not treat nodal reentry, which is commonly seen in the absence of heart disease. The reentry circuit lies within the atrioventricular node, and catheter ablation offers a definitive cure in over 95 percent of selected patients. Tell: a structurally normal heart with a nodal circuit needs ablation, not surgery.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 66-year-old woman collapses in a hospital hallway. The monitor shows chaotic, uncoordinated activity, and she has no pulse. Compressions have started and defibrillator pads are attached. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Delaying the shock to check electrolytes is wrong: pulseless ventricular fibrillation is treated as cardiac arrest, with defibrillation as soon as possible. Tell: the first shock is given as soon as possible; labs can come later.

Amiodarone is given when ventricular fibrillation persists after shocks, not before the first one. With pads attached, the first step is defibrillation as soon as possible. Tell: shock first; amiodarone comes after the second shock.

Synchronized cardioversion times the shock to a QRS complex, and ventricular fibrillation has no organized QRS to time against. It is treated with defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion). Tell: no pulse and no organized QRS mean an unsynchronized shock.

Correct. Chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no pulse is ventricular fibrillation, treated as cardiac arrest. With compressions underway and pads attached, she is defibrillated (unsynchronized cardioversion) as soon as possible, followed by 2 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation and epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 44-year-old man began having pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) pericardial pain 8 weeks ago. Despite treatment the symptoms have never fully gone away, with no symptom-free interval. Which term best describes his course?
opts: Correct. His symptoms have persisted for 8 weeks, beyond the 4 to 6 weeks of acute pericarditis but short of 3 months, with no symptom-free interval. Symptoms persisting more than 4 to 6 weeks and up to 3 months without a sustained remission define incessant pericarditis.

Effusive-constrictive pericarditis is underlying constriction with a coexisting effusion, recognized when constriction persists after drainage; it is a structural diagnosis, not a time label. He has unremitting pain at 8 weeks, which is incessant pericarditis. Tell: his stem gives a duration, with no effusion or drainage.

Chronic pericarditis requires symptoms for more than 3 months. At 8 weeks without remission he sits in the incessant window, beyond 4 to 6 weeks but under 3 months. Tell: count the weeks; chronic starts only after 3 months.
ruled out by a stated finding

Recurrence requires symptoms to return after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer, and he has never had such an interval. Unbroken symptoms at 8 weeks are incessant. Tell: no symptom-free gap, no recurrence.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
D.q: A 3-week-old infant born at 28 weeks is in the neonatal intensive care unit with a central venous catheter and parenteral nutrition. She develops feeding difficulty, tachycardia, hypotension and a new murmur, and echocardiography shows a right-sided vegetation. Which organism group is particularly tied to her risk factors?
opts: The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) gram-negative coccobacilli are not on the neonatal list, which is Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci and Candida, less often group B Streptococcus or enteric gram-negative rods. Tell: a catheter plus parenteral nutrition points to Candida.

Viridans group streptococci cause indolent disease in children over 1 year with congenital heart disease, not catheter-related infection in a premature newborn. Tell: her central line, parenteral nutrition, prematurity and intensive care stay are the fungal risk factors that point to Candida.

Correct. Neonatal fungal endocarditis is tied to central venous catheters, hyperalimentation (her parenteral nutrition), neonatal intensive care and prematurity, and she has all four. Neonatal disease is often catheter-related and right-sided, like her vegetation; Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci are the other common organisms.

Enterococci are less common in children than in adults and are not tied to central lines or parenteral nutrition in neonates. Tell: the neonatal organisms are Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci and Candida, and her catheter plus hyperalimentation singles out Candida.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 63-year-old man ran out of his metoprolol four days ago. He feels his heart racing, and his pulse is 118 and regular, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. He has no fever and is not bleeding. Which is the most likely cause of his tachycardia?
opts: Increased intracranial pressure is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, not sinus tachycardia. His fast sinus rate began after he stopped metoprolol, a listed drug-withdrawal cause. Tell: raised intracranial pressure slows the sinus node; beta blocker withdrawal speeds it.

Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, so it slows the sinus rate. His rate is fast at 118 and began after he ran out of metoprolol. Tell: hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism, sits on the sinus tachycardia list.

Increased vagal tone is not among the listed causes of sinus tachycardia, which are physiologic, pathologic or drug-related, including abrupt beta blocker withdrawal. A slow sinus rate, sinus bradycardia, is the adaptive response seen in well-conditioned athletes. Tell: a fast sinus rate four days after stopping metoprolol is withdrawal.

Correct. A regular rate of 118 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus tachycardia, and abrupt withdrawal of a beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is a listed drug cause. Running out of metoprolol four days ago, with no fever or bleeding to explain the rate, fits that cause.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: An 82-year-old woman taking digoxin for heart failure has nausea and fatigue. Her heart rate is 48 and regular, with narrow QRS complexes and retrograde P waves (inverted) just after each QRS in II, III and aVF. Which is the most likely cause of this rhythm?
opts: Correct. A slow, regular, narrow rhythm at 48 with inverted P waves just after each QRS in II, III and aVF is a junctional rhythm, and digoxin toxicity is a listed cause. Her nausea and fatigue while taking digoxin point to toxicity, which is treated with atropine and/or digoxin immune Fab (fragment antigen-binding).

Hyperthyroidism is a listed cause of sinus tachycardia, a fast rhythm with a P wave before each QRS. Her rhythm is slow at 48 with retrograde P waves after the QRS, a junctional rhythm. Tell: a slow junctional rhythm in a patient on digoxin points to digoxin toxicity, not the thyroid.

An accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) shows as pre-excitation, a short PR with a delta wave, and allows fast reentrant tachycardia. Her rhythm is slow and regular at 48 with retrograde P waves, a junctional rhythm. Tell: an accessory pathway goes with fast rhythms and delta waves, not a slow junctional rhythm.

Digoxin toxicity, not missed doses, is the listed digoxin-related cause of junctional rhythm, and digoxin is also a listed cause of sinus bradycardia. A slow junctional rhythm with nausea and fatigue in a patient on digoxin points to too much drug, not too little. Tell: digoxin excess slows the heart; missing doses would not.

D.q: A 63-year-old woman has been in the hospital for 9 days after hip surgery. She develops a new fever, and two sets of blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus; she has no indwelling catheter, and examination finds no wound or other source. Which diagnosis must be suspected?
opts: Dismissing both culture sets as contamination ignores the key rule: health care-associated endocarditis should be suspected in a hospitalized patient who develops fever with positive blood cultures and no apparent source. Tell: two concordant sets plus new fever in an inpatient demand an endocarditis workup.
ruled out by a stated finding

Postoperative atelectasis would not produce positive blood cultures. A hospitalized patient with new fever and positive cultures without an apparent source is exactly when health care-associated endocarditis should be suspected. Tell: bacteremia without a source in an inpatient points to the endocardium, not the lungs.

Correct. She has been in the hospital for 9 days and now has fever with two sets of positive blood cultures and no apparent source (no catheter, no wound). Health care-associated endocarditis is less common but should be suspected in exactly this situation, and 25-35% of native valve endocarditis is health care-associated.

Drug fever would not produce positive blood cultures. A new fever with two culture sets growing Staphylococcus aureus and no apparent source in a hospitalized patient raises health care-associated endocarditis. Tell: positive cultures make this an infection, not a drug reaction.

D.q: A 34-year-old woman has been hospitalized for four days receiving intravenous antibiotics through a peripheral catheter in her left forearm. She now has pain, redness and warmth along the course of the vein, and a firm, tender, palpable cord can be felt beneath the skin. She is afebrile, and the redness stays within the line of the vein. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A firm, tender cord tracking a single vein is not the picture of cellulitis; it is the indurated palpable cord of superficial thrombophlebitis, where tenderness, induration and erythema follow the vein's course. Her redness stays within the line of a recently cannulated vein.

Upper extremity deep vein thrombosis would involve the deep veins, while her findings sit in a superficial vein: a palpable cord with redness and warmth along its course. A palpable superficial cord after a peripheral catheter is superficial thrombophlebitis.

Septic thrombophlebitis is suggested by high fever, fluctuance or purulent drainage, or erythema extending significantly beyond the vein. She is afebrile and her redness stays within the line of the vein, so the process is superficial thrombophlebitis without signs of infection.

Correct. Pain, redness and warmth along the course of a superficial vein with an indurated, palpable cord after recent catheter use is superficial thrombophlebitis. She is afebrile and the redness stays within the line of the vein, so nothing suggests septic thrombophlebitis; recent intravenous catheter use is the most common cause in the arm.

D.q: A 76-year-old woman has had painful blue toes for several days after atheroemboli from proximal plaques. Which complication may follow in the affected digits?
opts: Correct. Her painful blue toes after atheroemboli reflect digital vascular occlusion causing ischemia, the blue toe syndrome. Digital necrosis and gangrene may develop, and localized tenderness, pallor and livedo reticularis occur at the sites of emboli.

Atheroemboli block small vessels of skin and muscle; they do not rupture large arteries such as the popliteal. Digital vascular occlusion leads to ischemia and blue toe syndrome, and digital necrosis and gangrene may develop in the affected toes. The complication stays in the digits.

Hoarseness comes from an aortic arch aneurysm involving the recurrent laryngeal nerve, nowhere near the toes. In her blue toes, atheroemboli occlude digital vessels, and digital necrosis and gangrene may follow. Match the complication to the tissue that lost its supply.

Heart block is unrelated to emboli lodged in the toes. Atheroembolic debris from proximal plaques occludes digital vessels, causing ischemia, blue toe syndrome and possibly digital necrosis and gangrene. The consequence is local tissue death, not a cardiac rhythm problem.

D.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
D.q: A 69-year-old woman being evaluated for endocarditis had a soft systolic murmur documented for 10 years. Today the murmur sounds a little louder. How does this change count under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Immunologic phenomena are glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor; a change in a murmur is not one of them. Tell: murmurs belong to the endocardial major criterion, where only new valvular regurgitation counts.
It does not meet the major criterion

Correct. New valvular regurgitation counts as evidence of endocardial involvement, a major criterion, but an increase or change in a preexisting murmur is specifically not sufficient. Her soft systolic murmur has been documented for 10 years, so a slightly louder version of it does not count.

A louder preexisting murmur does not count toward any criterion, so it cannot confirm anything. Definite endocarditis needs two major, one major plus three minor, or five minor criteria. Tell: an old murmur that got louder adds zero criteria.

Only new valvular regurgitation meets the endocardial major criterion; an increase or change in a preexisting murmur is specifically excluded, and her murmur has been present for 10 years. Tell: the word new is what matters, and her murmur is old.

D.q: A 61-year-old man underwent cardiac catheterization through the right femoral artery and vein ten days ago. He now has a continuous machine-like murmur over the puncture site with a palpable thrill (a vibration felt over the skin), and his right leg is swollen with prominent superficial veins. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Deep vein thrombosis of the leg

Deep vein thrombosis would not explain a continuous murmur and thrill over the puncture site, which are the clues to an abnormal artery-to-vein connection. Iatrogenic fistulas most commonly occur in the lower extremity after femoral access, exactly his history.

Correct. Femoral artery and vein access for catheterization, followed by a continuous murmur and thrill over the puncture site, points to an iatrogenic arteriovenous (AV) fistula. Fistula flow gives a thrill and bruit with both systolic and diastolic components; these fistulas most commonly affect the femoral vessels, and duplex ultrasound confirms the diagnosis.

Superficial thrombophlebitis is a clot in a superficial vein; it would not explain a continuous machine-like murmur and thrill at a femoral puncture site. Those findings after percutaneous groin access point to an iatrogenic arteriovenous fistula, which duplex ultrasound confirms.

A continuous murmur with a thrill, carrying both systolic and diastolic components, is the signature of flow from artery to vein rather than of a pseudoaneurysm. Puncture of both femoral vessels is the classic setting for an iatrogenic arteriovenous fistula, confirmed with duplex ultrasound.

D.q: A 64-year-old man had an anterior myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago. He now has fever, pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) chest pain eased by sitting forward, and a friction rub (a scratchy, three-part rubbing sound) at the left sternal border. Which drug should be avoided in treating his pericarditis?
opts: Correct. Fever, pleuritic pain eased by sitting forward and a rub 3 weeks after an anterior infarction make this post-infarction pericarditis. Nonsteroidal drugs such as ibuprofen are not given for post-infarction pericarditis, and in patients on aspirin as an antiplatelet agent, ibuprofen and indomethacin are avoided. Aspirin plus colchicine is used.

Colchicine is part of the treatment, not a drug to avoid; it pairs with the anti-inflammatory drug in first-line therapy. After an infarction, aspirin becomes that partner because nonsteroidal drugs such as ibuprofen are avoided. Tell: colchicine stays in every first-line regimen.

A proton pump inhibitor provides the gastrointestinal protection that anti-inflammatory therapy calls for, so it is added rather than avoided. The drug to avoid after an infarction is a non-aspirin nonsteroidal drug such as ibuprofen. Tell: gastrointestinal protection is recommended, not restricted.

Aspirin is the anti-inflammatory used for post-infarction pericarditis, paired with colchicine, because the other nonsteroidal drugs and glucocorticoids are avoided after an infarction. Tell: after a myocardial infarction, aspirin replaces ibuprofen rather than being the drug to avoid.

E.q: A 76-year-old man has had symmetric pitting swelling of both ankles for three weeks. He started amlodipine for hypertension one month ago. There is no warmth, redness, tenderness or skin discoloration, and he has no history of heart, kidney or liver disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Drug-induced edema sits on the differential of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) because it swells the legs, but it is often bilateral and usually lacks signs of inflammation. His symmetric swelling without warmth, redness or tenderness began a month after amlodipine, which points to the drug rather than clots in both legs.

Correct. Symmetric pitting swelling of both ankles that began after starting amlodipine, with no warmth, redness or tenderness, fits drug-induced edema. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine commonly cause it; the swelling is often bilateral and usually shows no signs of inflammation.

Chronic venous insufficiency in its post-thrombotic form follows a deep vein thrombosis by 6 to 24 months, and he has no history of a clot. His swelling is only three weeks old, bilateral, without skin discoloration, and began after amlodipine, which fits drug-induced edema.

Lymphedema is chronic edema of the extremities, usually with a history of pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy, none of which he has. The timing is the tell: his swelling started weeks after amlodipine was begun and is bilateral without inflammation, the pattern of drug-induced edema.

E.q: A 68-year-old man with Mobitz type II block found on a routine tracing declines a pacemaker because he feels perfectly well. Which risk should be explained to him?
opts: Mobitz type II does not drift back to normal. It carries a higher risk of progression to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death, which is why it is considered dangerous even in a patient who feels well. Tell: type II gets worse, not better.

Correct. Mobitz type II usually originates at the bundle of His, leaving a weak and unreliable escape rhythm, and carries a higher risk of progression to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death. It is considered dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression, so a permanent pacemaker is recommended.

Mobitz type II does not ease into first-degree block. Its risk runs the other way: progression to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death. Tell: the feared direction for type II is toward complete block.

Atrial fibrillation and stroke are not the risks tied to Mobitz type II. The feared outcome is progression to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death. Tell: the danger of this block is a worse block.

E.q: A 74-year-old woman with recurrent urinary tract infections was treated for pyelonephritis a month ago. She now has low-grade fevers, fatigue and a new murmur, and blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci. Which organism is most likely?
opts: Correct. Her recurrent urinary tract infections and recent pyelonephritis point to the genitourinary tract, the source of enterococci. Enterococci are a subacute and native valve cause, which fits her low-grade fevers, fatigue and new murmur.

Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus from the skin, best known as an early prosthetic valve organism. She has no prosthesis, and her infections come from the urinary tract. Tell: a genitourinary source points to enterococci, not skin staphylococci.

Viridans streptococci come from the oral cavity, and nothing in her history suggests a dental source. Her recurrent urinary infections and pyelonephritis point to the genitourinary tract. Tell: the mouth means viridans streptococci; the urinary tract means enterococci.

Streptococcus gallolyticus comes from the gastrointestinal tract, not the urinary tract. Her recurrent urinary infections and recent pyelonephritis point to enterococci. Tell: a bowel source suggests Streptococcus gallolyticus; a genitourinary source suggests enterococci.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: A 29-year-old woman has had a resting heart rate of 105 to 115 for a year. Thyroid tests, a blood count, a drug screen and an echocardiogram are normal, and she takes no medications or stimulants. Her electrocardiogram shows a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial flutter with 2:1 block shows two sawtooth waves for every QRS, at an atrial rate of 250 or more. She has one normal P wave before each QRS at about 110. Tell: one normal P wave per QRS is sinus; two sawtooth waves per QRS is flutter.

Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a paroxysmal, regular narrow tachycardia, usually 140 to 180, with hidden P waves. Hers is a persistent rate of 105 to 115 for a year with normal P waves visible before every QRS. Tell: sudden episodes with hidden P waves mean nodal reentry; a steady sinus rate with visible P waves does not.

Focal atrial tachycardia comes from a single ectopic focus outside the sinus node, with a consistently abnormal P wave, usually at 150 to 250, and abrupt-onset palpitations. Her P waves are normal and her rate is a steady 105 to 115. Tell: a normal P-wave shape points to the sinus node; an abnormal one points to an ectopic focus.

Correct. A resting rate of 105 to 115 for a year with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus tachycardia, and normal thyroid tests, blood count, drug screen and echocardiogram with no medications or stimulants exclude the secondary causes. A sinus tachycardia that stays unexplained after that is inappropriate sinus tachycardia, a diagnosis of exclusion.
