E.q: A 34-year-old woman without diabetes has ulcers on the posterior aspect of both lower legs. Her pedal pulses are strong, and there are no varicose veins, brown pigmentation or leg swelling. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Arterial insufficiency ulcers are painful, usually (not always) on the lateral aspect of the ankle, and come with weak pulses. Her strong pedal pulses and bilateral posterior ulcers point to erythema induratum instead.

Diabetic neuropathic ulcers belong to patients with diabetes, and she has none. Ulcers on the posterior aspect of both lower legs, in a woman with strong pulses, are the distribution of erythema induratum.

Venous ulcers occur at the medial ankle in a leg with chronic venous hypertension, typically with edema and brown pigmentation. She has no swelling, pigmentation or varicose veins, and her ulcers are posterior and bilateral, the pattern of erythema induratum.

Correct. Bilateral ulcers on the posterior aspect of the lower legs are the pattern of erythema induratum on the differential of leg ulcers. Her strong pulses argue against arterial ulcers, the lack of diabetes against neuropathic ulcers, and the absence of varicose veins, pigmentation and swelling against venous disease.

E.q: A 71-year-old man has a 4.8 cm descending thoracic aortic aneurysm, and he now has back pain that is attributed to the aneurysm. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: The over-6.0 cm threshold for descending aneurysms applies to asymptomatic patients. His 4.8 cm aneurysm now causes back pain, and repair is recommended for all symptomatic thoracic aortic aneurysms regardless of size. Symptoms override the size threshold.

Correct. Repair is recommended for all symptomatic thoracic aortic aneurysms. His 4.8 cm descending aneurysm is below the asymptomatic threshold of 6.0 cm, but back pain attributed to the aneurysm makes it symptomatic, and that alone indicates repair.

Imaging every 3 to 5 years is for asymptomatic aneurysms under 4.5 cm. His aneurysm is 4.8 cm and symptomatic, and repair is recommended for every symptomatic thoracic aneurysm. Both size and symptoms rule this out.

Imaging every 6 to 12 months is surveillance for an asymptomatic 4.5 to 5.4 cm thoracic aneurysm. His 4.8 cm aneurysm now causes back pain, so it is symptomatic, and all symptomatic thoracic aneurysms should be repaired. Symptoms end surveillance.

E.q: A 71-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy and marked biatrial enlargement has had palpitations for a week, and the electrocardiogram now shows atrial fibrillation. Which treatment reduces her risk of embolism?
opts: Surgical myectomy is not part of restrictive cardiomyopathy management and does nothing for embolism. With atrial fibrillation and marked biatrial enlargement, she needs anticoagulants to prevent embolism from atrial thrombi. Tell: the question asks about embolism, and only an anticoagulant prevents clots.

A positive inotrope is not on the restrictive cardiomyopathy list and does not prevent clots. The listed drugs are diuretics with caution, beta blockers or verapamil and diltiazem, and anticoagulants for atrial thrombi. Tell: embolism prevention means anticoagulation.

Diuretics treat pulmonary and systemic congestion but must be used with caution, because noncompliant ventricles depend on preload to maintain cardiac output, and they do not prevent emboli. Anticoagulants prevent embolism from atrial thrombi. Tell: diuretics for congestion, anticoagulants for clots.

Correct. In this woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy, marked biatrial enlargement and new atrial fibrillation, anticoagulants may be needed to prevent embolism from atrial thrombi. Beta blockers or verapamil and diltiazem may help filling time, but only anticoagulation addresses the embolic risk.

E.q: A 28-year-old woman has sudden palpitations after three energy drinks. She notices her neck throbbing, and examination shows a frog sign (rapid visible pulsations in the neck). Her heart rate is 172 and regular, with a narrow QRS and no visible P waves. She has no heart disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A sudden, regular narrow tachycardia at 172 with hidden P waves, neck pulsations (frog sign) and a caffeine trigger in a young woman without heart disease is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia. It is a reentry circuit within the node, far more common in women, and usually runs at 140 to 180.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves, often in older patients with hypertension, diabetes or heart disease. Her rhythm is regular, which points to a reentry circuit. Tell: both may show no P waves, but only atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular.
ruled out by a stated finding

Sinus tachycardia runs at over 100 to 160 with a uniform P wave before every QRS. Her rate is 172 with no visible P waves, a sudden onset and neck pulsations. Tell: a normal P wave before each QRS means sinus; hidden P waves with the frog sign point to nodal reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three P-wave shapes, and occurs in acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure. She is healthy and her rhythm is regular with no visible P waves. Tell: changing P waves in a sick lung patient is multifocal; hidden P waves after a stimulant is nodal reentry.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
E.q: A 70-year-old woman being treated for an acute aortic dissection develops a new diastolic murmur and worsening breathlessness. Which complication explains these findings?
opts: Correct. Aortic dissection can cause aortic regurgitation through dilatation of the aortic root, alongside its other presenting features of tearing chest pain, syncope and hypertension or hypotension. A new diastolic murmur with worsening breathlessness during treatment for a dissection fits that complication.

Carotid stenosis is an atherosclerotic narrowing that can produce a bruit and neurologic symptoms, not a diastolic murmur with breathlessness. In dissection, dilatation of the aortic root causes aortic regurgitation. Her findings are cardiac, not neurologic.

Mitral stenosis is not a listed consequence of aortic dissection. The valve affected in dissection is the aortic valve, through dilatation of the aortic root, producing aortic regurgitation. The anatomy points to the aortic root, not the mitral valve.

A pseudoaneurysm is a blood-filled cavity outside an arterial wall, usually the femoral artery after catheterization, causing local pain from swelling or nerve compression. It does not cause a new murmur. Her diastolic murmur reflects aortic regurgitation from root dilatation.

E.q: A 67-year-old woman with previous infective endocarditis brings an old wallet card that lists clindamycin for her dental prophylaxis. She has a penicillin allergy. Which counseling point is most accurate?
opts: She still needs prophylaxis, because previous infective endocarditis is on the list of qualifying conditions. Tell: what changed is the drug on her card, not her need for prophylaxis before dental work that manipulates the gums or roots or perforates the oral mucosa.

Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, so her old card is out of date. Tell: a penicillin-allergic patient now receives azithromycin, clarithromycin, doxycycline or, without a severe reaction history, cephalexin.

Correct. Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. Her previous endocarditis still qualifies her, so with a penicillin allergy she receives azithromycin or clarithromycin, doxycycline, or cephalexin if her reaction was not anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria.

Amoxicillin is a penicillin, and she has a penicillin allergy, so it is not an option. Penicillin-allergic patients who can take oral medication receive azithromycin, clarithromycin, doxycycline or cephalexin. Tell: the fix for an outdated clindamycin card is a non-penicillin alternative.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.q: A 49-year-old man has had a peripheral intravenous catheter in his right forearm for six days. He now has a fever of 39.2 degrees Celsius, a tender cord along the vein, purulent drainage at the insertion site, and redness that extends several centimeters beyond the vein margin. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis shows tenderness, induration and erythema along the vein, with a palpable cord. His high fever, purulent drainage and redness well past the vein margin go beyond that and suggest infection within the vein.

Correct. A fever of 39.2 degrees Celsius, purulent drainage and redness extending several centimeters beyond the vein margin after six days of cannulation indicate infection within the vein, suppurative or septic thrombophlebitis. Septic thrombophlebitis is uncommon without venous cannulation, which he has.

Cellulitis alone does not explain a tender cord along the cannulated vein with purulent drainage at the insertion site. High fever, purulence and erythema extending well beyond the vein margin place the infection within the vein: septic thrombophlebitis.

A deep vein clot would not produce purulent drainage at the insertion site or a tender superficial cord. Fever, purulence and redness beyond the vein margin after peripheral cannulation indicate septic thrombophlebitis, an infection within the vein.

E.q: A 24-year-old man with known obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the left sternal border that radiates to the suprasternal notch. At the bedside, the examiner tests how the murmur responds to changes in blood flow through the heart. Which maneuver would make his murmur louder?
opts: Correct. Anything that decreases blood flow in the heart increases outflow obstruction and makes the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy louder. The Valsalva maneuver and standing decrease preload, and amyl nitrite decreases afterload, so each increases this crescendo-decrescendo murmur.

Passive leg raising increases preload, which reduces outflow obstruction and softens the murmur. Decreasing preload with the Valsalva maneuver or standing makes it louder. Tell: raising the legs fills the heart and quiets the murmur.

Sustained handgrip increases afterload, which reduces outflow obstruction and softens the murmur rather than making it louder. Tell: handgrip sits with squatting and leg raising on the side that decreases the murmur.

Rapid squatting increases preload and so reduces outflow obstruction and softens the murmur. Standing or the Valsalva maneuver, which decrease preload, make it louder. Tell: squatting softens it; standing makes it louder.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
E.q: Acute pericarditis accounts for about what share of emergency department admissions for nonischemic chest pain?
opts: One percent understates it; acute pericarditis accounts for about 5% of emergency department admissions for nonischemic chest pain. Tell: much smaller figures belong to rarer conditions, such as cardiac tamponade at about 0.05% of hospital admissions.

Correct. Acute pericarditis is recorded in about 5% of patients admitted to the emergency department for nonischemic chest pain, with an annual incidence of about 27.7 per 100,000 people. Of those patients, about 15 to 30% go on to recurrent pericarditis.

A quarter would make pericarditis the dominant cause of nonischemic chest pain; the recorded figure is about 5% of such admissions. Tell: 15 to 30% is the recurrence rate after acute pericarditis, a different number that is easy to mix up with this one.

Half of all nonischemic chest pain admissions is far too high; acute pericarditis accounts for about 5%. Tell: the larger percentages in this topic describe recurrence (15 to 30%) or effusion prevalence in the general adult population (up to 6.5%), not emergency department chest pain.

E.q: Which lifestyle measures are advised for adults with cardiomyopathy?
opts: Caffeine avoidance and deliberate weight gain

Neither caffeine avoidance nor deliberate weight gain is listed. The adult lifestyle modifications are sodium restriction and alcohol cessation. Tell: the two lifestyle items are salt and alcohol, both cut back rather than added.

Correct. The adult lifestyle modifications for cardiomyopathy are sodium restriction and alcohol cessation. They sit alongside guideline-directed medical therapy (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta blockers, angiotensin receptor blockers, diuretics), device therapy and, in advanced cases, an assist device or transplant.
Strict bed rest and total fluid restriction

Strict bed rest and total fluid restriction are not adult strategies, and the elderly list even advises caution with diuretics. The lifestyle modifications are sodium restriction and alcohol cessation. Tell: the advice restricts salt, not all fluid.
Fluid loading and a high-salt diet plan

A high-salt plan is the reverse of the advice; adults are told to restrict sodium and stop alcohol. Tell: salt appears in the adult list only as something to restrict, alongside guideline-directed drugs and device therapy.

E.q: Which anticoagulation strategy is described as the classical, waning approach?
opts: Correct. The classical, but waning, strategy starts with heparin and then bridges to warfarin. The two newer strategies are parenteral therapy switched after 5 days to dabigatran or edoxaban, and oral monotherapy with rivaroxaban or apixaban using a loading dose then a maintenance dose.

Apixaban given with a loading dose and then a maintenance dose is the oral monotherapy strategy, one of the newer approaches. The classical, waning strategy starts with heparin and bridges to warfarin.

Parenteral therapy switched after 5 days to dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, is the second of the three strategies, not the classical one. The classical, waning approach starts with heparin and bridges to warfarin.

Oral rivaroxaban with a loading dose followed by maintenance is the oral monotherapy strategy, which needs no injection lead-in. The classical, waning approach is heparin first, then bridging to warfarin.

E.q: A 15-year-old girl nearly fainted twice while standing in the lunch line; both times she felt better once she lay down. She plays competitive soccer. A systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border that becomes louder with the Valsalva maneuver. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Clear her to play next week

Clearing her ignores that presyncope identifies high risk of sudden death, and sudden cardiac death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is highest in adolescents and related to extreme exertion. The work-up is urgent. Tell: a competitive athlete with presyncope must be evaluated before playing.
Recheck the murmur in a year

Waiting a year ignores a high-risk warning: presyncope on standing, relieved by lying down, identifies patients at high risk of sudden death, and the work-up is urgent. Tell: urgent and a year from now cannot both be right.

Correct. Presyncope that occurs on standing and is relieved by lying down identifies patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy at high risk of sudden death, so the work-up is urgent. Her murmur that grows louder with the Valsalva maneuver and her competitive soccer add to the concern, and echocardiography begins that urgent work-up.

Reassurance would delay an urgent work-up. Presyncope on standing that is relieved by lying down identifies patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy at high risk of sudden death. Tell: presyncope plus a murmur in an athlete is not a benign teenage faint.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
E.q: A 58-year-old man received chest radiation for lymphoma 20 years ago. He has 8 months of exertional dyspnea, fatigue, leg edema and ascites. His jugular venous pressure is elevated and shows the Kussmaul sign (it rises on inspiration instead of falling), and a pericardial knock (an early diastolic sound, slightly earlier than a third heart sound) is heard. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Eight months of fluid overload (edema, ascites) and diminished cardiac output (fatigue, exertional dyspnea), an elevated jugular venous pressure with the Kussmaul sign and a pericardial knock fit constrictive pericarditis. Prior chest radiation is a listed cause.

Nothing here suggests infection, and endocarditis does not account for the Kussmaul sign or a pericardial knock, which are signs of constriction. His prior chest radiation is a listed cause of constrictive pericarditis. Tell: Kussmaul sign plus knock plus fluid overload points to a stiff pericardium.

His course is 8 months of fluid overload and low output with a Kussmaul sign and a pericardial knock, a chronic picture rather than an acute one. Constrictive pericarditis presents this way, and prior radiation and past pericarditis are among its causes. Tell: months of edema and ascites with a knock point to constriction.

His findings point to the pericardium, not the heart muscle: the Kussmaul sign, a pericardial knock (a mid-frequency sound slightly earlier than a third heart sound) and fluid overload. Prior chest radiation is a listed cause of constriction. Tell: a knock with the Kussmaul sign after chest radiation means constriction.

E.q: A 64-year-old man with claudication, diabetes and continued smoking is taking a statin. Which low-density lipoprotein target applies to him?
opts: Correct. Lipid-lowering therapy in peripheral artery disease targets a low-density lipoprotein below 100 mg/dL, and below 70 mg/dL for high-risk patients such as those with diabetes or continued smoking. He has both, so his target is below 70 mg/dL.

Below 100 mg/dL is the standard target in peripheral artery disease. His diabetes and continued smoking make him high risk, which lowers the target to below 70 mg/dL. High-risk features drop the goal.

Below 130 mg/dL is looser than any target given for peripheral artery disease. The standard target is below 100 mg/dL, and for high-risk patients like him, with diabetes and continued smoking, below 70 mg/dL. Neither target is this high.

Below 160 mg/dL would leave him far above goal. With diabetes and continued smoking he is high risk, and the low-density lipoprotein target is below 70 mg/dL. The listed targets are 100 and 70 mg/dL only.

E.q: Uremic pericarditis is typically associated with a blood urea nitrogen above which level?
opts: A blood urea nitrogen of 10 mg/dL is far below the level tied to uremic pericarditis, which is above 60 mg/dL. Uremia sits with post-infarction, autoimmune, neoplastic and iatrogenic disease among the noninfectious causes. Tell: the uremic threshold is high, 60 mg/dL, not a value in the everyday range.

A blood urea nitrogen of 20 mg/dL is well short of the level associated with uremic pericarditis, which is above 60 mg/dL. Tell: the number to remember is 60, three times this value; a level of 20 would not point to uremia as the cause of pericarditis.

Correct. Uremia is a listed cause of pericarditis, tied to a blood urea nitrogen above 60 mg/dL. It sits among the noninfectious causes alongside post-infarction disease, autoimmune disease such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, neoplasm and iatrogenic injury.

Uremic pericarditis does not require a level as extreme as 200 mg/dL; it is associated with a blood urea nitrogen above 60 mg/dL. Tell: pick the stated threshold, not an extreme value that merely exceeds it.

E.q: A 22-year-old man has recovered from mild viral myocarditis and feels well at discharge. He asks whether he needs any long-term follow-up with a cardiologist. Which later complication does follow-up watch for?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is not a stated outcome of myocarditis. The later risk after mild myocarditis is dilated cardiomyopathy, which develops in one third of patients. Tell: the one-third figure belongs to dilated cardiomyopathy.

Takotsubo is not a stated sequel of myocarditis. One third of patients with mild symptoms subsequently develop dilated cardiomyopathy, which follow-up watches for. Tell: the late complication of myocarditis is dilated cardiomyopathy.

Correct. Most patients with mild myocarditis recover completely, as he has, but one third subsequently develop dilated cardiomyopathy. That later risk is what long-term follow-up with a cardiologist watches for.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy is not the stated sequel. After mild myocarditis most patients recover completely, but one third develop dilated cardiomyopathy. Tell: recovery for most, dilated cardiomyopathy for one third.

E.q: An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia with some rates approaching 300 appears in someone with a known accessory pathway. Which intravenous drug is used?
opts: Correct. An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia with some rates approaching 300 in someone with a known accessory pathway is atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. When Wolff-Parkinson-White is known, intravenous procainamide is used, and adenosine must never be given.

Intravenous magnesium is not the listed drug for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. An irregular, wide tachycardia in someone with a known accessory pathway is treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: a known pathway plus irregular wide complexes means procainamide.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. This tachycardia already approaches 300, the opposite problem. Tell: atropine is for slow and unstable rhythms; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.

Adenosine must never be used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White appears; it is first line only for ordinary orthodromic reentry. This irregular, wide rhythm with a known accessory pathway is that exception. Tell: a known accessory pathway plus a fast irregular rhythm rules adenosine out.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
E.q: A 64-year-old woman has been in the hospital for 2 weeks with a peripherally inserted central line. She develops fever, and two separate blood cultures grow a gram-positive coccus with no other source. Which organism causes the largest share of this setting's native valve endocarditis?
opts: Enterococci cause about 16% of health care-associated native valve endocarditis, a distant second to Staphylococcus aureus at about 52%. Tell: in a hospitalized patient with a central line, Staphylococcus aureus dominates.

Streptococci, the group that includes viridans streptococci, lead community-acquired native valve endocarditis (about 40%) but cause only about 13% of health care-associated cases. Tell: her 2-week hospital stay and central line shift the leading organism to Staphylococcus aureus.

Correct. She has been hospitalized for 2 weeks with a central line, making this health care-associated native valve endocarditis, and Staphylococcus aureus causes about 52% of those cases (versus about 28% of community-acquired cases). Methicillin resistance is common among these strains.

Coagulase-negative staphylococci cause about 11% of health care-associated native valve endocarditis; they lead early prosthetic valve and device infection instead. Tell: for a native valve in a hospitalized patient, Staphylococcus aureus leads at about 52%.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. E.q: What is the mainstay of treatment for acute myocarditis?
opts: Long antibiotic courses are not in the plan; the listed medications are vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulation, given as needed on top of supportive care. Tell: the mainstay is support, with treatment directed toward the clinical scenario.

Early transplant is not part of acute myocarditis management. The mainstay is supportive care, with aggressive hemodynamic stabilization if needed and vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics or anticoagulation as needed. Tell: treatment follows the clinical scenario.

Septal ablation infarcts part of a thickened septum with alcohol (myectomy is the surgery that excises it), a treatment for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not acute myocarditis. Myocarditis is treated with supportive care directed at the clinical scenario. Tell: myocarditis care is stabilization plus drugs as needed, not a septal procedure.

Correct. Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment for acute myocarditis, directed toward the clinical scenario. Some patients need aggressive hemodynamic stabilization, and medications are added as needed: vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulation.

E.q: A 62-year-old woman on chemotherapy for breast cancer comes to the emergency department with a calf 4 cm larger than the other, tenderness along the deep veins and no better explanation, so her Wells score is high. Her D-dimer, drawn at triage, is negative. Which action should be avoided?
opts: Ordering venous duplex ultrasound is exactly right: a high Wells score sends her to ultrasound whatever the D-dimer shows. Her negative result does not change that, so imaging is the step to take, not the one to avoid.

Measuring both calves is how the Wells item for calf swelling is scored: more than 3 cm larger than the other leg, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. It is part of a correct evaluation, not an error.

Asking about shortness of breath is not a misstep in evaluating a suspected clot; it costs nothing and does not alter the Wells pathway. The action to avoid is ending the work-up at a negative D-dimer, since a high score goes on to ultrasound regardless.
Ending the work-up at the D-dimer

Correct. Active cancer, calf swelling over 3 cm and deep venous tenderness give her a high Wells score. In high-risk patients the D-dimer is optional, and even a negative result leads on to ultrasound of the thigh, so stopping at the D-dimer would leave a likely deep vein thrombosis (DVT) unexamined.

E.q: A 54-year-old woman who started a new antibiotic three days ago faints briefly. Her electrocardiogram before the event showed a markedly prolonged QT. The monitor now shows a wide QRS tachycardia whose peaks rise and fall so that the complexes seem to twist around the baseline. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no organized QRS complexes. Wide complexes whose peaks rise and fall so they twist around the baseline, after a long QT, are torsades de pointes. Tell: twisting complexes are still organized QRS complexes.

Atrial flutter is not a wide ventricular rhythm. A wide QRS tachycardia whose complexes twist around the baseline, on a background of a markedly prolonged QT, is torsades de pointes. Tell: a long QT plus twisting complexes points to torsades.

Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia keeps one QRS shape. Complexes whose peaks rise and fall and twist around the baseline are polymorphic, and with a long QT that is torsades de pointes. Tell: one shape is monomorphic; twisting is torsades.

Correct. Torsades de pointes is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in which the QRS complexes appear to twist around the baseline, and a long QT is the risk factor. Her new antibiotic and markedly prolonged QT fit, and her brief faint shows how the rhythm can cause syncope.

E.q: A 68-year-old man is brought in confused, with a blood pressure of 76/40. The monitor shows a slow, regular rhythm at 36 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Which is the first-line treatment?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia, not the first step in an acute, unstable episode. The acute sequence is atropine, then a temporary pacemaker if atropine fails. Tell: acute and unstable means atropine first; a permanent device comes later if the problem is chronic.

Synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, treats hemodynamically unstable tachycardias such as supraventricular tachycardia or atrial fibrillation. His rhythm is slow at 36, the opposite problem. Tell: unstable and fast means a synchronized shock; unstable and slow means atropine.

Correct. A slow, regular rhythm at 36 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus bradycardia, and confusion with a blood pressure of 76/40 make it acute, symptomatic and hemodynamically unstable. Atropine is first line; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing a rhythm already at 36 in a confused, hypotensive man is the opposite of the goal. Tell: adenosine is for fast narrow rhythms; atropine is for unstable slow ones.

E.q: A 30-year-old cyclist with no symptoms has a rhythm in which the PR interval lengthens beat by beat until a QRS complex is dropped, after which the cycle starts again. Echocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Correct. A PR that lengthens beat by beat until a QRS drops, then restarts, is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block, which is usually asymptomatic. With no symptoms and a normal echocardiogram, no treatment is needed; a permanent pacemaker is considered only for symptomatic patients, and increased vagal tone is a named cause.

Cardiac ablation is itself a named cause of Mobitz type I, so it cannot be the treatment. A silent Wenckebach pattern with a normal echocardiogram needs no treatment. Tell: a procedure that causes a block cannot fix it.

Transcutaneous pacing is an emergency bridge for unstable high-grade block such as Mobitz type II or complete block. This cyclist has stable, silent Mobitz type I. Tell: emergency pacing needs an unstable, slow patient.

A permanent pacemaker is considered for symptomatic Mobitz type I, and this cyclist has no symptoms. Mobitz type II is the block paced even without symptoms. Tell: in type I, the decision to pace follows symptoms.

E.q: Which electrolyte disturbances are named triggers of premature ventricular contractions?
opts: Correct. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, along with hypercalcemia, are the electrolyte imbalances named as causes of premature ventricular contractions, together with hypoxemia, alcohol, caffeine and stimulants. These beats occur with or without structural heart disease.

High potassium and low sodium are not the named triggers; potassium matters here when it is low. The list is hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia. Tell: remember potassium and magnesium low, calcium high.

Low calcium is the wrong direction: hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia, is the named trigger of premature ventricular contractions, and sodium is not on the list. The named imbalances are hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia. Tell: potassium and magnesium low, calcium high.

Phosphate and chloride are not named triggers. The electrolyte imbalances listed are hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia, along with hypoxemia, alcohol, caffeine and stimulants. Tell: the electrolytes to check are potassium, magnesium and calcium.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
E.q: A 4-year-old with cyanotic congenital heart disease and a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt has 2 weeks of fever. The murmur sounds unchanged. Which finding would most suggest that the shunt is infected?
opts: An unchanged murmur is the expected finding in children with cyanotic congenital heart disease and systemic-pulmonary shunts, so it neither suggests nor excludes shunt infection. Tell: in shunted cyanotic children, watch the oxygen saturation, not the murmur.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. In children with cyanotic congenital heart disease and systemic-pulmonary shunts, the murmur may not change; instead, falling oxygen saturation can signal graft infection. This 4-year-old's 2 weeks of fever with an unchanged murmur makes saturation the sign to watch.

Rising blood pressure is not a listed sign of shunt infection. In children with cyanotic congenital heart disease and systemic-pulmonary shunts, falling oxygen saturation is the clue to graft infection. Tell: a shunt infection shows up as worsening oxygenation.

Osler nodes and other classic peripheral stigmata (Janeway lesions, Roth spots, splinter hemorrhages, splenomegaly) are considerably less common in children than in adults. Tell: in a shunted cyanotic child, falling oxygen saturation, not a peripheral stigma, signals graft infection.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
E.q: A 73-year-old man has new pauses and slow rates on an ambulatory monitor. He started verapamil and digoxin last month for palpitations. He feels mildly lightheaded but is otherwise well. Which is the most appropriate first step?
opts: Correct. New pauses and slow rates a month after starting verapamil, a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, and digoxin fit drug-induced sick sinus syndrome, since those medications are listed causes. Management starts with treating the underlying cause, and he is stable and only mildly lightheaded, so stopping the rate-slowing drugs comes first.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia. He is stable and only mildly lightheaded, and his slow rates have a reversible drug cause. Tell: a stable patient with a drug-induced slow rhythm needs the culprit stopped, not a rescue drug.

A permanent pacemaker is for symptomatic bradycardia in sick sinus syndrome once symptoms are shown to correlate with the slow rates, after the underlying cause is treated. His slow rates began with verapamil and digoxin, so treating that cause comes first. Tell: remove the reversible cause before committing to a device.

Catheter ablation is used for tachycardias, such as curing focal atrial tachycardia or an accessory pathway. His problem is pauses and slow rates caused by rate-slowing drugs. Tell: ablation removes a fast focus or circuit; it does not fix a slow sinus node.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
E.q: A 74-year-old man who smokes wakes most nights with burning pain in his forefoot and toes that eases when he hangs the leg over the bed; he now sleeps in a recliner. Which ankle-brachial index range would be expected?
opts: The 0.4 to 0.9 band is claudication, pain with activity relieved by rest. Waking at night with forefoot pain eased by hanging the leg over the bed, and sleeping in a recliner, is ischemic rest pain, which sits in the 0 to 0.4 band. Rest pain means a lower band than claudication.

Correct. Nightly forefoot and toe pain eased by dependency, so that he now sleeps in a recliner, is ischemic rest pain of critical limb ischemia. Rest pain and tissue loss, ulcer or gangrene, correspond to an ankle-brachial index of 0 to 0.4, below the claudication band of 0.4 to 0.9.

Above 0.9 up to 1.3 is the normal range, which cannot explain nightly ischemic pain relieved by dependency. His symptoms are rest pain, matching an index of 0 to 0.4. A normal index does not fit critical limb ischemia.

An index above 1.3 is abnormal because calcified, noncompressible arteries, as in a diabetic patient, give an unreliably high reading. The expected band for true ischemic rest pain is 0 to 0.4. A high value reflects stiff arteries, not severity.

E.q: A 69-year-old man has an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.7 cm on his latest ultrasound. Which referral is appropriate?
opts: Emergency surgery is for rupture, not a painless 4.7 cm aneurysm, and aneurysms rarely rupture until the diameter exceeds 5 cm. The appropriate step at 4.5 cm or larger is referral to a vascular specialist for observation and assessment.

Waiting for a repair threshold is too late for referral. From 4.5 cm a vascular specialist should observe and assess the aneurysm, and surgical referral is considered at 5.0 cm or larger. His 4.7 cm aneurysm already meets the referral size.

Correct. An aortic aneurysm of 4.5 cm or larger warrants vascular specialist referral for observation and assessment, so his asymptomatic 4.7 cm aneurysm qualifies. Urgent referral applies whenever there is aneurysmal pain, and surgical referral is considered at 5.0 cm or larger.

Echocardiography is not the evaluation for an abdominal aneurysm. From 4.5 cm the referral is to a vascular specialist for observation and assessment. His 4.7 cm aneurysm belongs with the vascular team, not cardiology.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
E.q: A 70-year-old woman was admitted with chest pain after a near drowning. Her electrocardiogram showed ST elevation with T-wave inversion, and echocardiography showed hypokinesis of the midsegment and apex of the left ventricle. Which catheterization finding is expected if this is stress cardiomyopathy?
opts: Correct. A 70-year-old woman with chest pain after a near drowning, ST elevation with T wave inversion, and hypokinesis of the midsegment and apex of the left ventricle fits stress cardiomyopathy. The diagnosis is confirmed with cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries.

Triple-vessel narrowing would point to coronary disease as the cause of her wall-motion abnormality. In Takotsubo, catheterization most often shows normal coronary arteries. Tell: in this syndrome the coronaries are typically normal, while the echo shows hypokinesis or akinesis of the midsegment and apex.

A proximal occlusion would make this acute coronary syndrome, which is what Takotsubo mimics. Stress cardiomyopathy is confirmed by catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries. Tell: her stressor, ST changes and mid and apical hypokinesis point to Takotsubo, whose coronaries are clean.

A ruptured coronary plaque would explain acute coronary syndrome, not stress cardiomyopathy, whose catheterization most often shows normal coronary arteries. Tell: Takotsubo looks like acute coronary syndrome on the electrocardiogram, troponin and echo, and only the coronary arteries tell them apart.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
E.q: A 64-year-old man in cardiac arrest is intubated by the team. Compressions continue. How should breaths now be given?
opts: One breath every 2 seconds is far too fast and over-ventilates. Once intubated, compressions continue without pauses and a breath is given every 6 seconds, about 10 breaths per minute. Tell: the number after intubation is 6 seconds.

Breaths do not stop after intubation. Compressions become continuous, and ventilation continues at 1 breath every 6 seconds. Tell: the tube lets breaths go in without pausing compressions; it does not end ventilation.

Thirty compressions to 2 breaths is the ratio used without an advanced airway. Once he is intubated, compressions are continuous and a breath is given every 6 seconds. Tell: the airway is what turns the 30:2 cycle into continuous compressions.

Correct. Once the patient is intubated, cardiopulmonary resuscitation continues as continuous chest compressions with 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths per minute). Compressions no longer pause for breaths, which keeps interruptions to a minimum.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: What is the first-line treatment for stable supraventricular tachycardia?
opts: Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, the setting in which adenosine must never be used. Ordinary stable supraventricular tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver. Tell: procainamide answers pre-excited atrial fibrillation, not routine supraventricular tachycardia.

Immediate synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia, the less common presentation. A stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver. Tell: the word stable points to the vagal maneuver; unstable points to the shock.

Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver. Adenosine follows, and may be repeated once, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to see P waves; a hemodynamically unstable patient instead gets immediate synchronized cardioversion.

Adenosine is the second step in stable supraventricular tachycardia, used if a vagal maneuver fails, and it may be repeated once. It may convert the rhythm to normal sinus rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Tell: first line means before any drug, which is the vagal maneuver.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
E.q: How is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia treated, even when the patient has a pulse?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. Polymorphic tachycardia is defibrillated (unsynchronized) even when a pulse is present, because it is never truly stable. Tell: a QRS that keeps changing shape gets an unsynchronized shock.

Correct. Even when the patient has a pulse and looks well, polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable; it is a short-lived transitional state. It is defibrillated, followed by urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization, and intravenous metoprolol or amiodarone may be added.

Observation is unsafe: even if the patient looks fine, polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is only a short-lived transitional state that will need defibrillation. Tell: 'never truly stable' means it is shocked as soon as it is seen, then followed by urgent coronary angiography.

Intravenous lidocaine alone is not enough: drug cardioversion is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, and lidocaine is otherwise the one antiarrhythmic allowed in torsades. Polymorphic tachycardia is never truly stable and is defibrillated. Tell: a pulse does not make polymorphic tachycardia safe.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
E.q: In high-income countries, which conditions are now the leading predisposing conditions for infective endocarditis?
opts: Hypertension and high cholesterol are not on the endocarditis risk-factor list at all. The leading predisposing conditions in high-income countries are now degenerative valve disease and intracardiac devices. Tell: endocarditis needs an abnormal valve or a device, not atherosclerotic risk.

Rheumatic heart disease is a listed risk factor but no longer the leading one in high-income countries, and syphilis is not listed. Degenerative valve disease and intracardiac devices now lead. Tell: in high-income countries, think aging valves and devices.

Atrial fibrillation and heart block are not listed risk factors. In high-income countries, degenerative valve disease and intracardiac devices are now the leading predisposing conditions. Tell: rhythm disorders are not substrates, although devices placed to treat them can be.

Correct. Degenerative valve disease and intracardiac devices are now the leading predisposing conditions in high-income countries. Other listed risk factors include congenital and rheumatic heart disease, prosthetic valves and injection drug use, and people over 60 account for more than 50% of cases.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
E.q: A 28-year-old man had a cold 10 days ago. He now has sharp, pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) substernal chest pain that is worse lying flat and eases when he leans forward. A pericardial friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound) is heard at the left sternal border, and the electrocardiogram shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and ST depression in aVR. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Sharp pleuritic substernal pain that is worse supine and eased by leaning forward, a friction rub at the left sternal border, and widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and reciprocal ST depression in aVR meet three of the four criteria; two suffice. A preceding cold fits, since most idiopathic cases are likely viral.

Myocardial infarction is a common differential, but pericardial pain is pleuritic and positional, unlike infarction, and his tracing shows the widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and reciprocal aVR changes that characterize pericarditis. A friction rub is highly specific for pericarditis. Tell: diffuse concave ST elevation plus PR depression points to the pericardium.

Pleuritis is a common differential, but a pleural rub is heard only during inspiration, while his is a pericardial rub at the left sternal border. Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression also places the problem in the pericardium. Tell: a rub at the left sternal border plus diffuse ST changes means pericarditis.

Pulmonary embolism is a less common differential for this chest pain, and nothing here fits it better than pericarditis: the pain eases on leaning forward, a friction rub is present, and the tracing shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression. Tell: positional pain plus a rub plus diffuse ST elevation meets the pericarditis criteria.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
E.q: What is the common site of a pseudoaneurysm?
opts: Pseudoaneurysm is not described as a bypass complication; bypass risks are myocardial infarction, stroke, graft infection and peripheral embolization. The common site of pseudoaneurysm is the femoral artery after cardiac catheterization. Think of the puncture site, not the graft.

Correct. The common site of a pseudoaneurysm is the femoral artery after cardiac catheterization, caused by laceration of the artery by the access needle. The leak forms a blood-filled cavity outside the vessel wall that seals as it thromboses.

The listed complications of carotid endarterectomy are stroke or nerve damage, not pseudoaneurysm. A pseudoaneurysm typically follows femoral artery puncture for cardiac catheterization. The access needle, not the endarterectomy, is the cause.

The abdominal aorta is the most common site of true aneurysm, and smoking is its strongest risk factor, but that is a true aneurysm involving all three wall layers. A pseudoaneurysm typically forms at the femoral artery after catheterization, from laceration by the access needle.

E.q: A 28-year-old woman with a stab wound to the abdomen arrives pulseless after losing a large amount of blood. The monitor shows an organized narrow rhythm. Compressions are underway. Besides compressions and epinephrine, which problem must be addressed urgently?
opts: Hypothermia is not one of the two leading causes of pulseless electrical activity, and nothing in her story points to it. Her massive blood loss means hypovolemia, which must be corrected. Tell: the two leading causes are hypovolemia and hypoxia.

Nothing in her story suggests a toxin. Her large blood loss from a stab wound means hypovolemia, one of the two leading causes of pulseless electrical activity in adults. Tell: match the cause to the story; bleeding means volume loss.

Hyperkalemia is not suggested by her story; her problem is hemorrhage. Hypovolemia, with hypoxia, is one of the two leading causes of pulseless electrical activity in adults. Tell: a stab wound with heavy bleeding points to hypovolemia.

Correct. A pulseless patient with an organized narrow rhythm has pulseless electrical activity, which is unshockable. Its two leading causes in adults are hypovolemia and hypoxia, and her large blood loss from a stab wound is hypovolemia that must be corrected along with compressions and epinephrine.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: A 33-year-old woman has abrupt-onset palpitations during a week of little sleep and heavy coffee. Her heart rate is 160 and regular, and every QRS is preceded by an identical P wave whose shape differs from her baseline P wave. She has no heart disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more that outnumber the QRS complexes. She has one discrete abnormal P wave before each QRS at 160. Tell: one P wave per QRS means an atrial focus; more sawtooth waves than QRS complexes means flutter.

Sinus tachycardia keeps a uniform P wave matching the normal sinus shape, and it can follow stimulants such as coffee. Her P wave differs from her baseline shape, which places the source outside the sinus node, and the onset was abrupt. Tell: compare with the baseline P wave; a new, consistent abnormal shape means an ectopic focus.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A regular tachycardia at 160 with one identical P wave before each QRS, shaped differently from her baseline P wave, comes from a single ectopic focus in the atria outside the sinus node: focal atrial tachycardia. It is commonly seen without heart disease when metabolic demand rises, and most people report abrupt-onset palpitations, as she does.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three P-wave shapes in the same lead, and usually arises in acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure. Her rhythm is regular with one identical abnormal P wave and no heart disease. Tell: one abnormal shape is focal; three or more is multifocal.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
E.q: A 72-year-old woman had a bioprosthetic aortic valve placed 5 months ago. She now has a fever of 39.0 °C (102.2 °F) and a new regurgitant murmur, and blood cultures have been drawn. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Penicillin G plus gentamicin is directed therapy for viridans streptococci once the organism is identified, not empiric therapy. Her cultures are still pending on a valve only 5 months old. Tell: a prosthetic valve in place 1 year or less calls for vancomycin, gentamicin and cefepime.

Correct. Her bioprosthetic valve was placed 5 months ago, so it has been in place 1 year or less, and empiric therapy for prosthetic valve endocarditis in that window is vancomycin plus gentamicin plus cefepime. Empiric therapy covers staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci and starts only after cultures are drawn.

Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is the empiric regimen for a subacute presentation, native valve endocarditis or a prosthetic valve in place more than 1 year. Her valve is only 5 months old. Tell: the 1-year mark decides it, and 1 year or less adds gentamicin and cefepime to vancomycin.

Ceftriaxone alone is not a listed empiric regimen; empiric therapy must cover staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci, and for a prosthetic valve in place 1 year or less that means vancomycin, gentamicin and cefepime. Tell: every listed empiric regimen includes vancomycin.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
E.q: A 53-year-old man on the cardiology ward develops jugular venous distension and a blood pressure of 88/60 a day after a catheter procedure. Before drainage, which bedside triad should be specifically checked for?
opts: Fever, a new murmur and splinters

Fever, a new murmur and splinter findings are not the triad for tamponade and do not match his picture of hypotension and distended neck veins after a procedure. The Beck triad is hypotension, distended jugular veins and muffled heart sounds. Tell: the tamponade triad describes compression, not infection.

Correct. New jugular venous distension and a blood pressure of 88/60 the day after a catheter procedure raise concern for tamponade. The Beck triad is distant (muffled) heart sounds, distended jugular veins and decreased arterial pressure, so he already shows two of the three, and muffled heart sounds should be checked.

Hypertension is the opposite of his low blood pressure, and this set does not describe pericardial compression. The Beck triad pairs decreased arterial pressure with distended jugular veins and distant heart sounds. Tell: tamponade lowers the blood pressure, so any triad starting with hypertension is wrong.

This mix is not the Beck triad, which is three bedside findings: decreased arterial pressure, distended jugular veins and distant heart sounds. Pulsus paradoxus is the companion sign to check alongside it. Tell: the triad named for tamponade is hypotension, neck veins and muffled sounds.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
E.q: A 45-year-old man with a first deep vein thrombosis is otherwise healthy and hemodynamically stable. The plan is oral anticoagulation monotherapy with a loading phase followed by maintenance, without any injection lead-in. Which drug fits this strategy?
opts: Fondaparinux is an indirect factor Xa inhibitor, not one of the two oral agents used for monotherapy. The oral strategy with a loading dose followed by maintenance, with no injection lead-in, uses rivaroxaban or apixaban.

Edoxaban is an anti-Xa agent, but it belongs to the strategy in which parenteral therapy is switched after 5 days to a novel anticoagulant. The plan here has no injection lead-in, which means rivaroxaban or apixaban.

Dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, is started after 5 days of parenteral therapy, so it requires the injection lead-in this plan avoids. Oral monotherapy with a loading dose then maintenance uses rivaroxaban or apixaban.

Correct. Oral monotherapy with a loading dose followed by a maintenance dose, with no injection lead-in, is the strategy that uses rivaroxaban or apixaban, both anti-Xa agents. Apixaban (Eliquis) is a direct factor Xa inhibitor, and he is stable and otherwise healthy, so the oral-only plan fits.

Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
E.q: An 82-year-old man is confused, with a blood pressure of 74/40 and a heart rate of 32. The electrocardiogram shows P waves and wide QRS complexes at two separate regular rates with no relationship between them. Which is the most appropriate immediate measure?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion terminates fast rhythms with a pulse. His rate is 32 from complete heart block, so there is nothing fast to convert. Tell: a slow, dissociated rhythm needs pacing, and the immediate form is transcutaneous pacing.

Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. He has a pulse and a slow, dissociated rhythm at 32 from complete block, which needs pacing. Tell: pace the slow, shock the fast.

Correct. P waves and wide QRS complexes at two unrelated rates with a ventricular rate of 32 are complete heart block, and confusion with a blood pressure of 74/40 make him unstable. Emergent options are atropine, epinephrine and transcutaneous pacing, which bridges him to the definitive permanent pacemaker.

Intravenous amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation; it does nothing to raise a rate of 32 from complete block. An unstable patient with complete block needs transcutaneous pacing. Tell: a slow rhythm needs pacing, not an antiarrhythmic.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
E.q: A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who takes no anticoagulant develops sudden, severe pain in her left leg two hours ago. The leg is cold and pale, pulses are absent below the femoral artery, and she has numbness over the dorsum of the foot. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Critical limb ischemia is chronic: constant rest pain in the forefoot and toes and nonhealing ulcers that build over time. Her pain began two hours ago in a previously normal leg, with a cold, pale, pulseless limb and untreated atrial fibrillation. Abrupt onset points to acute embolic occlusion.

Correct. Sudden severe pain with a cold, pale leg and absent pulses below the femoral artery is acute limb ischemia, sudden occlusion of a previously patent artery. Thromboemboli are most common and the heart is the source in 80 to 90% of cases, with atrial fibrillation a named source; numbness over the dorsum of the foot is an early neurologic sign.

Claudication is predictable exertional pain relieved by rest, usually within 10 minutes. Her pain began suddenly two hours ago with a cold, pale, pulseless leg and numbness over the dorsum of the foot. That is acute limb ischemia, a vascular emergency, not chronic exertional pain.

Atheroemboli lodge in small vessels of skin and muscle, so distal pulses usually stay palpable while the toes turn blue. Her pulses are absent below the femoral artery and the whole leg is cold and pale, which means a larger artery is occluded. Absent pulses argue against atheroembolism.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
E.q: A 63-year-old man is diagnosed with a first proximal deep vein thrombosis five days after knee replacement under two hours of general anesthesia. His clot is attributed to the venous stasis and endothelial trauma of the Virchow triad, both from the surgery. What duration of anticoagulation is appropriate?
opts: Indefinite anticoagulation is for an unprovoked first venous thromboembolism, one with no identifiable risk factor. His clot followed knee replacement under general anesthesia, a major transient trigger, so 3 months is enough.
Six weeks is shorter than the minimum: every acute first venous thromboembolism is anticoagulated for at least 3 months. His surgery-provoked clot gets exactly that minimum, 3 months.

Three to six months is for a clot provoked by a minor transient factor such as estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery or prolonged travel. Knee replacement under two hours of general anesthesia is a major factor, which calls for 3 months.

Correct. Knee replacement under two hours of general anesthesia is surgery under general anesthesia for more than 30 minutes, a major transient, reversible risk factor. A first venous thromboembolism (VTE) provoked by a major transient factor is treated for 3 months, which is also the minimum for any first VTE.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
E.q: A 36-year-old woman has had three episodes of pericarditis in 18 months, each treated in primary care with an anti-inflammatory and colchicine. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Three episodes in 18 months is recurrent pericarditis, and recurrences are a stated reason to refer to cardiology for further assessment. The other referral triggers are no response to conservative management and development of constrictive pericarditis.

Recurrence is a stated reason to refer to cardiology for further assessment, not directly to surgery. Cardiology is also the referral for no response to conservative therapy or for developing constriction. Tell: recurrences, nonresponse and constriction all route to cardiology first.

Gastroenterology is not a referral for recurrent pericarditis; her recurrences are a stated reason to refer to cardiology. Medication side effects are handled through counseling. Tell: the referral follows the heart problem, recurrence, not the side effects of treatment.

Nothing points to an infection, and recurrence itself is a stated reason to refer to cardiology for further assessment, as is no response to conservative management. Tell: three episodes in 18 months is recurrent pericarditis, and recurrent pericarditis goes to cardiology.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
E.q: A 26-year-old marathon runner is diagnosed with acute viral pericarditis and starts ibuprofen and colchicine. He asks when he can return to training. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Avoid exercise for the rest of his life

Lifelong restriction is not advised. Strenuous activity is avoided until symptoms resolve and C-reactive protein normalizes, and for at least 1 month after diagnosis. Tell: the restriction has an end point defined by symptoms, biomarkers and time.
Resume running once the chest pain stops

Pain resolution alone is not enough; C-reactive protein must also normalize, and the restriction lasts at least 1 month after diagnosis. Tell: symptoms are only one of three conditions, along with normal biomarkers and the 1-month minimum.
Run on alternate days during treatment

Running on alternate days is still strenuous activity, which is avoided during recovery; activity stays at a maximal heart rate under 100 beats per minute until symptoms resolve and C-reactive protein normalizes. Tell: the restriction is about intensity, not frequency.
Avoid strenuous activity for at least 1 month

Correct. Strenuous physical activity such as marathon training is avoided until symptoms resolve and biomarkers such as C-reactive protein normalize, for at least 1 month after diagnosis, with a maximal heart rate under 100 beats per minute. He can return once all of those conditions are met.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for pericardial disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 9. adult 10. elderly
E.q: A 76-year-old woman has needed prednisone for several months for pericarditis that did not respond to first-line therapy. Which complication of her treatment should be specifically anticipated?
opts: Bradycardia is not the corticosteroid concern named for older adults; the named risk is osteoporosis, which matters after months of prednisone at 76. Colchicine dose reduction is the other age-related drug adjustment. Tell: link long steroid courses in older adults to bone loss.

Hypoglycemia is not the complication flagged for older adults on corticosteroids; osteoporosis is. Her several months of prednisone at age 76 make bone loss the specific concern to plan for. Tell: in older adults, the steroid caution is about bone.

Correct. Corticosteroids increase the risk of osteoporosis, and in a 76-year-old on months of prednisone that risk should be specifically anticipated. Older adults also call for caution with anti-inflammatory drugs on the Beers list, with colchicine considered for dose reduction.

Hearing loss is not a corticosteroid concern named for this age group. The anticipated complication is osteoporosis, given her age and months of prednisone; anti-inflammatory drugs, by contrast, carry a Beers list caution. Tell: steroids plus older age equals bone risk.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
E.q: A 51-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy drinks most of a bottle of whiskey every night. He is on a beta blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, his ejection fraction is 30%, and he asks whether anything he does himself could help his heart recover. Which counseling point is most accurate?
opts: Damage is fixed once the heart dilates

With long-term excess alcohol as the cause, cardiac function can recover if intake is reduced or halted, so the damage is not necessarily permanent. Tell: alcohol is the cause on the list that comes with a stated chance of recovery.
Stopping alcohol may let function recover

Correct. Long-term excess alcohol consumption is a cause of dilated cardiomyopathy, and cardiac function can recover if alcohol intake is reduced or halted. For this man, who drinks most of a bottle of whiskey nightly, stopping alcohol is the step he can take himself, alongside his beta blocker and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
Wine would be safer than spirits for him

Switching drinks does not address the cause, which is long-term excess alcohol consumption of any kind. Function can recover only if alcohol intake is reduced or halted. Tell: the fix is less alcohol, not a different bottle.
Only a transplant could restore function

A transplant is not the only path here: when long-term excess alcohol is the cause, cardiac function can recover if intake is reduced or halted. Tell: a reversible cause comes with something he can do himself, and his is stopping alcohol.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
E.q: A 27-year-old woman has a new moderate pericardial effusion with joint aches and fatigue. She has not traveled and has no recent viral illness. Which test is most reasonable to add to her workup?
opts: Blood cultures are not part of the listed effusion workup, and nothing in her story points to infection. The workup adds an antinuclear antibody in a young woman with an effusion, which fits her joint aches and fatigue. Tell: young woman plus effusion is the stated cue for an antinuclear antibody.

A hemoglobin A1c is not part of the listed effusion workup and does not address her joint aches and fatigue. The workup includes blood counts, chemistry with renal function, thyroid-stimulating hormone, troponins and, in a young woman, an antinuclear antibody. Tell: choose tests on the workup list that fit her clues.

Serum lipase is not part of the effusion workup, and nothing suggests an abdominal process. In a young woman with a new effusion, the workup specifically allows for an antinuclear antibody. Tell: her age and sex are the clue the workup names.

Correct. The effusion workup includes a complete blood count, chemistry with renal function, thyroid-stimulating hormone and troponins, and possibly an antinuclear antibody, for example in a young woman with an effusion. At 27, with joint aches and fatigue and no travel or viral illness, she is that patient.

E.q: A 74-year-old man with advanced dilated cardiomyopathy has refractory symptoms on full medical therapy. Severe lung disease and frailty rule him out as a transplant candidate, and he wants to remain at home and mobile. Which treatment option fits his situation?
opts: Surgical myectomy is not part of dilated cardiomyopathy management; his problem is a failing, dilated pump with refractory symptoms. A left ventricular assist device as destination therapy fits a patient who cannot have a transplant. Tell: a weak pump needs support, not removal of muscle.

He has been ruled out as a transplant candidate because of severe lung disease and frailty, so listing is not an option. A left ventricular assist device as destination therapy is for exactly such patients. Tell: not a candidate means destination therapy.

Correct. A left ventricular assist device (LVAD), a pump that helps the left ventricle in heart failure, is used as destination therapy for patients who are not candidates for cardiac transplant, as his lung disease and frailty make him. Patients may stay alive over 5 years with the device.
Assist device as a bridge to transplant

Bridge therapy supports a patient waiting for cardiac transplantation or for cardiac function to return. He cannot receive a transplant, so the device would be destination therapy. Tell: a bridge needs somewhere to lead; without transplant, the device is the destination.

E.q: Which feature distinguishes Osler nodes from Janeway lesions?
opts: This reverses the two lesions. Osler nodes are painful, while Janeway lesions are nontender hemorrhagic lesions on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Tell: pain points to Osler nodes; painless points to Janeway lesions.

Osler nodes do not persist for months; they appear in crops and fade in 2-3 days. The feature that separates them from Janeway lesions is pain. Tell: Osler nodes are painful and transient, while Janeway lesions are nontender.

Correct. Osler nodes are painful lesions on the palms, soles and distal phalanges that appear in crops and fade in 2-3 days, from septic emboli or immune complexes. Janeway lesions are nontender hemorrhagic lesions on the palms and soles from septic emboli, so pain is the distinguishing feature.

Retinal lesions in endocarditis are Roth spots, white-centered hemorrhages from vasculitis of the small retinal arteries. Osler nodes sit on the palms, soles and distal phalanges. Tell: the eye finding is the Roth spot; the painful finger lesion is the Osler node.

E.q: A 34-year-old man who injects heroin has 4 days of fever to 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), rigors and a cough. A new holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border, and he looks toxic. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A mitral murmur is loudest at the apex rather than the left lower sternal border, and the valve named for people who inject drugs is the tricuspid.
Pneumonia would not explain a new holosystolic murmur in a person who injects drugs; fever, rigors, cough and that murmur point to tricuspid valve endocarditis.

Correct. In a person who injects drugs, fever, rigors and a new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border point to tricuspid valve endocarditis, the valve named for this group (Staphylococcus aureus causes 80-90% of their tricuspid infections); the lung, a listed embolic site, explains the cough.
Pericarditis brings positional chest pain and a friction rub, not a new holosystolic murmur with rigors in a person who injects drugs.

E.q: A 69-year-old man is recovering from a carotid endarterectomy for high-grade symptomatic stenosis. Which complications of the procedure should be monitored for?
opts: Retroperitoneal rupture describes a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, unrelated to a neck operation. The complications to monitor after carotid endarterectomy are stroke and nerve damage. Match the complication to the vessel operated on.

Correct. Carotid endarterectomy removes plaque from inside the artery through a surgical incision and is the gold standard for high-grade stenosis. Its named complications are stroke or nerve damage, so his recovery should be watched for new neurologic deficits.

Graft infection is a complication of lower extremity bypass grafting, along with myocardial infarction, stroke and peripheral embolization. After carotid endarterectomy, the named complications are stroke and nerve damage. He had no leg graft.

Wet gangrene is an infected, moist limb gangrene and a surgical emergency in critical limb ischemia. The complications of carotid endarterectomy are stroke and nerve damage. A neck procedure does not threaten the foot.

E.q: A 79-year-old man has a preoperative electrocardiogram before cataract surgery. He feels well. His heart rate is 70, every P wave is followed by a narrow QRS complex, and the PR interval is constant at 0.26 seconds on every beat. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A constant PR interval longer than 0.20 seconds (here 0.26) with every P wave conducted to a narrow QRS, at a regular rate of 70, is first-degree atrioventricular block. The prolonged PR can occur along with an underlying rhythm.

Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block lengthens the PR from beat to beat until a QRS is dropped. Here the PR is constant at 0.26 seconds and every beat conducts. Tell: a constant PR with no drops is first degree.
Mobitz type II keeps a constant PR but drops QRS complexes at random. Here every P wave is followed by a QRS, so nothing is dropped. Tell: no dropped beats means no second-degree block.

Complete block dissociates P waves from QRS complexes, so the atria and ventricles beat at two different rates. Here every P wave leads its own narrow QRS at a fixed 0.26-second interval. Tell: a fixed PR before every QRS rules out complete block.

E.q: A 68-year-old woman has atrial fibrillation found at a routine visit. Her heart rate is 84, she has no symptoms of instability, and her blood pressure is 128/76. Which is the most appropriate rate management?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation, and elective outpatient cardioversion comes only after 21 days of anticoagulation. She is stable with a blood pressure of 128/76, so rate control comes first.

Atropine is not part of atrial fibrillation management, which is synchronized cardioversion if unstable, intravenous rate control if stable in rapid ventricular response, and rate control if stable without it. Her rate of 84 needs no speeding up.

Correct. She is hemodynamically stable (blood pressure 128/76, no instability) and a rate of 84 is not a rapid ventricular response, so she gets rate control; the intravenous route is kept for stable patients in rapid ventricular response. Anticoagulation is then weighed for her, guided by her CHA2DS2-VASc stroke-risk score.

Intravenous rate control is for a hemodynamically stable patient in rapid ventricular response (RVR). Her rate of 84 is not rapid, so she gets rate control without the intravenous route; the tell is the heart rate, not her stability.

E.q: A 48-year-old man with a first calf deep vein thrombosis is hemodynamically stable, has low bleeding risk and normal kidney function, and has a supportive spouse who will bring him to every follow-up visit. Which is the best setting for treatment?
opts: Withholding treatment ignores that he qualifies for outpatient anticoagulation: he is stable, at low bleeding risk, with normal kidney function and reliable support. The outpatient options include rivaroxaban, apixaban, or low molecular weight heparin followed by dabigatran or edoxaban.

Admission is for an iliofemoral (proximal) clot, a concurrent symptomatic pulmonary embolism, high bleeding risk or comorbidities that warrant inpatient care. He has a calf clot and none of these, so he can be treated at home.

Intensive care monitoring is not needed for a hemodynamically stable man with a calf clot and low bleeding risk. Even ordinary hospital admission is reserved for iliofemoral clots, symptomatic pulmonary embolism, high bleeding risk or other serious comorbidities.

Correct. Outpatient therapy is appropriate for patients who are hemodynamically stable, have low bleeding risk and no renal insufficiency, and have good support and reliable follow-up. He meets every criterion, and his clot is in the calf, not an iliofemoral clot that would require admission.

E.q: A 57-year-old woman has frequent premature junctional contractions, more than 10 per minute, on a monitor. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. Premature junctional contractions are early beats from the atrioventricular junction, and frequent ones prompt a search for structural heart disease instead. Tell: frequent junctional beats lead to a structural workup, not anticoagulation.

A permanent pacemaker is for slow rhythms, such as a junctional rhythm caused by complete or high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome. She has frequent early beats, not a slow escape rhythm. Tell: frequent premature beats call for a structural workup and a beta blocker, not a device.

Reassurance alone suits premature junctional contractions that are asymptomatic and infrequent. Hers are more than 10 per minute, the frequency threshold that prompts a search for structural heart disease. Tell: more than 10 per minute or multifocal means evaluate and treat.

Correct. Premature junctional contractions that are frequent, more than 10 per minute or multifocal, prompt a search for underlying structural heart disease, and the beats are then treated with a beta blocker. Her rate of more than 10 per minute meets that threshold.
